echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth.
echoes.note: 'Be holy, for I am holy' — the imitatio Dei formula directly behind 'be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.'

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' — the Holiness Code's call to imitate God, reframed as perfection in v.48.

echoes.text: You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: 'You shall be blameless/perfect (tamim) before the LORD your God' — the LXX 'teleios' here closely matches 'be perfect.'

echoes.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.
echoes.note: 'Walk before me and be blameless (tamim)' — the call to integrity before God behind 'be perfect.'

echoes.text: Yahweh is good to all. His tender mercies are over all his works.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is good to all, his mercy over all he has made' — God's indiscriminate goodness behind 'he makes his sun rise on evil and good.'

echoes.text: Can his armies be counted? On whom does his light not arise?
echoes.note: 'Upon whom does his light not arise?' — God's light/sun given universally, paralleling v.45.

echoes.text: You visit the earth, and water it. You greatly enrich it. The river of God is full of water. You provide them grain, for so you have ordained it. You drench its furrows. You level its ridges. You soften it with showers. You bless it with a crop. You crown the year with your bounty. Your carts overflow with abundance. The wilderness grasslands overflow. The hills are clothed with gladness. The pastures are covered with flocks. The valleys also are clothed […]
echoes.note: God waters the earth and provides rain abundantly; background to 'sends rain on the just and the unjust.'

echoes.text: Neither do they say in their heart, ‘Let us now fear Yahweh our God, who gives rain, both the former and the latter, in its season; who preserves to us the appointed weeks of the harvest.’
echoes.note: God gives the rains in season for all; coheres with rain on just and unjust as common grace.

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: 'You are children of the LORD your God' — divine-sonship language behind 'that you may be children of your Father.'

echoes.text: Be as a father to the fatherless, And instead of a husband to their mother: So will you be as a son of the Most High, And he will love you more than your mother does.
echoes.note: Be like a father to orphans and you will be like a son of the Most High — deuterocanonical sonship-through-mercy parallel to v.45.

pericopes.text: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. Therefore when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

echoes.text: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
echoes.note: The command to give generously to the poor ('open wide your hand to your brother') is the Torah background for Jesus' presupposition that disciples 'do merciful deeds'; almsgiving is assumed righteousness, not optional.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' — the logic of God himself repaying the secret almsgiver (v.4) closely matches this proverb's reward-from-God motif.

echoes.text: With him the alms of a man is as a signet; And he will keep the bounty of a man as the apple of the eye.
echoes.note: Ben Sira: a person's almsgiving is 'like a signet ring' kept with God who guards it as a treasure — Second Temple development of almsgiving stored with God who rewards, paralleling the Father who sees in secret.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from one's substance, that almsgiving 'delivers from death' and 'stores up a good treasure,' is the closest Second Temple parallel to Jesus' theology of hidden, God-rewarded charity.

echoes.text: Good is prayer with fasting, alms, and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold. Alms delivers from death, and it purges away all sin. Those who give alms and do righteousness will be filled with life;
echoes.note: 'Prayer with fasting and almsgiving... is better than to lay up gold' and 'almsgiving saves from death' — the same triad of almsgiving/prayer/fasting that structures Mt 6:1-18, suggesting a shared piety pattern.

echoes.text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke? Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: Isaiah's true fast as sharing bread with the hungry links almsgiving and fasting as authentic versus performative piety, the very contrast Jesus draws.

pericopes.text: “When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward. But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. In praying, don’t use vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking. Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.

echoes.text: He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh.
echoes.note: Elisha 'shut the door' and prayed to the LORD in private before raising the child — a possible OT precedent for entering one's room and shutting the door (v.6) to pray unseen.

echoes.text: Come, my people, enter into your rooms, and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation is past.
echoes.note: 'Enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you' — striking verbal overlap with 'enter into your inner room, and having shut your door,' though the contexts differ (hiding from wrath vs. private prayer).

echoes.text: They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, nor any who answered. They leaped about the altar which was made. At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.” They cried aloud, and cut themselves in […]
echoes.note: The prophets of Baal cried aloud 'from morning until noon' with no answer — a possible backdrop for the Gentiles' 'much speaking' (v.7) imagining they are heard for many words.

echoes.text: Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
echoes.note: 'Let your words be few' before God in heaven — a wisdom warning against verbose prayer that closely matches the rebuke of 'vain repetitions' and 'much speaking.'

echoes.text: Prate not in the multitude of elders; And repeat not your words in your prayer.
echoes.note: 'Do not babble in the assembly of the elders, and do not repeat yourself in your prayer' — almost a direct Second Temple parallel to the warning against vain repetition.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: God knows the word on the tongue before it is spoken — grounds Jesus' claim that 'your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him' (v.8).

pericopes.text: Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen. ’

echoes.text: I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, which you have profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am Yahweh, says the Lord Yahweh, when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes.
echoes.note: 'I will sanctify my great name... and the nations will know that I am the LORD' — the divine self-hallowing of God's name is the OT engine behind 'hallowed be your name'; God hallows his name by his eschatological act, which the petition invokes.

echoes.text: But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name. Yes, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.
echoes.note: 'They will sanctify my name... and stand in awe of the God of Israel' — sanctifying/hallowing the divine Name as eschatological hope, the conceptual root of the first petition.

echoes.text: You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be made holy among the children of Israel. I am Yahweh who makes you holy,
echoes.note: 'You shall not profane my holy name, but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel' — the covenantal duty to hallow the Name underlies 'hallowed be your name.'

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: 'The God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed' — the prayer 'Let your Kingdom come' draws directly on Daniel's vision of God's everlasting kingdom breaking into history.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'Your God reigns!' — the proclamation of God's kingship/reign that 'your Kingdom come' petitions to be realized.

echoes.text: Saviors will go up on Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.
echoes.note: 'And the kingdom will be the LORD's' — terse OT articulation of the coming divine kingdom echoed in the second petition.

echoes.text: Nevertheless, as may be the will in heaven, so shall he do.
echoes.note: 'As may be the will in heaven, so let him do' — a Second Temple formula of submission to heaven's will closely paralleling 'your will be done.'

echoes.text: Praise Yahweh, all you armies of his, you servants of his, who do his pleasure.
echoes.note: The heavenly hosts 'do his will' (v.20-21) — the angelic obedience in heaven is the model for 'your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.'

echoes.text: Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth, in the seas and in all deeps;
echoes.note: 'Whatever the LORD pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth' — the heaven/earth scope of God's will echoes in the third petition's cosmic frame.

echoes.text: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me;
echoes.note: 'Feed me with the food that is needful for me' (Agur's prayer for neither poverty nor riches, just the daily portion) — the closest OT analogue to 'Give us today our daily bread,' both asking for sufficient daily provision.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: The manna gathered 'a day's portion every day' is the typological pattern for daily bread: God provides enough for today, teaching dependence rather than hoarding (cf. anxiety section vv.25-34).

echoes.text: Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.” Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and became foul: and Moses was angry with them.
echoes.note: The manna could not be stored overnight without rotting — reinforces the day-by-day reliance behind 'give us today our daily bread' and against laying up earthly treasure.

echoes.text: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray.
echoes.note: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray' — a remarkably close Second Temple parallel to the reciprocal forgiveness of the fifth petition and vv.14-15.

echoes.text: This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.
echoes.note: The sabbatical 'release' (remission) of debts colors 'forgive us our debts' — debt-remission language drawn from Torah jubilee/release practice applied to sins.

echoes.text: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered' — the divine forgiveness of sin/debt sought in 'forgive us our debts.'

echoes.text: For you will light my lamp, Yahweh. My God will light up my darkness. For by you, I advance through a troop. By my God, I leap over a wall. As for God, his way is perfect. Yahweh’s word is tried. He is a shield to all those who take refuge in him. For who is God, except Yahweh? Who is a rock, besides our God,
echoes.note: Petitions for God to deliver from the enemy/evildoer underlie 'deliver us from the evil one'; the Psalter's deliverance language saturates the final petition.

echoes.text: Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips. Don’t incline my heart to any evil thing, to practice deeds of wickedness with men who work iniquity. Don’t let me eat of their delicacies.
echoes.note: 'Incline not my heart to any evil thing' — a prayer not to be led toward evil that parallels 'bring us not into temptation.'

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: 'Yours, O LORD, is the greatness, the power... the kingdom... and the glory' — David's doxology is the verbatim source of the prayer's traditional closing ascription of kingdom, power, and glory to God.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this forever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of your people, and prepare their heart for you;
echoes.note: David asks God to keep his people's hearts directed toward him — continues the doxological context (29:11) from which the Lord's Prayer ending is drawn.

pericopes.text: “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

echoes.text: Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins?
echoes.note: 'Forgive your neighbor... and then your sins will be pardoned'; the wrathful man who holds anger cannot expect healing from God — the strongest Second Temple statement of conditional, reciprocal forgiveness mirroring vv.14-15.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge... but you shall love your neighbor' — the Torah ground for releasing others' trespasses as a condition of one's own standing before God.

echoes.text: ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
echoes.note: Joseph's brothers beg him to forgive their trespass and Joseph forgives — a narrative model of human forgiveness as the channel of restored relationship.

echoes.text: Wrath and anger, these also are abominations; And a sinful man will possess them. He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins.
echoes.note: Wrath and anger are abominations that the sinner holds tight, and 'the Lord will take vengeance' on the unforgiving — the immediate context preceding the forgiveness teaching of Sir 28:2.

pericopes.text: “Moreover when you fast, don’t be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces, that they may be seen by men to be fasting. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward. But you, when you fast, anoint your head, and wash your face; so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

echoes.text: ‘Why have we fasted,’ say they, ‘and you don’t see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and you take no knowledge?’ “Behold, in the day of your fast you find pleasure, and exact all your labors. Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness: you don’t fast this day so as to make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I have chosen? the day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head as a […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's polemic against fasting done for show ('to be heard on high'... bowing the head like a reed) versus the fast God chooses — the prophetic template for Jesus' contrast between hypocritical and hidden fasting.

echoes.text: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.
echoes.note: 'Rend your heart, and not your garments' — true fasting is inward not performative, the same heart-versus-display contrast Jesus presses against disfigured faces.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh month for these seventy years, did you at all fast to me, really to me? When you eat, and when you drink, don’t you eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves?
echoes.note: 'When you fasted... did you at all fast to me, even to me?' — God's challenge that ritual fasting may be self-directed rather than God-directed, paralleling fasting 'to be seen by men.'

echoes.text: Therefore wash yourself, anoint yourself, get dressed, and go down to the threshing floor, but don’t make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.
echoes.note: 'Wash yourself, anoint yourself' — anointing and washing as ordinary grooming (the opposite of mourning), the gesture Jesus prescribes to mask fasting (v.17).

echoes.text: Then David arose from the earth, and washed, and anointed himself, and changed his clothing; and he came into Yahweh’s house, and worshiped: then he came to his own house; and when he required, they set bread before him, and he ate.
echoes.note: David washes and anoints himself when he ceases mourning — the cultural background for anointing the head and washing the face to appear un-fasting.

echoes.text: Good is prayer with fasting, alms, and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold.
echoes.note: The triad 'prayer with fasting and almsgiving' commends fasting as genuine piety, paralleling the assumed practice of fasting that Jesus purifies of display.

echoes.text: I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine into my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled.
echoes.note: Daniel mourns and does NOT anoint himself while fasting — the very mourning-fast convention Jesus reverses by telling disciples to anoint themselves.

pericopes.text: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

echoes.text: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments... store up almsgiving in your treasuries, and it will rescue you from every misfortune' — the most direct Second Temple parallel to laying up treasure in heaven through righteous use of wealth.

echoes.text: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint. Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.
echoes.note: 'Don't weary yourself to be rich... riches sprout wings like an eagle and fly away' — the transience of earthly wealth behind 'treasures on earth, where... thieves break through and steal.'

echoes.text: Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare clothing as the clay; he may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver.
echoes.note: The wicked heaps up silver like dust but the just will wear it — the futility of hoarded wealth that another takes, echoing treasure consumed or stolen.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him.
echoes.note: The rich man 'carries nothing away' at death; his glory does not descend with him — undergirds the worthlessness of earthly treasure.

echoes.text: There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm. Those riches perish by misfortune, and if he has fathered a son, there is nothing in his hand. As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.
echoes.note: Riches kept by their owner to his hurt, perishing by misfortune, leaving nothing in hand — Qoheleth's meditation on perishable wealth.

echoes.text: for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity;
echoes.note: Almsgiving lays up 'a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity' — explicit treasure-storing-with-God language behind treasures in heaven.

echoes.text: Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me! But you say, ‘How have we robbed you?’ In tithes and offerings. You are cursed with the curse; for you rob me, even this whole nation. Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says Yahweh of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough for.
echoes.note: Bringing tithes into God's storehouse so that heaven's windows pour out blessing — a heaven-versus-earth economy of giving that resonates faintly with heavenly treasure.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: Kindness to the poor 'lends to the LORD' who repays — the mechanism by which earthly generosity becomes heavenly treasure.

pericopes.text: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: 'He who has a generous eye (bountiful eye) will be blessed' — the Hebrew idiom of the 'good/generous eye' versus the stingy eye underlies the 'sound' (single) eye and the 'evil eye,' linking the lamp saying to generosity (cf. surrounding treasure/mammon).

echoes.text: A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him.
echoes.note: 'A man with an evil eye hastens after riches' — the 'evil eye' as greed/stinginess, the very vice contrasted with the sound eye between the treasure and mammon sayings.

echoes.text: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: Warning against a 'wicked' (mean/evil) eye toward the needy brother — the evil eye as ungenerous miserliness, contextually fitting the eye/lamp logion's placement amid wealth teaching.

echoes.text: For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light. Reproofs of instruction are the way of life,
echoes.note: 'The commandment is a lamp... the way of life' — light/lamp as moral illumination, the metaphor field Jesus uses for the eye as the body's lamp.

echoes.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
echoes.note: 'Your word is a lamp to my feet' — lamp/light as inner moral guidance, the imagery undergirding the eye as the lamp of the body.

echoes.text: An evil eye is grudging of bread, And he is miserly at his table
echoes.note: 'An evil eye is grudging of bread' — Ben Sira's stingy 'evil eye' that begrudges sharing, fitting the generosity reading of the evil eye versus sound eye.

echoes.text: The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
echoes.note: 'The spirit of man is the LORD's lamp, searching all his innermost parts' — inner illumination imagery related to the lamp of the body.

pericopes.text: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: 'Love the LORD your God with all your heart' — the Shema's demand of undivided love is what divided service to two masters (God and Mammon) violates; one cannot love both wholly.

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'Choose this day whom you will serve' — the exclusive either/or of covenant allegiance behind 'no one can serve two masters.'

echoes.text: Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people answered him not a word.
echoes.note: 'How long will you waver between two opinions?' — Elijah's demand to choose between the LORD and Baal, the prophetic either/or pattern of single-master service.

echoes.text: “You shall have no other gods before me.
echoes.note: 'You shall have no other gods before me' — making wealth a rival master is functional idolatry, the first commandment's exclusivity reframed as God versus Mammon.

echoes.text: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.
echoes.note: The lover of gold cannot be justified; gold has been a stumbling block and ruin to many — Ben Sira on wealth as an idol-like snare, paralleling serving Mammon.

pericopes.text: Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they? “Which of you, by being anxious, can add one momentto his lifespan? Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith? “Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well. Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' — the antidote to anxiety is entrusting provision to God, the heart of 'don't be anxious for your life.'

echoes.text: I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread.
echoes.note: 'I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging bread' — God's reliable provision for the righteous undergirds 'your heavenly Father feeds them... how much more you.'

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God brings forth food and 'satisfies' creation — the Creator's provision for plants, beasts, and people grounds the argument from birds and lilies to human care.

echoes.text: These all wait for you, that you may give them their food in due season. You give to them; they gather. You open your hand; they are satisfied with good.
echoes.note: 'These all wait for you... you give them their food in due season' — God feeds all creatures, directly behind 'your heavenly Father feeds' the birds.

echoes.text: He provides food for the livestock, and for the young ravens when they call.
echoes.note: 'He gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens which cry' — God feeding the birds is the precise image of 'See the birds of the sky... your heavenly Father feeds them.'

echoes.text: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?
echoes.note: 'Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry?' — the divine-speech argument that God feeds wild birds, paralleling the lesson of v.26.

echoes.text: “But ask the animals, now, and they shall teach you; the birds of the sky, and they shall tell you. Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach you. The fish of the sea shall declare to you. Who doesn’t know that in all these, the hand of Yahweh has done this, in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?
echoes.note: 'Ask the animals... the birds of the sky' — they teach that God's hand holds all life; the pedagogy of learning providence from birds matches 'See the birds of the sky.'

echoes.text: It shall be, that you shall drink of the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan. The ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook.
echoes.note: Ravens feed Elijah at God's command — a narrative enactment of God using birds in provision, faintly behind the birds-fed-by-the-Father motif.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their clothing, and his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her. She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom. However I didn’t believe the words, […]
echoes.note: Solomon's surpassing glory and splendor (the queen of Sheba's awe) is the explicit comparison: 'even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these' (v.29).

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: The daily manna ('a day's portion') typifies the day-at-a-time trust of 'don't be anxious for tomorrow'; Israel's wilderness schooling in non-hoarding dependence.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: God let Israel hunger then fed with manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone' — provision as a lesson in dependence, behind seeking the Kingdom first over food.

echoes.text: God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, neither have asked riches for yourself, nor have asked the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice; behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a wise and an understanding heart; so that there has been no one like you before you, neither after you shall any arise like you. I have also given you […]
echoes.note: Solomon seeks wisdom (God's priority) and is given riches and honor 'as well' — the exact pattern of 'seek first God's Kingdom... and all these things will be added.'

echoes.text: Commit your deeds to Yahweh, and your plans shall succeed.
echoes.note: 'Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established' — entrusting one's concerns to God rather than anxious self-provision.

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'All flesh is grass... the grass withers' — the transience of grass that today is and tomorrow is burned (v.30) draws on Isaiah's grass-and-flower imagery of human frailty.

echoes.text: You sweep them away as they sleep. In the morning they sprout like new grass. In the morning it sprouts and springs up. By evening, it is withered and dry.
echoes.note: Humanity 'like grass which grows up. In the morning it flourishes... in the evening it is cut down' — the grass-of-the-field's day-long life behind v.30.

echoes.text: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.
echoes.note: 'As for man, his days are like grass... the wind passes over it, and it is gone' — reinforces the perishable grass imagery applied to the field's clothing.

echoes.text: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: Toil for bread and the field's produce under the curse — the labor of sowing/reaping and anxious provision that Jesus relativizes by pointing to birds that neither sow nor reap.

echoes.text: Therefore at that time also, converting itself into all forms, It ministered to your all-nourishing bounty, According to the desire of those who made supplication; That your sons, whom you loved, O Lord, might learn That it is not the growth of the earth’s fruits that nourishes a man, But that your word preserves those who trust you.
echoes.note: Manna provision teaches that 'it is not the production of crops that feeds humankind but your word that sustains those who trust in you' — Second Temple reflection on God-given sustenance versus anxious labor.

echoes.text: Envy and wrath shorten a man’s days; And care brings old age before the time.
echoes.note: 'Anxiety brings on premature old age' — Ben Sira on the harm of worry, faintly paralleling 'which of you by being anxious can add to his lifespan?'

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.
echoes.note: The ant gathers in summer — a nature-observation wisdom form ('consider the ant'); Jesus inverts the genre with 'consider the lilies' which do NOT toil, yet are clothed.

pericopes.text: “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
echoes.note: The Holiness Code's demand for righteous, unbiased judgment ('you shall not be partial... but in righteousness shall you judge') underlies Jesus' critique of hypocritical, self-exempting judging.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Reproof of 'your brother/neighbor' without bearing sin or grudge frames the speck-and-beam logic: correction must be cleansed of self-righteousness; 'brother' language matches Lev's love-of-neighbor unit.

echoes.text: David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who has done this is worthy to die! He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!” Nathan said to David, “You are the man. This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.
echoes.note: Nathan's 'You are the man!' — David condemns another's sin while blind to his own — is the narrative archetype of judging with a beam in one's eye.

echoes.text: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man, you will show yourself perfect. With the pure, you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
echoes.note: Measure-for-measure principle ('with the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the crooked, shrewd'): God deals back in kind, echoed in 'with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.'

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD' — leaving recompense to God, the disposition behind 'judge not, that you be not judged.'

echoes.text: While therefore you do chasten us, you scourge our enemies ten thousand times more, To the intent that we may ponder your goodness when we judge, And when we are judged may look for mercy.
echoes.note: God judges with measured forbearance so the righteous learn to be kind; a Second Temple articulation of the reciprocal-measure ethic.

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]
echoes.note: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong... and then your sins will be pardoned' — the reciprocity of judgment/forgiveness in wisdom tradition closely parallels 7:1-2.

pericopes.text: “Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.

echoes.text: Don’t speak in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.
echoes.note: 'Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words' — withholding precious teaching from those who will only scorn it parallels not casting pearls before swine.

echoes.text: He who corrects a mocker invites insult. He who reproves a wicked man invites abuse. Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise man, and he will love you.
echoes.note: Correcting a scoffer brings abuse ('reprove a scoffer and he will hate you'); the rebuffing 'dogs' who 'turn and tear you' echoes the futility of instructing scorners.

echoes.text: Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.
echoes.note: A gold ring in a swine's snout — wisdom tradition's pairing of something precious with a pig as image of incongruity.

echoes.text: “‘No stranger shall eat of the holy thing: a foreigner living with the priests, or a hired servant, shall not eat of the holy thing. But if a priest buys a slave, purchased by his money, he shall eat of it; and such as are born in his house, they shall eat of his bread. If a priest’s daughter is married to an outsider, she shall not eat of the heave offering of the holy things. But if a priest’s daughter is a widow, or divorced, and has no child, and has […]
echoes.note: 'That which is holy' (qodesh) — sacred offerings forbidden to the unconsecrated/profane — supplies cultic background for not giving the holy to dogs.

echoes.text: “You shall be holy men to me, therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by animals in the field. You shall cast it to the dogs.
echoes.note: Sacred meat is to be thrown to the dogs as the antithesis of holy use; the dog as the unclean recipient of holy things underlies the saying's logic.

pericopes.text: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you. For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened. Or who is there among you, who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!

echoes.text: You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.
echoes.note: 'You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart' — the seek/find promise behind 'Seek, and you will find.'

echoes.text: But from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: 'From there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search with all your heart' — covenantal seek-and-find assurance.

echoes.text: I love those who love me. Those who seek me diligently will find me.
echoes.note: Wisdom: 'those who seek me diligently find me' — the wisdom-tradition seek/find topos applied to prayer.

echoes.text: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call you on him while he is near:
echoes.note: 'Seek the LORD while he may be found, call upon him while he is near' — seeking and calling that meet divine availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him. He also will hear their cry, and will save them.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to all who call on him... he fulfills the desire of those who fear him' — the Father's reliable response to those who ask.

echoes.text: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you!
echoes.note: A mother cannot forget her nursing child — the a fortiori of parental compassion ('how much more your Father') has prophetic precedent.

echoes.text: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.
echoes.note: 'As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion' — the very father-to-children analogy of 7:11.

echoes.text: He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged. He will in no wise despise the supplication of the fatherless; Nor the widow, when she pours out her tale. Do not the tears of the widow run down her cheek? And is not her cry against him that has caused them to fall?
echoes.note: God hears the prayer of the wronged and does not ignore supplication — Second Temple confidence in answered petition.

pericopes.text: Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' — the Golden Rule reformulates the command Jesus elsewhere names as summing the Law (Mt 22:39-40), here explicitly 'the law and the prophets.'

echoes.text: And what you yourself hate, do to no man. Don’t drink wine to drunkenness, and don’t let drunkenness go with you on your way.
echoes.note: 'What you hate, do to no one' — the negative form of the Golden Rule in the deuterocanon; the closest verbal precedent to 7:12's reciprocity maxim.

echoes.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: Extension of neighbor-love to the resident alien ('love him as yourself') broadens the rule's scope to 'men' generally.

echoes.text: Consider your neighbor’s liking by your own; And be discreet in every point.
echoes.note: 'Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own' — wisdom-tradition empathic reciprocity anticipating the Golden Rule.

pericopes.text: “Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it. Hownarrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: The Mosaic 'two ways' — life and good vs. death and evil, with the call to 'choose life' — is the foundational template for the two gates/ways leading to life or destruction.

echoes.text: To this people you shall say, Thus says Yahweh: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.
echoes.note: 'I set before you the way of life and the way of death' — the explicit prophetic 'way of life / way of death' formula behind 7:13-14.

echoes.text: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.
echoes.note: 'The LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish' — the two-ways frame (the same Psalm informs 7:17-19 on trees/fruit).

echoes.text: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light, that shines more and more until the perfect day. The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.
echoes.note: The path of the righteous vs. the way of the wicked who stumble in darkness — wisdom's contrasted ways.

echoes.text: There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.
echoes.note: 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death' — the broad way that 'leads to destruction.'

echoes.text: The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; And at the last end thereof is the pit of Hades.
echoes.note: 'The way of sinners is smoothly paved... but at its end is the pit of Hades' — Second Temple two-ways with a broad/smooth road to destruction.

echoes.text: Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse: the blessing, if you listen to the commandments of Yahweh your God, which I command you this day; and the curse, if you do not listen to the commandments of Yahweh your God, but turn aside out of the way which I command you this day, to go after other gods, which you have not known.
echoes.note: The blessing-and-curse alternative set before Israel reinforces the binary-choice structure.

pericopes.text: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit. Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down, and thrown into the fire. Therefore by their fruits you will know them.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: Israel's princes are 'like wolves tearing the prey' for gain — the predatory-wolf image for corrupt leaders, here the false prophets 'inwardly ravening wolves.'

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day. Her prophets are arrogant and treacherous people. Her priests have profaned the sanctuary. They have done violence to the law.
echoes.note: Judah's officials are 'roaring lions,' her judges 'evening wolves,' her prophets 'treacherous' — prophets/leaders as wolves cloaking treachery.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies, Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you: they teach you vanity; they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of Yahweh. They say continually to those who despise me, Yahweh has said, You shall have peace; and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart they say, No evil shall come on you. For who has stood in the council of Yahweh, that he should perceive and hear his […]
echoes.note: Warning against false prophets who speak from their own minds, not the LORD; the test of true vs. false prophecy frames 'beware of false prophets.'

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]
echoes.note: The Torah test for a false prophet who leads astray though signs come true — background to discerning prophets 'by their fruits.'

echoes.text: But the prophet who speaks a word presumptuously in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.” You may say in your heart, “How shall we know the word which Yahweh has not spoken?” When a prophet speaks in Yahweh’s name, if the thing doesn’t follow, nor happen, that is the thing which Yahweh has not spoken. The prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You shall not be afraid of him.
echoes.note: The criterion for distinguishing the prophet who speaks presumptuously — judging the prophet by outcome/fruit.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The righteous as a tree yielding its fruit in season vs. the wicked as chaff — the good-tree/good-fruit and judgment imagery of Ps 1 underlies 7:17-19.

echoes.text: For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and shall not fear when heat comes, but its leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
echoes.note: The one trusting the LORD is a tree by water that 'does not cease to bear fruit' — fruitfulness as the mark of right relation to God.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The vineyard yielding wild/bad grapes instead of good is judged and destroyed — bad fruit signaling false standing and impending judgment.

echoes.text: Ephraim is struck. Their root has dried up. They will bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, yet I will kill the beloved ones of their womb.”
echoes.note: Ephraim 'blighted, their root dried up, they shall bear no fruit' — fruitlessness as ground for being cut off.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The coming day burns the evildoers like stubble; 'every tree that doesn't grow good fruit is... thrown into the fire' shares the burning-judgment image.

echoes.text: By the river on its bank, on this side and on that side, shall grow every tree for food, whose leaf shall not wither, neither shall its fruit fail: it shall produce new fruit every month, because its waters issue out of the sanctuary; and its fruit shall be for food, and its leaf for healing.
echoes.note: Trees whose fruit is for food, leaves for healing — the eschatological good-tree image as foil to the corrupt tree.

echoes.text: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.
echoes.note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree, so the expression of a thought discloses the heart' — wisdom maxim that fruit reveals inner character.

pericopes.text: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’

echoes.text: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for Yahweh has heard the voice of my weeping.
echoes.note: 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' — verbatim source of Jesus' dismissal sentence in 7:23.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name; I didn’t send them, neither have I commanded them, neither spoke I to them: they prophesy to you a lying vision, and divination, and a thing of nothing, and the deceit of their own heart.
echoes.note: Prophets prophesy lies 'in my name' though the LORD did not send them — 'didn't we prophesy in your name?' echoes false prophecy claiming the divine name.

echoes.text: For I have not sent them, says Yahweh, but they prophesy falsely in my name; that I may drive you out, and that you may perish, you, and the prophets who prophesy to you.
echoes.note: 'They prophesy falsely in my name' — the divine repudiation of those who invoke God's name without commission.

echoes.text: He said to Korah and to all his company, “In the morning, Yahweh will show who are his, and who is holy, and will cause him to come near to him. Even him whom he shall choose, he will cause to come near to him.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will make known who is his' — the motif of God knowing/owning his own, inverted in 'I never knew you.'

echoes.text: For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.
echoes.note: 'The LORD knows the way of the righteous' — divine 'knowing' as covenantal acknowledgment, denied to the iniquitous in 7:23.

echoes.text: They cry to me, ‘My God, we Israel acknowledge you!’ Israel has cast off that which is good. The enemy will pursue him.
echoes.note: Israel cries 'My God, we know you!' yet has spurned the good — claiming acquaintance with God while doing iniquity, repudiated.

pericopes.text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.”

echoes.text: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more; but the righteous stand firm forever.
echoes.note: 'When the storm passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever' — the storm that sweeps away the unfounded vs. the firmly founded, the core contrast of the two builders.

echoes.text: The wicked are overthrown, and are no more, but the house of the righteous shall stand.
echoes.note: 'The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand' — the standing vs. falling house image.

echoes.text: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. echoes.note: Psalm 103 pairs the two acts Jesus performs together: God 'forgives all your iniquity' and 'heals all your diseases.' Matthew's scene welds forgiveness ('your sins are forgiven') to the cure of paralysis, enacting the psalm's joined benefits and implying Jesus does what the LORD does.

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake.' The scribes' charge of blasphemy presupposes that only God forgives sins; Isaiah's first-person divine prerogative is the unstated premise Jesus claims, sharpening the christological provocation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins' fuses the Danielic 'one like a son of man' to whom dominion and authority (exousia/sholtan) are given. Matthew transfers heavenly enthronement authority into an earthly act of forgiveness, the key warrant for the healing.

echoes.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
echoes.note: 'He who blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death.' The scribes' verdict 'This man blasphemes' invokes the capital statute; the legal background charges the episode with the threat that will later kill Jesus.

echoes.text: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness. He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
echoes.note: 'Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity... he will tread our iniquities underfoot.' The hymn to the God who uniquely forgives stands behind the assumption that forgiveness is a divine, not human, act, which Jesus nonetheless exercises.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth, keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
echoes.note: The LORD 'forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin' is the foundational self-revelation of divine pardon; the paralytic's forgiveness re-presents this divine attribute in Jesus' speech.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom and the dominion... shall be given to the people of the holy ones.' The crowd's wonder that God 'had given such authority to men' may echo the Danielic transfer of dominion to a human collective, though the link is faint.

pericopes.text: As Jesus passed by from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax collection office. He said to him, “Follow me.” He got up and followed him. As he sat in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and sat down with Jesus and his disciples. When the Pharisees saw it, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do. But you go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Formula-marked citation, 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Verbatim from Hosea (LXX eleos ou thysian). Jesus deploys the prophetic preference for covenant loyalty over cultic act to justify table fellowship with sinners; Matthew alone repeats it at 12:7.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' Samuel's rebuke of Saul belongs to the same prophetic tradition prioritizing obedience/mercy over cult that Hosea 6:6 distills; it reinforces the scriptural logic Jesus wields against the Pharisees.

echoes.text: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to Yahweh than sacrifice.
echoes.note: 'To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.' A wisdom parallel to Hosea 6:6 corroborating the mercy-over-sacrifice principle invoked to defend eating with tax collectors.

echoes.text: Honor a physician according to your need of him with the honors due to him: For verily the Lord has created him. For from the Most High comes healing; And from the king he shall receive a gift. The skill of the physician shall lift up his head; And in the sight of great men he shall be admired. The Lord created medicines out of the earth; And a prudent man will have no disgust at them.
echoes.note: 'Honor the physician... the Lord created medicines.' Jesus' aphorism 'those who are sick need a physician' uses the physician topos; Sirach's Second Temple esteem for the healer is a contemporary backdrop, though the saying is proverbial rather than a specific borrowing.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: 'I will seek the lost... and bind up the injured.' The shepherd-God who goes after the sick and strayed anticipates Jesus' coming 'not to call the righteous but sinners,' the same pastoral logic, faintly heard here and developed at 9:36.

pericopes.text: Then John’s disciples came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples don’t fast?” Jesus said to them, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch would tear away from the garment, and a worse hole is made. Neither do people put new wine into old wine skins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved.”

echoes.text: Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.
echoes.note: 'My belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.' Elihu's image is the closest scriptural antecedent to Jesus' new-wine/bursting-old-skins saying, supplying the very mechanics (new wine, skins ready to burst) of the metaphor.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.' The prophetic depiction of God/the messianic age as bridegroom undergirds Jesus' self-identification as the bridegroom whose presence makes fasting impossible.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will betroth you to me forever.' The LORD's marriage to Israel frames the bridegroom imagery; coming from the same prophet quoted at 9:13, it suggests Jesus occupies the divine spouse's role in the renewed covenant.

echoes.text: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called. For Yahweh has called you as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit, even a wife of youth, when she is cast off,” says your God.
echoes.note: 'Your Maker is your husband.' Another strand of the bridegroom-God tradition reinforcing the nuptial joy that suspends mourning while the bridegroom is present.

echoes.text: The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.
echoes.note: 'The vats shall overflow with wine.' The eschatological abundance of new wine in the prophets colors Jesus' 'new wine' as the inbreaking new age incompatible with old structures.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.
echoes.note: 'The mountains shall drip sweet wine.' Like Joel, an eschatological new-wine motif faintly resonant with Jesus' claim that the new cannot be poured into the old.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and in the seventh month for these seventy years, did you at all fast to me, really to me?
echoes.note: 'When you fasted and mourned... was it for me?' Zechariah's critique of fasting that misses God anticipates Jesus' relativizing of John's-disciples' fasting in light of the bridegroom's presence.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
echoes.note: 'He was taken away.' Jesus' ominous 'the bridegroom will be taken away' foreshadows the passion; the Servant who is 'taken away' is a plausible typological reservoir, though the verbal link is slight.

pericopes.text: While he told these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” Jesus got up and followed him, as did his disciples. Behold, a woman who had an issue of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.” But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour. When Jesus came into the ruler’s house, and saw the flute players, and the crowd in noisy disorder, he said to them, “Make room, because the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him. But when the crowd was put out, he entered in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose. The report of this went out into all that land.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: The woman touches 'the fringe (kraspedon/tzitzit) of his garment.' The tassels commanded in Numbers mark the wearer as a Torah-keeping Israelite; Matthew specifies the fringe, framing the healing power as flowing through Jesus' faithful Israelite dress.

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]
echoes.note: The statute on a woman with a chronic 'discharge of blood' renders her and what she touches unclean. The twelve-year hemorrhage and her touching Jesus directly engage this purity law; rather than contracting impurity, Jesus communicates cleansing health.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow's dead son. The prophetic raising of a dead child is the primary type for Jesus entering, taking the girl by the hand, and raising her; Matthew presents Jesus as greater than Elijah.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raises the Shunammite's daughter, entering the room, acting on the child's body, and restoring her. The closest structural type (a girl, an anxious parent, prophet enters and revives), illuminating Jesus' act in the ruler's house.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaf)' — kanaf also meaning the garment-corner/fringe. The pun links the healing 'fringe' the woman grasps to the messianic promise of healing in the 'wings,' a suggestive but disputed resonance.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust... shall awake.' Jesus' 'the girl is not dead but sleeping' frames death as sleep, the idiom Daniel uses for resurrection, hinting that the raising prefigures eschatological awakening.

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: The martyr's hope: 'the King of the universe will raise us up.' Second Temple resurrection hope forms the conceptual horizon for the daughter's restoration being read as more than resuscitation; relevant but not a verbal borrowing.

pericopes.text: As Jesus passed by from there, two blind men followed him, calling out and saying, “Have mercy on us, son of David!” When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They told him, “Yes, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you.” Their eyes were opened. Jesus strictly commanded them, saying, “See that no one knows about this.” But they went out and spread abroad his fame in all that land.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened.' The opening of the two blind men's eyes enacts the signature sign of Isaiah's coming-of-God salvation oracle; Matthew uses it programmatically (cf. 11:5) to identify Jesus' deeds with the promised restoration.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The Davidic covenant promising David an everlasting offspring/throne is the root of the title 'Son of David' the blind men cry. Matthew's recurring Davidic christology (1:1) is voiced precisely by those seeking mercy and sight.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'Out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.' A second Isaianic blindness-reversal oracle reinforcing that restored sight is the mark of God's eschatological visitation now effected by Jesus.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant is called 'to open the eyes that are blind.' The opening of eyes as the Servant's commissioned task links Jesus' healing to Isaiah's servant-of-the-LORD vocation.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind.' The psalm ascribes eye-opening to the LORD himself; Jesus performing it implies the same divine agency the crowd marveled at in 9:8.

echoes.text: Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt.
