echoes.note: 'Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy.' The blind men's cry 'Have mercy on us' echoes the standard psalmic appeal for divine mercy, now addressed to the Son of David.

echoes.text: Raphael said, “I know, Tobias, that your father will open his eyes. Therefore anoint his eyes with the gall, and being pricked therewith, he will rub, and willl make the white films fall away. Then he will see you.” Anna ran to him, and fell upon the neck of her son, and said to him, “I have seen you, my child! I am ready to die.” They wept both. Tobit went toward the door and stumbled; but his son ran to him, and took hold of his father. He rubbed the […]
echoes.note: Tobit's blindness is cured and 'his eyes were opened.' The deuterocanonical healing-of-blindness narrative is a Second Temple precedent for restored sight as a sign of divine favor; thematically apt though not directly quoted.

pericopes.text: As they went out, behold, a mute man who was demon possessed was brought to him. When the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke. The multitudes marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!” But the Pharisees said, “By the prince of the demons, he casts out demons.”

echoes.text: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: 'The tongue of the mute shall sing for joy.' The mute man speaking when the demon is cast out completes the Isaiah 35 cluster (blind see in 9:30, mute speak here), presenting Jesus' miracles as the bundled signs of Isaiah's restoration.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: 'Who makes him mute... Is it not I, the LORD?' God's claim to sovereignty over speech and its impairment frames Jesus' loosing of the mute tongue as a divine prerogative exercised.

echoes.text: But I, as a deaf man, don’t hear. I am as a mute man who doesn’t open his mouth. Yes, I am as a man who doesn’t hear, in whose mouth are no reproofs. For in you, Yahweh, do I hope. You will answer, Lord my God.
echoes.note: 'Like a mute man who does not open his mouth... but for you, O LORD, do I wait.' The psalmic muteness-then-divine-help pattern faintly underlies the restoration of speech, though no verbal borrowing is present.

pericopes.text: Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses asks for a successor so the congregation 'may not be as sheep that have no shepherd.' Matthew's 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd' directly takes up this idiom; Jesus' compassion answers Israel's perennial need for a true shepherd-leader.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: Micaiah sees 'all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd.' The leaderless, scattered flock under failed kings is exactly Matthew's diagnosis of the crowds, with Jesus stepping into the vacant shepherd role.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: 'They were scattered because there was no shepherd.' Ezekiel's indictment of Israel's negligent shepherds and promise that God himself will shepherd the flock is the richest backdrop: Jesus' compassion enacts the LORD's pledge to seek the scattered sheep.

echoes.text: For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie; and they have told false dreams. They comfort in vain. Therefore they go their way like sheep. They are oppressed, because there is no shepherd.
echoes.note: The people 'wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd.' Zechariah's shepherdless, afflicted flock parallels Matthew's 'harassed' crowds, adding a prophetic voice to the shepherd-deficit motif.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them return every man to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: The Chronicler's parallel to 1 Kings 22:17 repeats 'all Israel scattered... as sheep that have no shepherd,' a second canonical attestation of the formula behind 9:36.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.' Jesus' 'the harvest is plentiful' picks up the prophetic harvest image; where Joel's harvest is judgment, Matthew turns it toward ingathering, asking for laborers from the Lord of the harvest.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that Yahweh will thresh from the flowing stream of the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt; and you will be gathered one by one, children of Israel.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will thresh... and you will be gathered one by one.' The eschatological gathering-harvest of Israel is a faint resonance behind the plentiful harvest needing laborers.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: 'I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David.' The promise of a single Davidic shepherd is figurally fulfilled as Jesus (the Son of David of 9:27) responds to the shepherdless crowds, binding this pericope to the Davidic christology of the chapter.

pericopes.text: He called to himself his twelve disciples, and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these. The first, Simon, who is called Peter; Andrew, his brother; James the son of Zebedee; John, his brother; Philip; Bartholomew; Thomas; Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus; Lebbaeus, who was also called Thaddaeus; Simon the Canaanite; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.

echoes.text: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his blessing.
echoes.note: The number Twelve is the structuring datum of the apostle list. Jacob's twelve sons becoming the twelve tribes is the obvious typological template: Jesus constitutes a renewed Israel of twelve, an eschatological re-founding of the people (cf. Mt 19:28, the Twelve judging the twelve tribes). The figural reading is widely held.

echoes.text: Moses wrote all Yahweh’s words, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar under the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
echoes.note: Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars 'according to the twelve tribes of Israel' at the covenant ratification. The setting-apart of twelve representatives at a covenant moment is a thematic analogue to the appointment of the Twelve; faint and dependent on the broader twelve-tribe pattern.

echoes.text: These are those who were numbered, whom Moses and Aaron numbered, and the princes of Israel, being twelve men: they were each one for his fathers’ house.
echoes.note: The census appoints twelve tribal leaders, 'every one for the house of his fathers.' A possible background for the twelve named representatives commissioned for a task on Israel's behalf, but the link is purely numerical and structural.

pericopes.text: Jesus sent these twelve out, and commanded them, saying, “Don’t go among the Gentiles, and don’t enter into any city of the Samaritans. Rather, go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. As you go, preach, saying, ‘The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!’ Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, and cast out demons. Freely you received, so freely give. Don’t take any gold, nor silver, nor brass in your money belts. Take no bag for your journey, neither two coats, nor shoes, nor staff: for the laborer is worthy of his food. Into whatever city or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy; and stay there until you go on. As you enter into the household, greet it. If the household is worthy, let your peace come on it, but if it isn’t worthy, let your peace return to you. Whoever doesn’t receive you, nor hear your words, as you go out of that house or that city, shake off the dust from your feet. Most certainly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city.

echoes.text: My people have been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have turned them away on the mountains; they have gone from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.
echoes.note: 'My people have been lost sheep' (Jer 50:6) supplies the exact image and idiom behind 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (10:6). The phrase is a deliberate scriptural designation of Israel as a flock gone astray under failed shepherds, which the mission of the Twelve is sent to gather.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's flock 'scattered because there was no shepherd' and the sheep that 'wandered through all the mountains' is the controlling background for Israel-as-lost-sheep. Ezek 34:16, 'I will seek that which was lost,' frames the apostolic mission as God's promised search for the strays.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Israel as a congregation 'as sheep which have no shepherd,' Moses' prayer for a successor. Matthew uses this very phrase at 9:36 immediately before this commissioning, so it bleeds directly into the 'lost sheep' rationale for sending the Twelve.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray.' Reinforces the lost-sheep idiom for Israel's straying, though without the verbal specificity of Jeremiah or Ezekiel.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky. He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
echoes.note: 'Sodom and Gomorrah' (10:15) names the archetypal city of judgment whose destruction by fire becomes the proverbial worst-case fate. Jesus says it will be 'more tolerable' for them than for a town that rejects the apostles — a direct invocation of the Genesis paradigm of inhospitality and overthrow.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The hospitality/inhospitality axis governing the worthy-household and shake-off-the-dust instructions (10:11-15) culminates in the Sodom comparison; Abraham's reception of the visitors vs. Sodom's refusal is the implicit contrast. The sin of Sodom as failed hospitality (cf. Ezek 16:49) underlies the whole judgment logic.

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: The Passover departure 'with your staff in your hand' and sandals on, ready to travel light, sits in ironic counterpoint to the mission's stripping away of staff, sandals (in the Markan form), and provisions. A possible inversion of the exodus travel kit, but the parallel is contested and the Matthean list differs.

echoes.text: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the face of the child.”
echoes.note: Elisha sends Gehazi with staff and the urgent command not to greet anyone on the road — a prophetic-commission travel instruction with the same terse, single-minded haste as the mission charge. Faint and disputed.

echoes.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even thus be he shaken out, and emptied.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. The people did according to this promise.
echoes.note: Nehemiah shakes out the fold of his garment as a prophetic sign-act of rejection and curse against those who break faith. A possible cultural background for 'shake off the dust from your feet' (10:14) as a gesture of testimony against, though the dust-of-the-feet gesture is not identical.

pericopes.text: “Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. But beware of men: for they will deliver you up to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you. Yes, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the nations. But when they deliver you up, don’t be anxious how or what you will say, for it will be given you in that hour what you will say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. “Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents, and cause them to be put to death. You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved. But when they persecute you in this city, flee into the next, for most certainly I tell you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel, until the Son of Man has come.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: 'Be wise as serpents' (10:16) trades on the serpent of Eden being 'more subtle/cunning than any beast of the field.' Jesus redeems the proverbial shrewdness of the serpent for the disciples' survival among hostile men; the verbal link to the Genesis serpent's craftiness is the most natural source.

echoes.text: Her princes in its midst are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, that they may get dishonest gain.
echoes.note: Israel's predatory leaders are 'like wolves ravening the prey.' Combined with Zeph 3:3 this supplies the biblical 'wolves' menacing the flock, now the danger the sheep-disciples are sent into the midst of (10:16).

echoes.text: Her princes in the midst of her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
echoes.note: 'Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves.' Reinforces the wolves-among-the-flock danger and specifically locates the threat in officials and judges — apt for 10:17-18, the councils, governors, and kings before whom disciples are dragged.

echoes.text: What fellowship shall the wolf have with the lamb? So is the sinner to the godly.
echoes.note: 'What fellowship has the wolf with the lamb? No more has the sinner with the godly.' Second Temple wisdom uses the wolf/lamb pairing precisely for the irreconcilable hostility between the righteous and the wicked — close to the 'sheep among wolves' logic of the persecuted mission.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for to whoever I shall send you, you shall go, and whatever I shall command you, you shall speak. Don’t be afraid because of them; for I am with you to deliver you,” says Yahweh. Then Yahweh stretched out his hand, and touched my mouth; and Yahweh said to me, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.
echoes.note: God's promise to the prophet sent to kings and nations — 'I have put my words in your mouth' — is the prophetic-call template behind 10:19-20: do not be anxious what to say, for it will be given you in that hour; it is the Spirit of your Father speaking in you. The handing-over of words to a divinely commissioned spokesman before hostile rulers is the same scene.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.' Moses' commissioning, where God overrides the inadequate speaker by supplying the very words, is the foundational background for 'it will be given you in that hour what you will say' and 'it is not you who speak' (10:19-20).

echoes.text: “The Spirit of Yahweh spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit of the LORD spoke by me, and his word was in my tongue.' David's last words present the same pattern of the Spirit speaking through a human mouth, a faint background for the Spirit of the Father speaking in the disciples (10:20).

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 'The son dishonoreth the father... a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Micah's portrait of the collapse of household loyalty in a day of distress stands behind 10:21 ('brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child; children will rise up against parents'). The same text is quoted more fully at 10:35-36; here it surfaces in the persecution context of intra-familial betrayal unto death.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is he that waiteth and cometh... thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.' Daniel's eschatological endurance-to-the-end-and-be-vindicated theme underlies 10:22, 'he who endures to the end will be saved,' set amid tribulation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' 10:23, 'until the Son of Man has come,' draws its title and its coming-in-judgment expectation from Daniel's vision; the apocalyptic horizon of the persecution sayings is Danielic.

pericopes.text: “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord. It is enough for the disciple that he be like his teacher, and the servant like his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household!

echoes.text: Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover of this sickness.” But Yahweh’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel, that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
echoes.note: 'Beelzebul' (10:25) derives from Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consults. The name of the rejected foreign deity becomes the slander hurled at 'the master of the house'; the disciples should expect the same naming, 'how much more those of his household.'

pericopes.text: Therefore don’t be afraid of them, for there is nothing covered that will not be revealed; and hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in the ear, proclaim on the housetops. Don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. Rather, fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. “Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls on the ground apart from your Father’s will, but the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows.

echoes.text: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.
echoes.note: 'Neither fear ye their fear... Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.' Isaiah's command to fear God rather than the conspiracy of men is the precise logic of 10:28: do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who can destroy soul and body. The double 'do not fear / rather fear' structure is Isaianic.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind. Therefore behold, the days come”, says Yahweh, “that it shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter; for they shall bury in Topheth, until there is no place to bury.
echoes.note: 'Gehenna' (10:28) is the valley of Hinnom (Topheth), the site of child-sacrifice that Jeremiah declares will become 'the valley of slaughter.' The OT condemnation of this valley as the place of fiery judgment supplies the term for the place where God can destroy both soul and body.

echoes.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
echoes.note: Josiah defiles Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so none could pass a child through fire to Molech. Reinforces the Gehenna background as the defiled valley of fire that becomes the figure of final destruction (10:28).

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: 'There shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground.' The idiom of every hair guarded as a token of total providential protection (cf. 2 Sam 14:11; 1 Kgs 1:52) lies directly behind 10:30, 'the very hairs of your head are all numbered,' assuring the disciples of God's exhaustive care amid persecution.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: God keeps count of the sufferer's wanderings and bottles his tears. A thematic analogue to the divine bookkeeping of hairs and the fall of sparrows (10:29-31) — God's minute attention to the afflicted — though without verbal overlap.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' The wisdom maxim that proper fear is owed to God alone undergirds the redirection of fear in 10:28, but the connection is general rather than verbal.

pericopes.text: Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, him I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.' A faint analogue to confessing Christ before men without shame (10:32), continuous with the 'testimony before governors and kings' of 10:18. Disputed and thematic only.

pericopes.text: “Don’t think that I came to send peace on the earth. I didn’t come to send peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man at odds against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s foes will be those of his own household. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me isn’t worthy of me. He who doesn’t take his cross and follow after me, isn’t worthy of me. He who seeks his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 10:35-36 is a near-verbatim rendering of Micah 7:6: 'the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Matthew reproduces the three paired antagonisms (father/son here as father, daughter/mother, daughter-in-law/mother-in-law) and the climactic 'a man's foes will be those of his own household' almost word for word. This is the strongest, formula-grade allusion in the chapter.

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi 'said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren... for they have observed thy word.' The blessing praises placing covenant loyalty above family bonds — the same demand as 10:37, loving God above father, mother, son, daughter. A recognized OT precedent for cult loyalty overriding kinship.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites slay brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command and are thereby 'consecrated.' A harsh background for loyalty to God dividing even kin (10:34-37); thematically apt but lexically distant and contested.

echoes.text: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]
echoes.note: The Aqedah — Abraham not withholding his son for the sake of God — is a possible figural backdrop to 'he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me' (10:37): supreme love of God above the dearest child. Suggestive typology rather than verbal echo.

pericopes.text: He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me. He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward. Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.”

echoes.text: “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.” She said, “As […]
echoes.note: The widow of Zarephath receives the prophet Elijah and is rewarded with sustained meal and oil and her son's restoration. This is the paradigm narrative for 10:41, 'he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet's reward' — hospitality to God's messenger drawing the messenger's blessing.

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: The Shunammite woman receives Elisha, builds him a room, and is rewarded with a son and his resurrection. Together with the Zarephath account this supplies the OT pattern that receiving a prophet yields a prophet's reward (10:41).

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: The man who brings provisions to Elisha and 'the servant of the prophet' setting it before the people — a faint analogue to ministering to God's agents and not losing one's reward (10:42), within the same Elisha hospitality cycle.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: Giving the thirsty water to drink as a rewarded act of mercy is a wisdom analogue to 'a cup of cold water... he will in no way lose his reward' (10:42), though the proverb concerns an enemy. Thematic and disputed.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had finished directing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. Now when John heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear,the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.”

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: Jesus' catalog of signs answers John by weaving Isaiah's vision of the redeemed: 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped' — 'the blind receive sight, the deaf hear' borrows verbatim imagery, marking the dawning kingdom.

echoes.text: Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: 'Then shall the lame man leap as a hart' directly underlies 'the lame walk'; Isaiah 35 is the controlling subtext for Jesus' reply, signaling that the eschatological restoration has arrived.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: 'to preach good news to the poor' (anointed Servant) supplies the climactic 'the poor have good news preached to them' — the same verb/theme Jesus claims as his own programmatic mission (cf. Luke 4:18).
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'the dead are raised up' echoes Isaiah's resurrection hope, 'Your dead shall live... the earth shall give birth to the dead,' folded into the kingdom-signs list.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'In that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' — a parallel Isaianic oracle reinforcing the deaf/blind reversal, part of a recurring Isaianic cluster.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant 'to open the blind eyes' resonates with restoring sight; strengthens the Servant-mission reading of Jesus' self-presentation.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see.
echoes.note: 'Hear, you deaf; and look, you blind, that you may see' — further Isaianic deaf/blind language drawn into the answer to John.

echoes.text: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,
echoes.note: 'the lepers are cleansed' presumes the Torah cleansing rite for the healed leper; the only OT framework for leprosy cleansing, evoked figurally as fulfilled.

echoes.text: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
echoes.note: Naaman's cleansing is the paradigmatic prophetic leprosy healing; a faint precedent for 'lepers are cleansed' as a sign of prophetic power.

pericopes.text: As these went their way, Jesus began to say to the multitudes concerning John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in king’s houses. But why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and much more than a prophet. For this is he, of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer; yet he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptizer until now, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. If you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah, who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you' is a formula citation ('of whom it is written') of Mal 3:1, 'Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me,' identifying John as the eschatological forerunner.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send an angel before you, to keep you by the way, and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.
echoes.note: 'Behold, I send a messenger before you' (LXX wording 'before your face') is conflated with Mal 3:1 in the citation; the second-person 'before your face' tracks Exodus more closely than Malachi's 'before me.'

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'this is Elijah, who is to come' directly invokes Mal 4:5, 'I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD,' interpreting John as the returning Elijah.

echoes.text: It was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
echoes.note: The Elijah identification draws on the whole Elijah cycle; the wilderness/mantle prophet of austere dress stands behind the contrast with 'soft clothing' and the desert setting.

echoes.text: They answered him, “He was a hairy man, and wearing a leather belt around his waist.” He said, “It is Elijah the Tishbite.”
echoes.note: Elijah 'a hairy man, with a leather belt' grounds the John-as-Elijah figure and the contrast with kingly 'soft clothing'; cf. Matthew's own description of John's garb.

echoes.text: The voice of one who calls out, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness! Make a level highway in the desert for our God.
echoes.note: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see?' evokes the wilderness-voice preparing the way, the same way-preparation motif as the Mal 3:1 citation.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'born of women' as a marker of mortal human descent is biblical idiom (cf. Job 14:1; 15:14; 25:4); the phrase frames John as the greatest of mortals.

echoes.text: “Man, who is born of a woman, is of few days, and full of trouble.
echoes.note: 'Man who is born of a woman is of few days' supplies the idiom 'born of women' for finite humanity, against which John's greatness and the kingdom's superiority are measured.

pericopes.text: “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call to their companions and say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you didn’t dance. We mourned for you, and you didn’t lament.’ For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is justified by her children.”

echoes.text: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.
echoes.note: 'wisdom is justified by her children' personifies Wisdom as in Proverbs 8, where Lady Wisdom calls and her children/sons heed her; Jesus and John are vindicated as Wisdom's offspring.

echoes.text: Wisdom exalts her sons, And takes hold of those who seek her.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom exalts her sons and lays hold of those who seek her' — Second Temple Wisdom personification standing directly behind 'wisdom is justified by her children.'

echoes.text: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
echoes.note: 'a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance' faintly underlies the children's complaint about piping/dancing and mourning/lament.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars.
echoes.note: Wisdom's banquet invitation supports the wider Wisdom-vindicated theme; contested as a specific source.

pericopes.text: Then he began to denounce the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they didn’t repent. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades. For if the mighty works had been done in Sodom which were done in you, it would have remained until this day. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom, on the day of judgment, than for you.”

echoes.text: The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of Tarshish! For it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in. From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them.
echoes.note: The oracle against Tyre (and Sidon, v.4) is the prophetic backdrop for naming Tyre/Sidon as proverbially judged Gentile cities now declared less culpable than the unrepentant Galilean towns.

echoes.text: therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's extended judgment on Tyre ('I am against you, O Tyre') makes Tyre the type of a doomed city; invoked to shame Chorazin and Bethsaida.

echoes.text: Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against it,
echoes.note: 'Set your face against Sidon' — the companion oracle completing the Tyre/Sidon judgment pair Jesus names.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
echoes.note: Sodom's fiery overthrow is the archetypal divine judgment; 'more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment' presupposes Genesis 19 as the benchmark of destroyed wickedness.

echoes.text: You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north!
echoes.note: 'You, Capernaum, exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades' reworks the taunt against Babylon's king: 'I will ascend into heaven... yet you shall be brought down to Sheol' (Isa 14:13-15).

echoes.text: Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.
echoes.note: 'brought down to Sheol' is the direct verbal pattern behind 'go down to Hades'; the proud-exaltation-then-abasement form is borrowed wholesale.

echoes.text: As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, Sodom your sister has not done, she nor her daughters, as you have done, you and your daughters.
echoes.note: Ezekiel compares Jerusalem unfavorably to Sodom ('Sodom your sister has not done as you'), the same rhetorical move — guilty Israel worse than proverbial Sodom — Jesus makes against Capernaum.

echoes.text: For the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom, That was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands were laid on her.
echoes.note: 'the punishment of my people is greater than the punishment of Sodom' parallels the comparative-judgment logic; contested as direct source.

echoes.text: The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
echoes.note: 'repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes' echoes Nineveh's repentance in sackcloth and ashes, the model Gentile-repentance the Galilean towns failed to match.

echoes.text: and that all of its land is sulfur, salt, and burning, that it is not sown, doesn’t produce, nor does any grass grow in it, like the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which Yahweh overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath;
echoes.note: Sodom and Gomorrah's overthrow as covenant-curse paradigm reinforces 'the land of Sodom' as judgment shorthand.

pericopes.text: At that time, Jesus answered, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight. All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him.

echoes.text: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding;
echoes.note: 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth' echoes Daniel's blessing of the God who 'gives wisdom to the wise' yet reveals hidden things — the same revelation-to-the-lowly, concealment-from-the-wise pattern.

echoes.text: I thank you, and praise you, you God of my fathers, who have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we desired of you; for you have made known to us the king’s matter.
echoes.note: 'I thank you... you have given me wisdom... made known to us the king's matter' supplies the thanksgiving-for-revelation form behind Jesus' prayer.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among this people, even a marvelous work and a wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men will perish, and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.”
echoes.note: 'the wisdom of their wise men shall perish' grounds the reversal in which God hides 'these things from the wise and understanding' — the same Isaianic critique of human wisdom.

echoes.text: I will give thanks to you, O Lord, O King, And will praise you, O God my Saviour: I do give thanks to your name:
echoes.note: Sirach 51 opens 'I will give thanks to you, O Lord and King' — a sage's thanksgiving immediately preceding the Wisdom-yoke invitation (Sir 51:23ff) that Matthew 11:28-30 reworks; the thanksgiving + invitation sequence parallels Matthew's.

echoes.text: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?
echoes.note: 'What is his name, and what is his son's name?' faintly anticipates the exclusive Father-Son mutual knowing of v.27; contested.

echoes.text: He professes to have knowledge of God, And names himself servant of the Lord.
echoes.note: The righteous one 'calls himself a child of the Lord' and claims knowledge of God, a Second Temple anticipation of the Son's unique knowledge of the Father.

pericopes.text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

echoes.text: Draw near to me, you unlearned, And lodge in the house of instruction.
echoes.note: Wisdom's invitation 'Draw near to me, you who are untaught... Put your neck under the yoke, and let your souls receive instruction' is the closest analogue: 'Come to me... Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.' Jesus speaks as incarnate Wisdom issuing her summons.

echoes.text: Put your neck under the yoke, And let your soul receive instruction: She is hard at hand to find.
echoes.note: 'Put your neck under her yoke, and let your soul receive instruction... See with your eyes how I have labored little and found for myself much rest' — supplies yoke + labor + rest in the same cluster Jesus uses.

echoes.text: Behold with your eyes, How that I laboured but a little, And found for myself much rest.
echoes.note: 'I have labored little and found for myself great rest' lies directly behind 'I will give you rest' / 'rest for your souls' joined to taking up the yoke.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’
echoes.note: 'ask for the old paths... and you will find rest for your souls' is verbatim behind 'you will find rest for your souls' (Mt 11:29); Jesus offers the rest Jeremiah's generation refused.

echoes.text: And bring your feet into her fetters, And your neck into her chain.
echoes.note: 'Put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her collar/yoke... at last you will find her rest' — Sirach's earlier Wisdom-yoke passage doubling the yoke-and-rest motif.

echoes.text: For at the last you will find her rest; And she will be turned for you into gladness.
echoes.note: 'at last you will find the rest she gives, and she will be changed into joy for you' reinforces the Wisdom-yoke-rest pattern adopted in vv.28-30.

echoes.text: He said, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.”
echoes.note: 'My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest' is the foundational divine promise of rest; 'I will give you rest' assumes God as the giver of rest.

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: 'gentle and lowly in heart' echoes the humble/meek king who comes 'lowly and riding on a donkey' (Mt 21:5 cites it); the same praus self-description.

echoes.text: Now the man Moses was very humble, above all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
echoes.note: 'the man Moses was very meek, above all men' offers a precedent for 'I am gentle (meek) and lowly,' figuring Jesus as a new Moses giving an easy yoke.

echoes.text: that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot on my mountains. Then his yoke will leave them, and his burden leave their shoulders.
echoes.note: 'his yoke shall depart... his burden depart from off their shoulder' — the relief-from-yoke/burden imagery faintly contrasts with Jesus' light yoke and easy burden.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters' is the open invitational form ('Come to me, all') of prophetic Wisdom-summons.

pericopes.text: At that time, Jesus went on the Sabbath day through the grain fields. His disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But the Pharisees, when they saw it, said to him, “Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” But he said to them, “Haven’t you read what David did, when he was hungry, and those who were with him; how he entered into God’s house, and ate the show bread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Or have you not read in the law, that on the Sabbath day, the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath, and are guiltless? But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here. But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

echoes.text: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?” David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me a business, and has said to me, ‘Let no man know anything of the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you; and I have appointed the young men to such and such a place.’ Now therefore what is under your hand? Give me five loaves […]
echoes.note: David, hungry, enters the house of God and eats the bread of the Presence (showbread), unlawful for any but priests. Jesus cites this episode by name ('what David did') as the controlling precedent for need overriding cultic restriction. Strong verbal and narrative borrowing: David + companions + hunger + eating the consecrated bread.

echoes.text: “You shall take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes of it: two tenth parts of an ephah shall be in one cake. You shall set them in two rows, six on a row, on the pure gold table before Yahweh. You shall put pure frankincense on each row, that it may be to the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire to Yahweh. Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting […]
echoes.note: The legislation behind the showbread: twelve loaves set before the LORD, to be eaten only by Aaron and his sons 'in a holy place.' Jesus' phrase 'not lawful... but only for the priests' depends directly on this statute, which makes David's act a transgression that incurs no condemnation.

echoes.text: “‘On the Sabbath day, two male lambs a year old without defect, and two tenth parts of an ephah of fine flour for a meal offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering: this is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, besides the continual burnt offering, and its drink offering.
echoes.note: The Sabbath burnt offerings (two lambs, with grain and drink offerings) — the legally mandated priestly labor on the Sabbath. This is the 'work' Jesus means when he says priests 'profane the Sabbath and are guiltless,' an a fortiori argument that the temple service licenses Sabbath labor.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Formula-marked, near-verbatim citation: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Matthew uniquely inserts this Hosea line (cf. 9:13) as the hermeneutical key to the whole controversy; condemning the 'guiltless' violates God's own stated priority of mercy over cult.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Decalogue Sabbath command is the implicit law under dispute ('not lawful to do on the Sabbath'); the entire pericope is a halakhic argument over its proper scope.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: The second Decalogue's Sabbath command, grounding the rest in liberation; relevant background to the dispute over what the Sabbath is for and whom it serves.

echoes.text: “Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest: in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.
echoes.note: 'In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest' — the specific Sabbath rule sometimes read to forbid reaping; the disciples' plucking of grain would be construed as reaping under this line. Contested as the precise statute the Pharisees invoke.

echoes.text: When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, then you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor’s standing grain.
echoes.note: Plucking grain heads by hand from a neighbor's standing crop is explicitly permitted (gleaning by hand, not sickle); the disciples' act is lawful as such — the dispute is only the Sabbath, not theft. Explains why the Pharisees object to the day, not the deed.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath' — the title carries the dominion granted to the Danielic 'one like a son of man,' here extended over the Sabbath itself. Contested whether the title here is titular-Danielic or generic 'man.'

echoes.text: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
echoes.note: The Sabbath's creational institution: God rests and hallows the seventh day. Jesus' lordship over the Sabbath claim resonates against the divine origin and purpose of the day.

echoes.text: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?”
echoes.note: Ahimelech the priest at Nob is the figure who gives David the bread; Matthew's general 'house of God' (not yet the Jerusalem temple) tracks the Nob sanctuary setting of the source.

pericopes.text: He departed there, and went into their synagogue. And behold there was a man with a withered hand. They asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day?” that they might accuse him. He said to them, “What man is there among you, who has one sheep, and if this one falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, won’t he grab on to it, and lift it out? Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.” Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out; and it was restored whole, just like the other. But the Pharisees went out, and conspired against him, how they might destroy him.

echoes.text: When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself. The altar also was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word. The king answered the man of God, “Now entreat the favor […]
echoes.note: The withered/restored hand motif: Jeroboam's hand dries up and is restored at the man of God's word. Closest OT precedent for a 'withered hand' miraculously made whole, providing the verbal-thematic template Matthew's healing fulfills.

echoes.text: You shall not see your brother’s donkey or his ox fallen down by the way, and hide yourself from them. You shall surely help him to lift them up again.
echoes.note: 'You shall not see your brother's ox or sheep fallen by the way and hide yourself; you shall help him lift them up.' The rescue-of-fallen-animal obligation underlies Jesus' a fortiori: if you lift a sheep from a pit, how much more do good for a man.

echoes.text: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.
echoes.note: Obligation to relieve even an enemy's overburdened or straying animal — Torah's positive duty of mercy to beasts, which Jesus leverages to argue that doing good cannot be a Sabbath violation.

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: Again the Sabbath command is the contested law; the healing is staged as a deliberate test case of what 'lawful to do on the Sabbath' includes.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: The mercy-over-cult principle just cited (12:7) governs this scene too: 'it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath' enacts 'I desire mercy.' Thematic continuity links the two Sabbath controversies.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'How much more value is a man than a sheep' presupposes humanity's higher worth, rooted in creation in God's image; faint background to the lesser-to-greater argument.

pericopes.text: Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all, and commanded them that they should not make him known: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen; my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations. He will not strive, nor shout; neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory. In his name, the nations will hope.”

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations. He will not shout, nor raise his voice, nor cause it to be heard in the street. He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick. He will faithfully bring justice. He will not fail nor be discouraged, until he has set justice in the earth, and the islands will wait for his law.”
echoes.note: Matthew's longest formula quotation, explicitly marked 'fulfilled... through Isaiah.' The Servant Song: 'Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul delights; I will put my Spirit on him; he will proclaim justice to the nations... a bruised reed he will not break, a smoldering wick he will not quench... and in his name the nations will hope.' Matthew adapts the LXX/Hebrew to interpret Jesus' withdrawal, healing, and command to silence as the meek, non-clamorous Servant's mission.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'My chosen... in whom my soul delights, I will put my Spirit on him' verbally underlies the baptismal voice (Matt 3:17) and the Spirit endowment; Matthew here makes explicit the Servant-Christology already signaled at the baptism.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit. The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The Spirit-resting-on the Davidic shoot who judges the poor with righteousness; coheres with 'I will put my Spirit on him... he will proclaim justice,' and with the crowd's 'son of David' question following in 12:23.

echoes.text: Listen, islands, to me; and listen, you peoples, from far: Yahweh has called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother has he made mention of my name: and he has made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand, he has hidden me: and he has made me a polished shaft; in his quiver has he kept me close: and he said to me, “You are my servant; Israel, in whom I will be glorified.” But I said, “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength […]
echoes.note: Servant Song extending the servant's mission to the nations ('a light to the nations'); thematically reinforces 12:18/21 'justice to the nations... the nations will hope.'

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'My beloved' (agapetos) echoes the 'beloved son' Isaac language that LXX uses; faint resonance binding the Servant quotation to the beloved-son theme.

pericopes.text: Then one possessed by a demon, blind and mute, was brought to him and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw. All the multitudes were amazed, and said, “Can this be the son of David?” But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not cast out demons, except by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.” Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? If I by Beelzebul cast out demons, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can one enter into the house of the strong man, and plunder his goods, unless he first bind the strong man? Then he will plunder his house. “He who is not with me is against me, and he who doesn’t gather with me, scatters.

echoes.text: Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover of this sickness.” But Yahweh’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel, that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
echoes.note: Beelzebul/Baal-zebub, 'the god of Ekron' whom Ahaziah consults; the demonic name the Pharisees use derives from this Philistine deity, recast as 'prince of the demons.' Source of the loaded name.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The crowd's 'Can this be the son of David?' invokes the Davidic-messianic hope of the dynastic promise; Matthew frames Jesus' exorcisms as evidence of Davidic/messianic identity.

echoes.text: Shall the plunder be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captives be delivered? But thus says Yahweh, “Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the plunder of the terrible shall be delivered; for I will contend with him who contends with you, and I will save your children.
echoes.note: 'Shall the prey be taken from the mighty?... I will contend... and save your children.' The strong-man-bound-and-plundered image directly draws on Isaiah's promise that the spoil will be wrested from the tyrant — Jesus binding 'the strong man' (Satan) to plunder his house.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'He shall divide the spoil with the strong' — the Servant despoiling the mighty resonates with 'plunder his goods'; coheres with the Servant frame just quoted in 12:18-21.

echoes.text: Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God:” and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them; as Yahweh had spoken.
echoes.note: 'This is the finger of God' — Pharaoh's magicians concede the plagues' divine origin. Luke's parallel reads 'finger of God'; Matthew's 'Spirit of God cast out demons, then the Kingdom of God has come' carries the same Exodus echo: God's power directly at work signals the kingdom's arrival.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: Satan as the adversary rebuked by the LORD; background to the 'If Satan casts out Satan' / kingdom-of-Satan logic.

echoes.text: In the days of those kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, nor shall its sovereignty be left to another people; but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever.
echoes.note: The kingdom of God that breaks and supplants all other kingdoms; 'the Kingdom of God has come upon you' resonates with Daniel's eschatological kingdom overthrowing rival dominions (here Satan's).

echoes.text: If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose this day whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.”
echoes.note: 'He who is not with me is against me' carries the covenantal either/or of choosing allegiance ('choose this day whom you will serve'); faint thematic resonance of forced decision.

pericopes.text: Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men. Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in that which is to come. “Either make the tree good, and its fruit good, or make the tree corrupt, and its fruit corrupt; for the tree is known by its fruit. You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things. I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

echoes.text: But they rebelled, and grieved his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.
echoes.note: 'They rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; therefore he turned to be their enemy.' Background to the unforgivable 'blasphemy against the Holy Spirit' — opposing the Spirit's manifest work (the exorcisms just performed) provokes irrevocable judgment.

echoes.text: “‘But the soul who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, the same blasphemes Yahweh. That soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off. His iniquity shall be on him.’”
echoes.note: The sin done 'with a high hand' that despises the LORD's word and finds no atonement ('that person shall be cut off'); OT precedent for a sin beyond forgiveness, coherent with blasphemy against the Spirit.

echoes.text: If one man sin against another, God shall judge him; but if a man sin against Yahweh, who shall entreat for him?” Notwithstanding, they didn’t listen to the voice of their father, because Yahweh intended to kill them.
echoes.note: 'If a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?' — a sin against God himself leaving no mediation; faint resonance with the unpardonable blasphemy.

echoes.text: The fruit of a tree declares the husbandry thereof; So is the utterance of the thought of the heart of a man.
echoes.note: 'The fruit discloses the cultivation of a tree; so a person's speech discloses the cultivation of his mind.' Striking parallel to 'the tree is known by its fruit' applied to speech ('out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks'). Second Temple wisdom on word-as-fruit.

echoes.text: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. The work of a man’s hands shall be rewarded to him.
echoes.note: 'From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good' — wisdom linking words to fruit and to one's standing (justification/condemnation by speech), undergirding 'by your words you will be justified.'

echoes.text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.
echoes.note: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' — words carry decisive judicial weight, coherent with 'by your words... justified... condemned.'

echoes.text: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.
echoes.note: 'A gentle tongue is a tree of life' — wisdom's tree-and-speech imagery; faint background to the good/corrupt tree and its fruit of words.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'God will bring every deed into judgment... whether good or evil' — background to 'every idle word... in the day of judgment,' extending judgment to speech.

pericopes.text: Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.” But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, but no sign will be given it but the sign of Jonah the prophet. For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, someone greater than Jonah is here. The queen of the south will rise up in the judgment with this generation, and will condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, someone greater than Solomon is here.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: 'Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the fish' — Jesus quotes this near-verbatim ('three days and three nights in the belly of the whale') as the type of 'the Son of Man... three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.' Figural fulfillment of Jonah's burial-and-deliverance.

echoes.text: Then Jonah prayed to Yahweh, his God, out of the fish’s belly. He said, “I called because of my affliction to Yahweh. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice. For you threw me into the depths, in the heart of the seas. The flood was all around me. All your waves and your billows passed over me. I said, ‘I have been banished from your sight; yet I will look again toward your holy temple.’ The waters surrounded me, even to the […]
echoes.note: Jonah's prayer 'out of the belly of Sheol' and deliverance on the third day is the typological pattern for Jesus' descent into 'the heart of the earth' and resurrection. The whole Jonah-in-the-deep scene is read as a sign of death and rising.

echoes.text: The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least. The news reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. He made a proclamation and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, “Let neither man nor animal, herd nor flock, taste anything; let them not feed, […]
echoes.note: 'The men of Nineveh... repented at the preaching of Jonah.' Jesus cites Nineveh's repentance as testimony against 'this generation' that refuses the greater preacher. Direct narrative borrowing from Jonah 3.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to prove him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bore spices, and very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions: there was not anything hidden from the king which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had […]
echoes.note: The queen of Sheba comes 'from the ends of the earth' to hear Solomon's wisdom. Jesus invokes 'the queen of the south' as a witness who sought wisdom, contrasting 'something greater than Solomon.' Verbal and narrative dependence on 1 Kings 10.

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to prove Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great train, and camels that bore spices, and gold in abundance, and precious stones: and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him of all that was in her heart. Solomon told her all her questions; and there was not anything hidden from Solomon which he didn’t tell her. When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of […]
echoes.note: Parallel account of the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon; reinforces the 'queen of the south' allusion, drawn from the Chronicler's as well as the Kings narrative.

echoes.text: He said, “I called because of my affliction to Yahweh. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice.
echoes.note: 'Out of the belly of Sheol I cried' — 'heart of the earth' language for the realm of death echoes Jonah's Sheol/deep imagery specifically.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'On the third day he will raise us up' — the 'third day' resurrection schema possibly informs Jesus' 'three days' beyond the Jonah figure alone. Contested as a contributing intertext.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'A perverse and crooked generation' — the Song of Moses' indictment lies behind Matthew's recurrent 'evil and adulterous generation'; covenantal-prophetic language for a faithless people.

echoes.text: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.
echoes.note: 'A perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness' — reinforces the 'evil and adulterous generation' charge as a Mosaic Song echo.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness; For their mother has played […]
