echoes.note: 'Adulterous' for the unfaithful covenant people draws on the prophetic marriage metaphor (Israel as faithless spouse); grounds 'adulterous generation' in Hosea's idiom.

echoes.text: I saw, when, for this very cause that backsliding Israel had committed adultery, I had put her away and given her a bill of divorce, yet treacherous Judah, her sister, didn’t fear; but she also went and played the prostitute. Because she took her prostitution lightly, the land was polluted, and she committed adultery with stones and with wood.
echoes.note: Israel's 'adultery' / divorce for unfaithfulness; further prophetic backdrop to 'adulterous generation.'

echoes.text: God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and very great understanding, even as the sand that is on the seashore. Solomon’s wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east, and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame was in all the nations all around. He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs were one thousand five. […]
echoes.note: The breadth and fame of Solomon's wisdom that drew rulers from afar; background to why the queen came and why 'greater than Solomon' is a weighty claim.

pericopes.text: But the unclean spirit, when he is gone out of the man, passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Even so will it be also to this evil generation.”

echoes.text: But wild animals of the desert will lie there, and their houses will be full of jackals. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will frolic there.
echoes.note: Desert/waterless ruins as the haunt of demons and wild creatures ('goat-demons will dance there'); background to the unclean spirit roaming 'waterless places' as the abode of demons.

echoes.text: The wild animals of the desert will meet with the wolves, and the wild goat will cry to his fellow. Yes, the night creature shall settle there, and shall find herself a place of rest.
echoes.note: Lilith and desert demons resting in the desolate waste; reinforces 'waterless places, seeking rest' as the conventional demonic wilderness habitat in prophetic imagery.

echoes.text: But the goat, on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before Yahweh, to make atonement for him, to send him away for the scapegoat into the wilderness.
echoes.note: Azazel/the scapegoat driven into the wilderness; the desert as the place to which uncleanness is dispatched, faint background to the spirit's wilderness wandering.

echoes.text: When the demon smelled that smell, it fled into the uppermost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound him.
echoes.note: The demon Asmodeus flees to 'the remotest parts of Egypt' / the desert and is bound; Second Temple narrative of a routed demon driven to desolate regions, parallel to the unclean spirit expelled to waterless places.

echoes.text: As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly.
echoes.note: 'As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly' — wisdom proverb on relapse to a worse state, thematic kin to the spirit's return making 'the last state worse than the first.'

pericopes.text: While he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him. One said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.” But he answered him who spoke to him, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” He stretched out his hand towards his disciples, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi 'disowned his brothers and ignored his children' for covenant loyalty — kin-ties subordinated to obedience to God. Background to Jesus redefining family by doing 'the will of my Father' over natural kinship.

echoes.text: then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, “Whoever is on Yahweh’s side, come to me!” All the sons of Levi gathered themselves together to him. He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and […]
echoes.note: The Levites side with Moses against their own kin at the golden calf, gaining a 'blessing' for putting covenant before family; faint resonance with kinship redefined by allegiance to God's will.

echoes.text: I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”
echoes.note: 'I delight to do your will, O my God' — doing the Father's will as the mark of true belonging coheres with 'whoever does the will of my Father.'

echoes.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. In the midst of the assembly, I will praise you.
echoes.note: 'I will tell of your name to my brothers' — the messianic figure naming the faithful as kindred ('brothers'); faint background to Jesus' new-family declaration.

pericopes.text: On that day Jesus went out of the house, and sat by the seaside. Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat, and sat, and all the multitude stood on the beach. He spoke to them many things in parables, saying, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow. As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them. Others fell on rocky ground, where they didn’t have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth. When the sun had risen, they were scorched. Because they had no root, they withered away. Others fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them. Others fell on good soil, and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The word/seed that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, yielding seed and bread; the sower-and-word matrix governs the parable, made explicit in the later interpretation (v.19, 'the word of the Kingdom').

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: 'Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns' — the contrast of receptive ground vs. thorn-choked soil maps directly onto Jesus' soils; thorns that choke recur in v.7, 22.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: 'Sow righteousness... break up your fallow ground' — agricultural sowing-and-reaping imagery for response to God's word; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold (LXX 'hekatosteuousan') in the same year — the only clear OT 'hundredfold' agricultural blessing, possible backdrop for the good soil's hundredfold yield (v.8).

echoes.text: For as the husbandman sows much seed upon the ground, and plants many trees, and yet not all that is sown shall come up in due season, neither shall all that is planted take root: even so those who are sown in the world shall not all be saved.
echoes.note: Second Temple (4 Ezra): the farmer sows much seed but not all that is sown takes root or is saved — a near-contemporary Jewish sower parable of differential reception; cf. also 2 Esdras 9:31.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: God plants/sows expecting fruit and is disappointed by a barren yield; thematic kinship with fruit-bearing soils but no verbal overlap.

pericopes.text: The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them. For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance, but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has. Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand. In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive: for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and should turn again; and I would heal them.’ “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear. For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: Formal fulfillment quotation (v.14-15): 'hearing you will hear and not understand, seeing you will see and not perceive... this people's heart has grown callous.' Verbatim LXX citation explaining why parables both reveal and harden.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, ears to hear' — the same eyes/ears/heart triad governing whether revelation is 'given' (v.11); the verb 'given/not given' echoes Deuteronomy's grant-of-perception language.

echoes.text: ‘Hear now this, foolish people, and without understanding; who have eyes, and don’t see; who have ears, and don’t hear:
echoes.note: 'Foolish people without understanding, who have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear' — close parallel to v.13's 'seeing they do not see, hearing they do not hear.'

echoes.text: Son of man, you dwell in the midst of the rebellious house, who have eyes to see, and don’t see, who have ears to hear, and don’t hear; for they are a rebellious house.
echoes.note: 'A rebellious house, who have eyes to see but do not see, ears to hear but do not hear' — the same idiom of perceptual organs that fail in the obstinate.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.
echoes.note: 'There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries (mysteria)' — the only OT source of the technical 'mysteries' disclosed to the elect, behind 'to know the mysteries of the Kingdom' (v.11).

echoes.text: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.
echoes.note: 'The wicked shall not understand, but the wise shall understand' — an eschatological have/have-not of understanding paralleling v.11-12.

echoes.text: Instruct a wise man, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
echoes.note: 'Give to a wise man and he will be wiser still' — the principle of v.12, 'to him who has, more will be given,' resembles wisdom's accumulative reward.

echoes.text: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.
echoes.note: 'Open my eyes that I may behold wondrous things' — the blessing on eyes that see (v.16) inverts the prayer for opened perception; thematic only.

pericopes.text: “Hear, then, the parable of the farmer. When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom, and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes, and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside. What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word, and immediately with joy receives it; yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles. What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful. What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word, and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit, and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.”

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The interpretation names the seed 'the word of the Kingdom' (v.19), confirming the Isaiah 55 word-as-seed substrate that bears or fails to bear fruit.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: Sowing among thorns reappears interpretively (v.22, thorns = cares and riches that choke the word), echoing Jeremiah's warning not to sow among thorns.

echoes.text: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.
echoes.note: 'Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth' — the cursed ground's thorns as the agents of unfruitfulness; faint thematic backdrop to thorns choking the word.

pericopes.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away. But when the blade sprang up and produced fruit, then the darnel weeds appeared also. The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did this darnel come from?’ “He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’ “But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' — harvest as the set time of eschatological judgment and separation, directly behind 'at the harvest time I will tell the reapers' (v.30).

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The coming day burns like an oven, consuming the wicked as stubble; the burning of bundled weeds (v.30) anticipates this fiery consumption of evildoers.

echoes.text: I will utterly sweep away everything off of the surface of the earth, says Yahweh. I will sweep away man and animal. I will sweep away the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. I will cut off man from the surface of the earth, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: God will utterly sweep away / gather and remove the wicked from the land; gathering-for-removal imagery parallels gathering the weeds first.

echoes.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
echoes.note: 'Those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same' — the enemy who sows evil seed and its harvest of judgment; proverbial sowing/reaping morality.

pericopes.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field; which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The planted sprig becomes a noble cedar 'and birds of every kind will nest in it, in the shade of its branches' — the closest verbal source for 'the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches'; a Kingdom-tree sheltering the nations.

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's great tree under which the beasts find shade and 'the birds of the air dwelt in its branches' (cf. 4:21) — a world-empire tree image transposed to the Kingdom of Heaven.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Assyria as a towering cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the air made their nests' — reinforces the prophetic tree-of-empire-sheltering-birds motif.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: 'Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches' — birds nesting in branches as an image of creational shelter.

pericopes.text: He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast, which a woman took, and hid in three measuresof meal, until it was all leavened.”

echoes.text: Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
echoes.note: Abraham tells Sarah to take 'three measures (seahs) of fine flour' and make cakes for the divine visitors — the specific 'three measures of meal' is a distinctive verbal echo, a generous/hospitality-scaled quantity now hiding the Kingdom's leaven.

echoes.text: Gideon went in, and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal. He put the meat in a basket and he put the broth in a pot, and brought it out to him under the oak, and presented it.
echoes.note: Gideon prepares an ephah of flour (roughly three seahs) for the angelic visitor — another theophany-meal of this large measure.

echoes.text: When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young.
echoes.note: Hannah brings an ephah of flour to the house of the LORD — large-measure meal in a sacred context; faint.

echoes.text: They are all adulterers. They are burning like an oven that the baker stops stirring, from the kneading of the dough, until it is leavened.
echoes.note: The leaven left to rise by the baker; one of the few OT uses of leavening as a process working through dough, here neutral-to-positive rather than the usual negative valence.

pericopes.text: Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the multitudes; and without a parable, he didn’t speak to them, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.”

echoes.text: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,
echoes.note: Formal fulfillment quotation: 'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.' Asaph's didactic psalm of Israel's history is cited as prophecy of Jesus' parabolic teaching.

echoes.text: I will incline my ear to a proverb. I will open my riddle on the harp.
echoes.note: 'I will incline my ear to a proverb (mashal); I will open my riddle (hidah) on the harp' — parallel 'open my mouth / utter hidden things' diction; wisdom disclosing concealed truth.

echoes.text: to understand a proverb, and parables, the words and riddles of the wise.
echoes.note: To understand 'a proverb (mashal) and a figure, the words of the wise and their riddles' — the mashal/riddle pairing underlying parabolic, hidden speech.

echoes.text: You have heard it; see all this; and you, will you not declare it? “I have shown you new things from this time, even hidden things, which you have not known.
echoes.note: 'Hidden things you have not known' newly declared — disclosure of things hidden, faint backdrop to 'things hidden from the foundation of the world.'

pericopes.text: Then Jesus sent the multitudes away, and went into the house. His disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the darnel weeds of the field.” He answered them, “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man, the field is the world; and the good seed, these are the children of the Kingdom; and the darnel weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. As therefore the darnel weeds are gathered up and burned with fire; so will it be at the end of this age. The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling, and those who do iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars' — the direct source of 'the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father' (v.43).

echoes.text: and whoever doesn’t fall down and worship shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.
echoes.note: The 'furnace of blazing fire' (kaminos tou pyros) into which the disobedient are cast — verbal source for casting the wicked 'into the furnace of fire' (v.42).

echoes.text: I will sweep away man and animal. I will sweep away the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. I will cut off man from the surface of the earth, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: LXX: God will remove the lawless and 'the stumbling-blocks (ta skandala) together with the wicked' — strikingly close to 'gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling (ta skandala) and those who do iniquity' (v.41).

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The day burning like a furnace that consumes the wicked as stubble — the fiery end-of-age judgment behind the burning of the weeds (v.40-42).

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The Son of Man receiving an everlasting kingdom — Jesus self-identifies as 'the Son of Man' who has a Kingdom from which his angels gather the wicked (v.37, 41); the Danielic Son-of-Man/kingdom matrix.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: Harvest = judgment reaffirmed: 'the harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels' (v.39) interprets the harvest motif drawn from Joel.

echoes.text: And in the time of their visitation they will shine forth, And as sparks among stubble they will run to and fro.
echoes.note: Second Temple: 'In the time of their visitation the righteous will shine forth and run like sparks through the stubble' — a near-contemporary parallel to the righteous shining (v.43), pairing radiance with the burning of the wicked.

echoes.text: “So let all your enemies perish, Yahweh, but let those who love him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.” Then the land had rest forty years.
echoes.note: 'Let those who love him be like the sun rising in its might' — solar radiance as the destiny of the faithful; faint verbal kinship with shining 'like the sun.'

pericopes.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a treasure hidden in the field, which a man found, and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has, and buys that field.

echoes.text: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:
echoes.note: Seek wisdom 'as silver and search for it as hidden treasures' — the joyful search-and-sell-all for hidden treasure mirrors wisdom literature's treasure-hunt for the supreme good.

echoes.text: Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is out of sight, What profit is in them both?
echoes.note: Second Temple: 'Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure — what use is either?' — wisdom imaged as concealed treasure, faint backdrop to the field's hidden treasure.

echoes.text: I will give you the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that you may know that it is I, Yahweh, who call you by your name, even the God of Israel.
echoes.note: 'I will give you the treasures of darkness and hoards in secret places' — God-given hidden treasure imagery; thematic only.

pericopes.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls, who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had, and bought it.

echoes.text: No mention shall be made of coral or of crystal. Yes, the price of wisdom is above rubies.
echoes.note: 'The price of wisdom is above pearls/jewels' — wisdom surpassing precious gems; the pearl of supreme value for which all is sold echoes wisdom's incomparable worth.

echoes.text: She is more precious than rubies. None of the things you can desire are to be compared to her.
echoes.note: Wisdom 'is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire compares with her' (cf. 8:11) — the surpassing-value formula behind the one pearl worth selling everything.

echoes.text: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:
echoes.note: Seeking wisdom as for hidden treasure; the merchant's diligent seeking (v.45) parallels the wisdom-seeker's quest.

pericopes.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a dragnet, that was cast into the sea, and gathered some fish of every kind, which, when it was filled, they drew up on the beach. They sat down, and gathered the good into containers, but the bad they threw away. So will it be in the end of the world. The angels will come and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth.”

echoes.text: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad. Therefore he sacrifices to his net, and burns incense to his dragnet, because by them his life is luxurious, and his food is good. Will he therefore continually empty his net, and kill the nations without mercy?
echoes.note: Men caught like fish in a net and dragnet, drawn up and gathered — the dragnet (sagene) cast into the sea collecting people is anticipated by Habakkuk's image of catching humanity in a net.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]
echoes.note: Fishermen spread nets and catch 'fish of very many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea' in the river from the temple — close to the dragnet gathering 'fish of every kind' (v.47).

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: The fiery end-of-age judgment recurs: the wicked separated and cast 'into the furnace of fire' (v.50), reusing the Malachi furnace motif.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Eschatological separation of the righteous and the wicked at the end; angels separating the evil from the just (v.49) parallels the two-fate resurrection.

pericopes.text: Jesus said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” They answered him, “Yes, Lord.” He said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple in the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new and old things.”

echoes.text: The mandrakes produce fragrance. At our doors are all kinds of precious fruits, new and old, which I have stored up for you, my beloved.
echoes.note: 'All choice fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for you, my beloved' — the distinctive 'new and old things' brought out of one's store closely matches the scribe's treasure of 'new and old.'

echoes.text: You shall eat old store long kept, and you shall move out the old because of the new.
echoes.note: 'You shall eat old store long kept, and you shall clear out the old to make way for the new' — old and new produce drawn from the storehouse of blessing.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, ‘Where is the good way?’ and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’
echoes.note: 'Stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths' — the discipled scribe honoring the old alongside the new; faint thematic link of valuing inherited wisdom.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there. Coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom, and these mighty works? Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother called Mary, and his brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas? Aren’t all of his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all of these things?” They were offended by him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country, and in his own house.” He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;
echoes.note: The men of Anathoth, Jeremiah's own town, seek his life and forbid him to prophesy (cf. 12:6, his own family deals treacherously) — the prophet rejected in his homeland and household, behind v.57.

echoes.text: I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother’s children.
echoes.note: 'I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's children' — rejection by one's own family, paralleling 'in his own house' (v.57) where brothers and sisters are named.

echoes.text: When all who knew him before saw that, behold, he prophesied with the prophets, then the people said one to another, “What is this that has come to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” One of the same place answered, “Who is their father?” Therefore it became a proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
echoes.note: 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' — neighbors' astonishment that a known local figure now prophesies, like the townsfolk's 'where did this man get this wisdom?' (v.54).

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: 'Despised and rejected by men' — the Servant's rejection foreshadows the prophet dishonored among his own; thematic, no verbal overlap.

echoes.text: Amaziah also said to Amos, “You seer, go, flee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: but don’t prophesy again any more at Bethel; for it is the king’s sanctuary, and it is a royal house!”
echoes.note: Amaziah orders Amos to flee and stop prophesying at the king's sanctuary — a prophet driven out by the local establishment; faint analogue to hometown rejection.

pericopes.text: At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus, and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead. That is why these powers work in him.” For Herod had laid hold of John, and bound him, and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. For John said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” When he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet. But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced among them and pleased Herod. Whereupon he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask. She, being prompted by her mother, said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptizer.” The king was grieved, but for the sake of his oaths, and of those who sat at the table with him, he commanded it to be given, and he sent and beheaded John in the prison. His head was brought on a platter, and given to the young lady: and she brought it to her mother. His disciples came, and took the body, and buried it; and they went and told Jesus.

echoes.text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
echoes.note: Herodias driving the execution of the prophet John echoes Jezebel, who pursues the prophet Elijah's life after he confronts the royal house. Matthew has already cast John in Elijah's mantle (3:4; 11:14), so the wicked queen consort hounding the Elijah-prophet is a deliberate figural pairing: Herodias is the new Jezebel, Herod the weak Ahab.

echoes.text: But there was no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do that which was evil in the sight of Yahweh, whom Jezebel his wife stirred up.
echoes.note: Ahab is the king whom 'Jezebel his wife stirred up' to do evil; Herod likewise acts at the prompting of Herodias and her daughter ('being prompted by her mother'). The motif of a king led into killing by his wife reinforces the Ahab/Jezebel typology.

echoes.text: in the third year of his reign, he made a feast for all his princes and his servants; the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him. He displayed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honor of his excellent majesty many days, even one hundred eighty days. When these days were fulfilled, the king made a seven day feast for all the people who were present in Shushan the palace, both great and small, in the […]
echoes.note: The royal birthday banquet at which a king, pleased and bound by his word, grants a woman 'whatever she asks' closely mirrors the banquet-and-rash-promise scenario of the Persian court, where the setting of feasting, courtiers, and a king committed to honor his pledge generates the plot.

echoes.text: Then the king asked her, “What would you like, queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you even to the half of the kingdom.”
echoes.note: Herod's oath, 'to give her whatever she should ask,' verbally echoes Ahasuerus to Esther: 'What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom' (cf. Esther 5:6; 7:2). The extravagant open-ended royal promise is the same narrative device, here turned to murder rather than deliverance.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife. It is your brother’s nakedness.
echoes.note: John's charge, 'It is not lawful for you to have her,' rests directly on the Torah prohibition against uncovering the nakedness of one's brother's wife; Lev 20:21 specifies the explicit ban on taking a brother's wife. John's rebuke is a halakhic citation of this statute.

echoes.text: “‘If a man takes his brother’s wife, it is an impurity. He has uncovered his brother’s nakedness. They shall be childless.
echoes.note: 'If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity... they shall be childless.' This is the precise legal ground for John's 'It is not lawful for you to have her' against Herod's marriage to Herodias, his brother Philip's wife.

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The killing of a righteous prophet/messenger who rebukes the ruling house belongs to the deuteronomistic pattern of the murdered prophet (cf. Jer 26:20-23), which Matthew thematizes elsewhere (23:29-37). John's death extends this pattern of Israel slaying its prophets.

echoes.text: On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief cup bearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants. He restored the chief cup bearer to his position again, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand; but he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
echoes.note: Pharaoh's birthday feast, at which a beheading is decreed among the assembled officials, is the only other named royal birthday in Scripture and supplies a faint precedent for a birthday banquet that ends in an execution.

pericopes.text: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat, to a deserted place apart. When the multitudes heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities. Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them, and healed their sick. When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, “This place is deserted, and the hour is already late. Send the multitudes away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves food.” But Jesus said to them, “They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat.” They told him, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.” He said, “Bring them here to me.” He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes. They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces. Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves and there is some left over, against the servant's objection that it is too little. Matthew's feeding shares the structure: a prophet, an inadequate supply of loaves, a disciple's protest, a command to give it to the people, all eating, and a surplus remaining. Jesus is the greater Elisha.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not. It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.” Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought […]
echoes.note: The miraculous feeding of a multitude in a 'deserted place' (wilderness) where there is no bread evokes the manna narrative: God provides bread in the desert, all eat and are satisfied, and the gathering is measured. The new-Moses typology frames Jesus as the one who gives bread in the wilderness.

echoes.text: Where could I get meat to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, ‘Give us meat, that we may eat.’ I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me. If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.” Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people, and officers over […]
echoes.note: Moses' despairing question, 'Where am I to get meat to give all this people?... Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them?' mirrors the disciples' helplessness before the hungry crowd. The motif of an overwhelmed leader confronting an impossible feeding in the wilderness is shared.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: The shepherd who makes his flock lie down in green grass and spreads a table sounds through the detail that Jesus has the crowd 'sit down on the grass' and feeds them to the full. Matthew omits Mark's explicit 'sheep without a shepherd' yet retains the green-grass/feeding tableau of the LORD as shepherd.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The crowd 'like sheep without a shepherd' (Moses' prayer for a successor to lead Israel out and in) underlies Jesus' compassion on the shepherdless multitude; Matthew states this compassion (cf. 9:36) and enacts the shepherd's provision here.

echoes.text: I will feed them with good pasture; and on the mountains of the height of Israel shall their fold be: there shall they lie down in a good fold; and on fat pasture shall they feed on the mountains of Israel. I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down, says the Lord Yahweh. I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which […]
echoes.note: God's promise to shepherd his scattered flock himself, feeding them in good pasture and seeking the lost and sick, resonates with Jesus healing the sick and feeding the crowd in the open country. The Davidic-shepherd hope of Ezekiel is being enacted.

echoes.text: Yes, they spoke against God. They said, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Behold, he struck the rock, so that waters gushed out, and streams overflowed. Can he give bread also? Will he provide flesh for his people?” Therefore Yahweh heard, and was angry. A fire was kindled against Jacob, anger also went up against Israel, because they didn’t believe in God, and didn’t trust in his salvation. Yet he commanded the skies above, and opened the doors […]
echoes.note: 'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?' Israel's doubting question is answered as God rains down bread and the people 'ate and were well filled.' Matthew's 'They all ate, and were filled' echoes this wilderness-banquet vindication of God's power to feed in the desert.

echoes.text: The eyes of all wait for you. You give them their food in due season. You open your hand, and satisfy the desire of every living thing.
echoes.note: 'You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing.' The theme of God satisfying the hungry crowd to the full coheres with Jesus blessing and distributing until all are filled.

echoes.text: I will abundantly bless her provision. I will satisfy her poor with bread.
echoes.note: 'I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread.' A faint thematic resonance with the abundant provision of bread to the multitude in Zion's hope.

echoes.text: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.” Elisha said to her, “What shall I do for you? Tell me: what do you have in the house?” She said, “Your handmaid has nothing in the house, except a pot of oil.” Then he said, “Go, borrow containers from of all your […]
echoes.note: Elisha's multiplication of the widow's oil, where a small supply expands to abundance with a surplus, is a sibling miracle to the loaf-multiplication and reinforces the Elisha-as-feeder/provider background.

echoes.text: At meal time Boaz said to her, “Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar.” She sat beside the reapers, and they reached her parched grain, and she ate, and was satisfied, and left some of it.
echoes.note: Boaz feeds Ruth so that 'she ate and was satisfied, and had some left over' — the same pattern of eating to the full with a remainder. A faint verbal-thematic parallel to the satisfied crowd and twelve leftover baskets.

echoes.text: As soon as you have come into the city, you shall immediately find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he come, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you shall find him.”
echoes.note: Samuel 'blesses' before the people eat at the sacrificial meal; the gesture of a prophet looking up and blessing the food before distribution faintly echoes the prophetic table-blessing convention.

pericopes.text: Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away. After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone. But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary. In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.” Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased. Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”

echoes.text: He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea.
echoes.note: 'Who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea' (LXX: walks on the sea as on dry ground). Jesus walking on the sea enacts a divine prerogative ascribed to God alone in Job; the act itself is a theophanic self-disclosure.

echoes.text: Your way was through the sea; your paths through the great waters. Your footsteps were not known.
echoes.note: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen.' God's path through the sea (in the Exodus retelling) underlies Jesus' way across the waters; the psalm makes sea-treading a uniquely divine mode of salvation.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: Jesus' self-identification, 'It is I' (egō eimi), reprises the divine self-naming 'I AM' given to Moses at the bush. Combined with the sea-walking theophany and 'Don't be afraid,' the egō eimi reads as a claim to the divine name and presence.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.
echoes.note: 'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you'; and Isa 43:10-13, 25; 51:12 repeatedly pair the divine 'I am he' (egō eimi) with 'do not fear.' Jesus' 'It is I; don't be afraid' fuses the reassurance-formula and the divine self-identification of Deutero-Isaiah amid the waters.

echoes.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; These see Yahweh’s works, and his wonders in the deep. For he commands, and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up its waves. They mount up to the sky; they go down again to the depths. Their soul melts away because of trouble. They reel back and forth, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end. Then they cry to Yahweh in their trouble, and he brings them out of their […]
echoes.note: Those who go down to the sea, caught in a storm with waves mounting, cry to the LORD, who stills the storm to a whisper and brings them to harbor. Matthew's contrary wind, distressed boat, terror, cry, and the ceasing of the wind map onto this sea-rescue psalm where the LORD masters the deep.

echoes.text: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck! I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
echoes.note: 'Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck... I sink in deep mire.' Peter's sinking cry, 'Lord, save me!' echoes the psalmist's drowning plea, casting Peter's near-drowning in the language of the lament for rescue from the waters.

echoes.text: He sent from on high. He took me. He drew me out of many waters.
echoes.note: 'He reached down from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters.' Jesus stretching out his hand to seize the sinking Peter enacts the divine rescue-from-the-waters gesture of this royal thanksgiving.

echoes.text: Stretch out your hand from above, rescue me, and deliver me out of great waters, out of the hands of foreigners;
echoes.note: 'Stretch out your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from the many waters.' A close verbal sibling to Ps 18:16 reinforcing the 'outstretched hand from the waters' rescue motif applied to Peter.

echoes.text: You rule the pride of the sea. When its waves rise up, you calm them.
echoes.note: 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them.' The stilling of the contrary wind when Jesus enters the boat enacts the Creator's sovereignty over the sea's tumult ascribed to the LORD.

echoes.text: “Have you entered into the springs of the sea? Or have you walked in the recesses of the deep?
echoes.note: 'Have you... walked in the recesses of the deep?' God's challenge to Job implies that traversing the deep belongs to God alone; Jesus' walking on the sea answers the rhetorical question in his own person.

echoes.text: You trampled the sea with your horses, churning mighty waters.
echoes.note: 'You trampled the sea with your horses, the surging of mighty waters.' The theophanic image of God treading the sea in the prophet's vision faintly underlies the sea-walking theophany.

echoes.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all the night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. The children of Israel went into the midst of the sea on the dry ground, and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left.
echoes.note: The Red Sea crossing — God making a way through the sea by night to deliver his people from fear — is the Exodus archetype standing behind the night-time mastery of the waters and the deliverance of the disciples; Ps 77 explicitly reads the sea-treading as Exodus.

echoes.text: He answered, Look, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are unharmed; and the aspect of the fourth is like a son of the gods.
echoes.note: The disciples' confession 'You are truly the Son of God' has a faint resonance with the recognition that one 'like a son of the gods' walks unharmed amid a deadly element; the title here, however, is more securely rooted in Matthew's own Christology (3:17; 16:16).

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The boat's confession 'You are truly the Son of God' draws on the royal-messianic sonship of the enthronement psalm, the same Scripture echoed at Jesus' baptism (3:17). The post-theophany worship names Jesus in Davidic-divine sonship terms.

echoes.text: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
echoes.note: The Spirit/wind of God hovering over the face of the waters at creation provides a faint backdrop: the one who walks upon the deep and masters the wind exercises the Creator's authority over the primordial waters.

pericopes.text: When they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. When the people of that place recognized him, they sent into all that surrounding region, and brought to him all who were sick, and they begged him that they might just touch the fringe of his garment. As many as touched it were made whole.

echoes.note: Beyond the three-days motif, Jonah's preaching of repentance to Nineveh stands behind the rebuke of 'this generation': a pagan city repented at a sign, but the present generation will receive only Jonah's sign. Thematic coherence with Matthew's wider Jonah typology.

echoes.text: “But draw near here, you sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the prostitute.
echoes.note: 'An evil and adulterous generation' draws on the prophetic idiom of Israel as an adulterous people ('sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer'), where covenant infidelity is figured as adultery/idolatry.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness;
echoes.note: The 'adulterous generation' charge echoes Hosea's sustained metaphor of faithless Israel as an adulterous spouse. Faint and one of several possible prophetic backgrounds.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
echoes.note: Demanding 'a sign from heaven' to validate Jesus inverts the Deuteronomic test of a prophet: a sign alone does not authenticate; covenant fidelity does. Conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?”
echoes.note: The Pharisees and Sadducees 'testing' Jesus by demanding a sign recalls Israel testing the LORD at Massah; the verb of testing carries the wilderness-rebellion overtone. Faint thematic.

pericopes.text: The disciples came to the other side and had forgotten to take bread. Jesus said to them, “Take heed and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” They reasoned among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” Jesus, perceiving it, said, “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, ‘because you have brought no bread?’ Don’t you yet perceive, neither remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up? Nor the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up? How is it that you don’t perceive that I didn’t speak to you concerning bread? But beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Then they understood that he didn’t tell them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

echoes.text: “‘Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even the first day you shall put away yeast out of your houses, for whoever eats leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.
echoes.note: The warning against 'the yeast/leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees' trades on the Passover/Unleavened Bread association of leaven with pervasive corruption that must be purged from the house. The metaphor's intelligibility presupposes this cultic background.

echoes.text: Unleavened bread shall be eaten throughout the seven days; and no leavened bread shall be seen with you, neither shall yeast be seen with you, in all your borders.
echoes.note: Reinforces the leaven-as-defilement imagery from the Feast of Unleavened Bread, where no leaven may be seen within the borders. Secondary to Exodus 12:15.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: The disciples' anxiety over bread and the rebuke 'you of little faith' recall Israel's distrust over daily provision in the wilderness, where the LORD rained bread from heaven to test their faith. Thematic coherence with Matthew's two feeding miracles invoked here.

echoes.text: but now we have lost our appetite. There is nothing at all except this manna to look at.” The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like the appearance of bdellium. The people went around, gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in mortars, and boiled it in pots, and made cakes of it. Its taste was like the taste of fresh oil. When the dew fell on the camp in the night, the manna fell on it.
echoes.note: The grumbling-over-food motif behind the disciples' worry resonates with Israel's complaint about manna; the contrast is between miraculous provision already witnessed and persistent forgetfulness. Faint.

pericopes.text: Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” They said, “Some say John the Baptizer, some, Elijah, and others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. I also tell you that you are Peter,and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hadeswill not prevail against it. I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.” Then he commanded the disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus the Christ.

echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: 'I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven... bind... loose' draws on the Eliakim oracle: 'I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open and none shut, shut and none open.' The key-of-stewardship granting authority to admit and exclude is the controlling image. Strong verbal and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?
echoes.note: 'The gates of Hades will not prevail' echoes 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you?' — the underworld as a fortified city whose gates symbolize the realm and power of death. Verbal touchpoint ('gates' of death/Hades).

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, Yahweh. See my affliction by those who hate me, and lift me up from the gates of death;
echoes.note: 'You who lift me up from the gates of death' supplies the same 'gates of death/Hades' idiom; deliverance from death's gates is precisely what Jesus' resurrection-grounded assembly will enjoy. Reinforces Job 38:17.

echoes.text: I said, “In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol. I am deprived of the residue of my years.”
echoes.note: Hezekiah's 'I shall go through the gates of Sheol' offers another close instance of the 'gates of the underworld' figure standing behind 'gates of Hades.'

echoes.text: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?
echoes.note: Peter's confession of Jesus as 'the Son of the living God' employs the covenant title 'the living God,' contrasting Israel's God with lifeless idols. The epithet recurs across the OT and grounds the confession in covenant monotheism.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'Sons of the living God' supplies the specific collocation 'living God' with sonship language that Peter's title brings together. Faint verbal overlap.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The popular identification of Jesus with Elijah ('some say... Elijah') depends on Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, an expectation Matthew engages elsewhere (11:14; 17:10-13).

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'On this rock I will build' may play on the 'rock from which you were hewn' (Abraham) imagery for the founding of the people of God on a chosen progenitor. Disputed; rock-foundation imagery is diffuse.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah being named among the guesses for Jesus' identity reflects his stature as the suffering, rejected prophet of judgment on Jerusalem; the allusion is to Jeremiah as a prophetic type rather than a specific text. Faint.

pericopes.text: From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up. Peter took him aside, and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” But he turned, and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.”

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'must... suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Suffering Servant who was despised, rejected, and stricken; the divine necessity ('must') of the Messiah's suffering reflects Matthew's Servant Christology.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'The third day be raised up' echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him,' the OT text most plausibly underlying the recurrent 'third day' resurrection formula.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' as a rebuke of the adversary echoes 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan' — Peter unwittingly plays the satan/accuser opposing God's purpose. Thematic and verbal resonance with the rebuke-of-Satan formula.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The figure of 'the satan' as the adversary who would divert God's servant from his path stands behind naming Peter 'Satan' for setting his mind on human things. Faint, conceptual.

pericopes.text: Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life? For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to everyone according to his deeds. Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste of death, until they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.”

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'He will render to everyone according to his deeds' closely cites 'to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you render to a man according to his work.' Near-verbatim formula of eschatological recompense; the clearest source-citation in the chapter.

echoes.text: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?
echoes.note: Parallel near-verbatim source for 'render to everyone according to his deeds': 'will he not repay each according to his work?' Matthew's wording fuses the Psalms and Proverbs recompense formula. Together with Psalm 62:12 this is a high-confidence citation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels... coming in his Kingdom' draws directly on the 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to whom dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom are given. Strong verbal ('Son of Man,' 'coming,' 'kingdom,' 'glory') and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: 'What will a man give in exchange for his life?' echoes 'no man can ransom his brother or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly.' The futility of buying back one's soul with wealth is the shared logic, sharpened by 'gains the whole world but forfeits his life.'

echoes.text: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
echoes.note: 'Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life' resonates with the rhetorical 'what will a man give in exchange for his life?' — the supreme value placed on life. Faint, possibly coincidental proverbial overlap.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'With his angels' / 'in the glory of his Father' resonates with 'the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him,' a theophany of the divine coming with the heavenly host that informs the parousia imagery.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' is a further OT recompense text reinforcing the Psalm 62 / Proverbs 24 citation of judgment according to works.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical 'he will repay to man according to his deeds' continues the Second Temple development of the recompense formula behind 16:27, attesting the currency of the idea in Jesus' milieu.

echoes.text: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
echoes.note: Individual accountability — each judged for his own conduct, 'the soul who sins shall die' — undergirds the 'render to everyone according to his deeds' principle. Faint, conceptual.

pericopes.text: After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him. Peter answered, and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.
echoes.note: The glory of the LORD settles on Sinai and the cloud covers it 'six days,' and on the seventh day God calls Moses out of the cloud. Matthew's opening 'after six days' plus the high mountain, the cloud, and the divine voice from the cloud reproduce this Sinai theophany sequence with striking specificity; the strongest structural anchor for the new-Sinai reading.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him. Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses spoke to them. […]
echoes.note: Coming down Sinai Moses' face shone (LXX dedoxastai) so that he had to veil it. Jesus' face 'shone like the sun' figurally surpasses Moses: where Moses reflected borrowed glory, Jesus radiates his own. The shining-face motif is a deliberate Mosaic borrowing.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'You are my Son' — the royal-enthronement decree. The heavenly voice 'This is my beloved Son' weaves the Davidic/messianic sonship of Ps 2 into the composite oracle; widely recognized as one of the three texts fused at the baptism and transfiguration.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'My chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him.' 'In whom I am well pleased' (eudokesa) echoes the Servant designation. The voice fuses royal Son (Ps 2) with Servant (Isa 42), framing the glorified Son as the suffering Servant on the way to the cross.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will raise up for you a prophet like me... you shall listen to him' (autou akousesthe). The command 'Listen to him' is verbatim from the prophet-like-Moses promise; appended to the voice it identifies Jesus as the eschatological prophet, the climactic clause of the composite oracle.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: Elijah sent before the great Day. His appearance with Moses on the mountain anticipates the Elijah-must-come discussion of vv.10-13 and frames the scene eschatologically.

echoes.text: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. Yahweh showed him all the land of Gilead, to Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, to the western sea, and the south, and the Plain of the valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, to Zoar. Yahweh said to him, “This is the land which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to […]
echoes.note: Moses ascends a high mountain (Nebo), is shown the land, and dies in a manner the LORD conceals; later tradition held God buried/took him. His reappearance pairs with Elijah (who never died, 2 Kings 2) as the two who left earth extraordinarily, hence fit witnesses of glory.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Elijah taken up to heaven in a whirlwind/chariot of fire — never tasting death. His presence on the mountain trades on the tradition of his heavenly translation, qualifying him to appear in glory alongside Moses.

echoes.text: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle. Moses wasn’t able to enter into the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud stayed on it, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.
echoes.note: The bright cloud (the kabod/Shekinah) overshadowing and filling the tent of meeting. 'A bright cloud overshadowed them' (episkiazo) draws on the tabernacle-cloud of divine presence, reinforced by Peter's wish to build three skenai (tents).

echoes.text: You shall dwell in booths seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths, that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.’”
echoes.note: The Feast of Booths (Sukkot): dwelling in tents to recall the wilderness. Peter's instinct to erect three skenai may evoke the festival of God dwelling with Israel; some read an eschatological-ingathering nuance. Faint and disputed.
