echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'The wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky... like the stars.' The luminous transformation ('face shone like the sun,' garments 'white as the light') draws on apocalyptic resurrection-glory imagery, anticipating the risen state foreshadowed in v.9.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The Son of Man coming with clouds. The cloud plus the Son-of-Man saying in v.9 may activate the Danielic glorification motif; faint here, stronger elsewhere in Matthew.

echoes.text: He said, “Please show me your glory.” He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.” He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.” Yahweh also said, “Behold, there is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. It will happen, while my glory passes by, that I will put you in a cleft of […]
echoes.note: Moses asks to see God's glory and is hidden in the rock as the glory passes. The disciples falling on their faces in terror at the glory echoes the dangerous holiness of seeing divine glory on Sinai. Thematic.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'Your son, your only/beloved son.' The 'beloved Son' (agapetos, the LXX rendering of yahid in the Aqedah) may carry an Isaac-typology overtone of the beloved son led toward sacrifice, dovetailing with the passion predictions framing the chapter.

echoes.text: God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and his praise filled the earth. His splendor is like the sunrise. Rays shine from his hand, where his power is hidden.
echoes.note: God comes in radiance, 'his brightness was like the light, rays flashing from his hand.' The garments 'white as the light' may draw on theophanic light-imagery. Faint.

pericopes.text: As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, “Don’t tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” His disciples asked him, saying, “Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things, but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.” Then the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptizer.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: 'I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day... he will turn (restore) the hearts.' The scribal expectation 'Elijah must come first' and Jesus' 'Elijah indeed comes first and will restore all things' (apokatastesei panta) directly cite this oracle; identified with John the Baptist.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'I send my messenger to prepare the way before me.' The forerunner role attached to Elijah/John builds on the messenger of Mal 3, the companion text to 4:5 in the prophecy of the coming Day.

echoes.text: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.
echoes.note: Of Elijah: 'destined... to calm the wrath of God, to turn the heart of the parent to the child, and to restore (katastesai) the tribes of Jacob.' This Second Temple text supplies the 'restore all things' language and shows the developed Elijah-redivivus expectation Jesus engages. Deuterocanonical.

echoes.text: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!” When he saw that, he arose, and went for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die, and said, […]
echoes.note: Jezebel seeks Elijah's life and he flees; 'they did to him whatever they wanted' may echo the suffering/persecution of the historical Elijah, mapped onto John (and onward to the Son of Man). Thematic-typological.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: 'They did to him whatever they wanted to' — the maltreatment of the Elijah-figure (John) parallels Israel's rejection of the prophets generally; faint verbal, strong thematic continuity with the persecuted-prophet motif.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: 'Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them' pivots to the Servant's rejection and suffering, linking the fate of the forerunner to the passion. Faint here, the Servant frame recurs in the chapter.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'Until the Son of Man has risen from the dead' uses the Danielic Son-of-Man title; the resurrection-secret links glory to vindication. Title-level echo.

pericopes.text: When they came to the multitude, a man came to him, kneeling down to him, saying, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is epileptic, and suffers grievously; for he often falls into the fire, and often into the water. So I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.” Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation! How long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you? Bring him here to me.” Jesus rebuked him, the demon went out of him, and the boy was cured from that hour. Then the disciples came to Jesus privately, and said, “Why weren’t we able to cast it out?” He said to them, “Because of your unbelief. For most certainly I tell you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you. But this kind doesn’t go out except by prayer and fasting.”

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'A perverse and crooked generation' (genea skolia kai diestrammene, LXX). Jesus' rebuke 'O faithless and perverse generation' (genea apistos kai diestrammene) borrows the Song of Moses' indictment of the wilderness generation, casting the unbelieving crowd as the new faithless Israel.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? and how long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?
echoes.note: 'How long will this people despise me? How long will they refuse to believe (ou pisteuousin) in me?' The doubled 'How long...?' lament over unbelief and 'faithless' echoes God's wilderness frustration with Israel through Moses. Strengthens the Moses-typology of the descent from the mountain.

echoes.text: He said, “I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end will be; for they are a very perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness.
echoes.note: 'They are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faithfulness.' Continues the Song-of-Moses language behind 'faithless and perverse generation'; reinforces the Deut 32 frame.

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain.' The proverb of removing a mountain by God's power/Spirit may stand behind 'you will tell this mountain, Move from here.' Thematic.

echoes.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain.
echoes.note: 'Every mountain and hill made low.' The mountain-moving saying may draw on eschatological mountain-leveling imagery as a figure of God overcoming all obstacles. Faint.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The righteous shall live by his faith.' The whole pericope's contrast of unbelief versus mustard-seed faith resonates with the prophetic valuation of faith, though no verbal borrowing. Thematic.

echoes.text: because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice;
echoes.note: The wilderness generation tested God ten times and did not believe; 'How long will I bear with you?' echoes the divine forbearance toward a faithless people. Faint thematic.

pericopes.text: While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered up into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and the third day he will be raised up.” They were exceedingly sorry.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man is about to be delivered up (paradidotai) into the hands of men, and they will kill him.' The passive 'delivered up' echoes the Servant who 'was handed over for our sins' (Isa 53:6, 12 LXX paredothe), framing the death as the Servant's vicarious handing-over.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'His soul was delivered up to death... he was numbered with transgressors.' The being 'delivered into the hands of men' draws on the Servant's surrender; the divine-passive points to God's purpose behind the betrayal.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'On the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' 'The third day he will be raised up' may draw on this resurrection-on-the-third-day text, a candidate source for the early 'third day' formula.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The 'Son of Man' title carries the Danielic vindicated-one freight; the prediction couples humiliation with resurrection-vindication. Title-level echo.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: 'Three days and three nights'; Matthew elsewhere makes the Jonah-resurrection link explicit (12:40), so the 'third day' here may carry a faint Jonah resonance. Very faint.

pericopes.text: When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma coins came to Peter, and said, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?” He said, “Yes.” When he came into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive toll or tribute? From their children, or from strangers?” Peter said to him, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him, “Therefore the children are exempt. But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin.Take that, and give it to them for me and you.”

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them. They shall give this, everyone who passes over to those who are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary; (the shekel is twenty gerahs;) half a shekel for an offering to […]
echoes.note: The half-shekel atonement-money each Israelite pays for the service of the sanctuary. The didrachma (= the temple tax, the equivalent of the half-shekel) collected in v.24 is this Mosaic census/sanctuary levy; the whole exchange presupposes Exod 30 as the legal background of the temple tax.

echoes.text: The silver of those who were numbered of the congregation was one hundred talents, and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary: a beka a head, that is, half a shekel, after the shekel of the sanctuary, for everyone who passed over to those who were numbered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty men.
echoes.note: The reckoning of the half-shekel (a beka) from each man counted. Confirms the fixed temple contribution behind the 'didrachma' question; the Pentateuchal institution of the sanctuary tax.

echoes.text: Also we made ordinances for ourselves, to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God; for the show bread, and for the continual meal offering, and for the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, for the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.
echoes.note: The post-exilic community pledges a third/(later half-)shekel yearly 'for the service of the house of our God.' Documents the developing annual temple-tax practice the collectors enforce, the contemporary form of the Exodus levy.

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'The earth is the LORD's and its fullness.' Jesus' logic that the king's own children are free, and the provision of the coin from the sea/fish, plays on God's ownership of all things — the Son not being a stranger in his Father's house (the temple). Thematic.

echoes.text: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, then where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is the respect due me? Says Yahweh of Armies to you, priests, who despise my name. You say, ‘How have we despised your name?’
echoes.note: 'A son honors his father.' The Father-Son / sons-of-the-king argument that the children are exempt may resonate with the sonship-over-against-temple logic; Jesus as Son is not a stranger to the Father's house. Faint.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: A fish as divine instrument/provision at sea; the miraculous coin-bearing fish may carry a faint resonance of God's sovereign use of the sea-creature, though no verbal link. Very faint.

pericopes.text: In that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?” Jesus called a little child to himself, and set him in their midst, and said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn, and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child, the same is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven. Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me,

echoes.text: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
echoes.note: The reversal at the heart of the saying — 'whoever humbles himself... is the greatest' — restates the wisdom maxim that pride brings a person low while the humble in spirit obtain honor. The exaltation-through-humility logic is a sustained sapiential pattern.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility.
echoes.note: 'Before honor is humility' supplies the proverbial frame for greatness defined by lowering oneself; recurs at Prov 18:12, reinforcing thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me.
echoes.note: The image of becoming 'as little children' before God resonates with the psalmist's quieted, weaned-child posture of trust and renounced ambition. Verbal overlap is thin, so the link is thematic/figural rather than lexical.

echoes.text: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat; The calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them.
echoes.note: 'A little child shall lead them' offers an eschatological valorization of the child as figure of the messianic order, a possible backdrop to the child set 'in their midst' as model of the kingdom. Faint and disputed.

pericopes.text: but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a huge millstone should be hung around his neck, and that he should be sunk in the depths of the sea. “Woe to the world because of occasions of stumbling! For it must be that the occasions come, but woe to that person through whom the occasion comes!

echoes.text: “‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The skandalon ('stumbling block') vocabulary draws on the Holiness Code prohibition against placing a stumbling block before the blind; Matthew moralizes the cultic-ethical image into causing 'these little ones' to fall.

echoes.text: Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land!
echoes.note: The 'Woe' (ouai) oracle form against the world and against the agent of stumbling reproduces the prophetic woe-cry, of which Isaiah 5 is the paradigmatic chain. Formal echo, not verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot; and you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
echoes.note: Being 'sunk in the depths of the sea' may invert Micah's image of God casting sins into the depths of the sea: here it is the offender, not the sin, that is drowned. Suggestive but uncertain.

echoes.text: It shall be, when you have made an end of reading this book, that you shall bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of the Euphrates: and you shall say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise again because of the evil that I will bring on her; and they shall be weary. Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.
echoes.note: A stone bound to a scroll and sunk in the Euphrates as a sign of irreversible sinking judgment ('thus shall Babylon sink') parallels the millstone-and-sea image of inescapable doom. Contested.

pericopes.text: If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off, and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life maimed or crippled, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into the eternal fire. If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out, and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into the Gehennaof fire.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The 'eternal fire' / 'Gehenna of fire' draws directly on Isaiah's closing vision of the dead whose 'worm shall not die, nor their fire be quenched' — the classic source-image for unquenchable eschatological fire, set in the valley outside Jerusalem.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.
echoes.note: Gehenna = the Valley of (the son of) Hinnom (ge-hinnom), where children were burned at Topheth; Jeremiah's condemnation of that valley made it the topographic seed of the later place-of-fiery-judgment.

echoes.text: and have built the high places of Baal, to burn their sons in the fire for burnt offerings to Baal; which I didn’t command, nor spoke it, neither came it into my mind: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.
echoes.note: Jeremiah renames Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom 'the Valley of Slaughter,' a judgment site; reinforces the Gehenna toponym's punitive force behind 'cast into the eternal fire.'

echoes.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
echoes.note: Josiah's defilement of Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom contributes to the valley's afterlife as a place of refuse and judgment underlying Gehenna. Background rather than verbal source.

pericopes.text: See that you don’t despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost.

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.
echoes.note: 'Their angels always see the face of my Father' presumes the guardian-angel motif of 'he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.'

echoes.text: and the next to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom),
echoes.note: Angels who 'see the face' of the Father use the royal-court idiom for the highest courtiers — those who 'saw the king's face' and had access to his presence (cf. the seven princes who saw Ahasuerus's face). The little ones' angels hold rank in the heavenly court.

echoes.text: and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and five men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe, the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the city.
echoes.note: 'Those who saw the king's face' as a class of privileged courtiers parallels the access-language applied to the angels. Idiomatic background, contested.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: V.11 ('the Son of Man came to save that which was lost') directly evokes the shepherd-God's oracle 'I will seek the lost, and bring back the strayed' — and prepares the lost-sheep parable that follows.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man' in v.11 ultimately reaches back to Daniel's heavenly figure, though here in a saving rather than enthroned register. Faint at this point.

echoes.text: I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and go in before the glory of the Holy One.”
echoes.note: Raphael as one of the angels who 'stand and enter before the glory of the Lord' offers a Second Temple analogue to the angels who 'always see the face' of the Father. Deuterocanonical background, contested.

pericopes.text: “What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray? If he finds it, most certainly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray. Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: The shepherd who leaves the flock to 'seek that which has gone astray' and rejoices to find it directly enacts God's oracle: 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost, and bring back the strayed.' High volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the precise pairing of straying and being sought that the parable dramatizes.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical statement of the sheep-going-astray motif underlying the one that 'goes astray.'

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: The oracle against shepherds who scatter and fail to seek the flock, with God's promise to gather the strays, shares the shepherd/lost-sheep field. Contributory background.

echoes.text: My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: 'My sheep wandered through all the mountains... and none searched or sought' supplies the specific detail of the shepherd going 'to the mountains' to seek the strayed one.

pericopes.text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother. But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
echoes.note: 'Go, show him his fault between you and him alone' enacts the Holiness Code command 'you shall surely reprove your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him' — private, loving rebuke that does not let sin fester into hatred.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: 'At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established' is a near-verbatim citation of the Deuteronomic law of evidence ('on the testimony of two or three witnesses a matter shall be established'). The clearest formula-level borrowing in the chapter.

echoes.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
echoes.note: The two-or-three-witnesses standard is doubled in Deuteronomy's capital-case law ('on the evidence of two or three witnesses he shall be put to death'), reinforcing the juridical weight of the procedure Jesus prescribes for the assembly.

echoes.text: Reprove a friend; it may be he did it not: And if he did something, that he may do it no more. Reprove your neighbor; it may be he said it not: And if he has said it, that he may not say it again. Reprove a friend; for many times there is slander: And trust not every word. There is one that slips, and not from the heart: And who is he that has not sinned with his tongue? Reprove your neighbor before you threaten him; And give place to the law of the Most […]
echoes.note: 'Question a friend, perhaps he did not do it... reprove a neighbor before you threaten him' is the closest Second Temple parallel to the graduated, presumption-of-innocence rebuke of Mt 18:15. Deuterocanonical wisdom on fraternal correction.

pericopes.text: Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven. Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in their midst.”

echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: Binding/loosing as authoritative juridical decision shares the open/shut imagery of the 'key of the house of David... he shall open and none shut.' The connection is firmer at Mt 16:19; here it is reasserted communally and is more diffuse.

echoes.text: Then those who feared Yahweh spoke one with another; and Yahweh listened, and heard, and a book of memory was written before him, for those who feared Yahweh, and who honored his name.
echoes.note: 'Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst' resonates with those who feared the Lord speaking together while 'the Lord took note and a book of remembrance was written' — the divine presence attending the small gathered company. Contested.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: The 'two or three' of v.20 re-uses the witness-count of v.16, transposing the legal quorum into a quorum of prayer and presence. The verbal carryover from the Deuteronomic formula is deliberate.

pericopes.text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.

echoes.text: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
echoes.note: 'Until seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven') deliberately reverses Lamech's boast 'If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold': the same numbers that measured escalating vengeance now measure limitless forgiveness. The LXX of Gen 4:24 reads hebdomekontakis hepta, matching Jesus' phrasing.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron;
echoes.note: Peter's 'seven times' as a presumed limit may echo the prophetic 'for three transgressions and for four' idiom of a fixed tally of offenses before judgment; Jesus dissolves the tally. Faint formal parallel.

pericopes.text: Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who wanted to reconcile accounts with his servants. When he had begun to reconcile, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. The servant therefore fell down and kneeled before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’ The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt. “But that servant went out, and found one of his fellow servants, who owed him one hundred denarii,and he grabbed him, and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’ “So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’ He would not, but went and cast him into prison, until he should pay back that which was due. So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told to their lord all that was done. Then his lord called him in, and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt, because you begged me. Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’ His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors, until he should pay all that was due to him. So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]
echoes.note: The parable's logic — God forgives the one who forgives, and withholds mercy from the unmerciful — is the narrative form of Sirach's teaching: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' The closest extracanonical parallel to the whole pericope.

echoes.text: At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts. This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.
echoes.note: The king who 'releases' (aphiemi) his servant and 'forgives the debt' enacts the sabbatical-year release of debts (shemittah): every creditor shall release what he has lent. The unforgiving servant violates the release he himself received.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave.
echoes.note: The command to sell the debtor 'with his wife and children' reflects the legal reality of debt-slavery regulated in the Jubilee laws ('if your brother becomes poor and sells himself to you'), the very bondage the king's compassion suspends.

echoes.text: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”
echoes.note: A creditor coming to seize the debtor's children as slaves (the widow's plea to Elisha) supplies the social backdrop for selling the man 'with his wife, his children, and all that he had.'

echoes.text: Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children. Behold, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters have been brought into bondage. Neither is it in our power to help it; for other men have our fields and our vineyards.”
echoes.note: The outcry that 'we are forcing our sons and daughters to be slaves' to pay debts parallels the parable's seizure of family for an unpayable obligation. Contributory social context.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered' is the proverbial kernel of the parable: the servant who refuses his fellow's plea forfeits the mercy he had begged and received.

echoes.text: Whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker. He who is glad at calamity shall not be unpunished.
echoes.note: 'He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker; he who is glad at calamity shall not go unpunished' supports the measure-for-measure judgment on the merciless servant. Faint.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's counsel to the king to 'break off your sins by showing mercy to the oppressed' links royal forgiveness with the showing of mercy demanded of the forgiven — a possible backdrop to the king/mercy frame. Contested.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee, and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan. Great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there.

echoes.text: The children of Israel traveled, and encamped in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho.
echoes.note: The setting 'beyond the Jordan' in the region of Judea/Perea uses the standard wilderness-itinerary formula for Israel encamped 'beyond the Jordan' opposite Jericho; faint geographic resonance only.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: Jesus healing the great multitudes who follow him faintly recalls the eschatological healing of Isaiah's highway-of-the-redeemed; thematic, not verbal.

pericopes.text: Pharisees came to him, testing him, and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” He answered, “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall join to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?’ So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” They asked him, “Why then did Moses command us to give her a bill of divorce, and divorce her?” He said to them, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so. I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her when she is divorced commits adultery.”

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'He who made them from the beginning made them male and female' verbatim cites Genesis 1:27 ('male and female created he them'); explicit appeal to creation order as the warrant against divorce.

echoes.text: He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them “Adam”.
echoes.note: Genesis 5:2 repeats 'male and female created he them, and blessed them'; the doublet reinforces the 'from the beginning' creation argument and may stand behind Jesus' formulation alongside 1:27.

echoes.text: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
echoes.note: 'For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall join to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh' is a verbatim quotation of Genesis 2:24, the foundational one-flesh text.

echoes.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house.
echoes.note: The Pharisees' 'Moses commanded us to give her a bill of divorce' directly cites the Mosaic divorce permission of Deuteronomy 24:1 ('let him write her a bill of divorcement'); the crux of the dispute.

echoes.text: If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, who took her to be his wife; her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before Yahweh. You shall not cause the land to sin, which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
echoes.note: The full Deuteronomic divorce ordinance (vv.1-4, the prohibition of remarrying a twice-divorced wife) frames Jesus' redefinition of remarriage-after-divorce as adultery.

echoes.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For I hate divorce”, says Yahweh, the God of Israel, “and him […]
echoes.note: Malachi's covenant theology of marriage ('the wife of thy youth... did he not make one?... I hate divorce') anticipates Jesus' one-flesh-from-creation argument against putting away a wife.

echoes.text: The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
echoes.note: 'Bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh' establishes the one-flesh unity that 2:24 articulates and Jesus invokes as 'no more two but one flesh.'

echoes.text: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked.
echoes.note: Jesus' explanation that Moses permitted divorce 'because of the hardness of your hearts' draws on the Deuteronomic idiom of the uncircumcised/hardened heart of stubborn Israel.

echoes.text: Circumcise yourselves to Yahweh, and take away the foreskins of your heart, you men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
echoes.note: Prophetic 'hardness of heart' / circumcise-your-heart language underlies Jesus' diagnosis of why the Mosaic concession was given.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise to remove the heart of stone faintly contrasts with the 'hardness of heart' that necessitated the divorce concession 'from the beginning it was not so.'

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: Jesus' charge that remarriage after unlawful divorce 'commits adultery' presupposes the Decalogue prohibition (Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18).

echoes.text: went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah.
echoes.note: 'Male and female' as a fixed creational pair also appears in the ark narrative; faint reinforcement of the binary-pair language Jesus cites.

pericopes.text: His disciples said to him, “If this is the case of the man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” But he said to them, “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”

echoes.text: Neither let the foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people”; neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says Yahweh, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast my covenant: to them I will give in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, […]
echoes.note: 'Eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven's sake' inverts and fulfills Isaiah's promise that faithful eunuchs receive 'a name better than of sons and daughters' within God's house; the strongest scriptural ground for valuing the eunuch in the kingdom.

echoes.text: He who is emasculated by crushing or cutting shall not enter into Yahweh’s assembly.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy bars the emasculated from the assembly of the LORD; Jesus' commendation of voluntary 'eunuchs for the kingdom' figurally reverses that exclusion, echoing the Isaian abrogation.

echoes.text: And happy is the eunuch which has wrought no lawless deed with his hands, Nor imagined wicked things against the Lord; For there will be given him for his faithfulness a peculiar favor, And a lot in the sanctuary of the Lord more delightsome than wife or children.
echoes.note: Wisdom blesses the eunuch 'which hath wrought no iniquity... for unto him shall be given the special gift of faith,' a Second Temple anticipation of the eunuch honored in God's kingdom.

pericopes.text: Then little children were brought to him, that he should lay his hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them. But Jesus said, “Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these.” He laid his hands on them, and departed from there.

echoes.text: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham […]
echoes.note: Jesus laying hands on the children to bless echoes Israel/Jacob laying hands on Ephraim and Manasseh to bless them; patriarchal blessing-by-imposition-of-hands prefigured.

echoes.text: From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength, because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger.
echoes.note: The kingdom belonging to little children resonates with the Psalmist's 'out of the mouth of babes' as the locus of God's praise/strength; thematic only.
echoes.lxxText: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou perfected praise, because of thine enemies; that thou mightest put down the enemy and avenger.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him. Set him before Eleazar the priest, and before all the congregation; and commission him in their sight. You shall give authority to him, that all the congregation of the children of Israel may obey. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before Yahweh. At his word they shall go out, and at his […]
echoes.note: Laying on of hands as a means of transmitting blessing/commission (Moses on Joshua) lies behind the gesture the disciples sought to prevent.

pericopes.text: Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?” He said to him, “Why do you call me good?No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’ ‘Honor your father and mother.’And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?” Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder.
echoes.note: 'You shall not murder' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:13 / Deuteronomy 5:17).

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: 'You shall not commit adultery' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18).

echoes.text: “You shall not steal.
echoes.note: 'You shall not steal' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:15 / Deuteronomy 5:19).

echoes.text: “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: 'You shall not offer false testimony' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:16 / Deuteronomy 5:20).

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you.
echoes.note: 'Honor your father and mother' verbatim from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:12 / Deuteronomy 5:16).

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' is a verbatim quotation of Leviticus 19:18, appended by Jesus as the summary of the second table.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: The whole sequence Jesus recites follows the second-table Decalogue as given in Deuteronomy's repetition; the Matthean order (honor-parents last, plus Lev 19:18) reflects this catechetical cluster.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Keep the commandments' to 'enter into life' echoes Leviticus 18:5, 'which if a man do, he shall live in them'; the Torah principle of life-by-obedience the young man invokes.

echoes.text: It shall be righteousness to us, if we observe to do all this commandment before Yahweh our God, as he has commanded us.”
echoes.note: Doing 'all these commandments' as righteousness/life lies behind the young man's claim to have kept them and the question 'what do I still lack?'

echoes.text: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
echoes.note: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good but God' resonates with the recurrent confession 'the LORD is good' (Ps 118:1; 106:1; 136:1); only God is the source of the predicate 'good.'

echoes.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless.
echoes.note: 'If you want to be perfect (teleios)' echoes the call to Abraham, 'walk before me and be thou perfect/blameless,' the Septuagint sense of wholehearted covenant integrity.

echoes.text: You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: 'You shall be perfect/blameless with the LORD your God' stands behind Jesus' 'if you would be perfect,' framing discipleship as covenantal completeness.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven' enacts 'He that hath pity on the poor lendeth unto the LORD'; almsgiving as deposit with God.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's counsel that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure against the day of necessity' is the closest Second Temple parallel to 'sell what you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.'

echoes.text: Lose your money for a brother and a friend; And let it not rust under the stone to be lost. Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges 'lay up thy treasure according to the commandments... it shall bring thee more profit than gold,' directly paralleling treasure-in-heaven-through-almsgiving.

pericopes.text: Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty. Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.” When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?” Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'With God all things are possible' is the strongest verbal kin to 'Is anything too hard (impossible) for the LORD?' spoken at the promise of Isaac; divine omnipotence over the humanly impossible.

echoes.text: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.
echoes.note: Job's confession 'I know that thou canst do all things, and that no purpose of thine can be withheld' closely matches 'with God all things are possible.'

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'If it be marvelous... should it also be marvelous in mine eyes? saith the LORD' grounds the contrast between what is impossible for men and possible for God in the restoration promise.

echoes.text: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,
echoes.note: 'There is nothing too hard for thee' (cf. 32:27, 'is there any thing too hard for me?') is a near-equivalent declaration of God's unlimited power.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Has Yahweh’s hand grown short? Now you will see whether my word will happen to you or not.”
echoes.note: 'Is the LORD's hand waxed short?' belongs to the same idiom of God overcoming the humanly impossible.

echoes.text: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: The difficulty of the rich entering the kingdom resonates with the Psalmist's verdict that wealth cannot ransom a life; riches as no security before God.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”
echoes.note: The Abraham-Sodom dialogue's confidence in God ('shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?') shares the setting of the same 'too hard for the LORD?' passage Jesus echoes.

pericopes.text: Then Peter answered, “Behold, we have left everything, and followed you. What then will we have?” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive one hundred times, and will inherit eternal life. But many will be last who are first; and first who are last.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: 'When the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging' draws on Daniel's vision of thrones set, the Ancient of Days, and judgment convened; the throne-and-judgment imagery.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man... on the throne of his glory' alludes to the Danielic 'one like a son of man' given dominion and an everlasting kingdom.

echoes.text: until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom.
echoes.note: 'Judgment was given to the saints of the Most High' grounds the disciples' role of sitting in judgment over the twelve tribes.

echoes.text: where the tribes go up, even Yah’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to Yahweh’s name. For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David’s house.
echoes.note: 'There are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David'—Jerusalem as the seat where the tribes are judged—stands behind the twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

echoes.text: They will judge nations, and have dominion over peoples; And the Lord will reign over them for evermore.
echoes.note: 'They shall judge the nations, and have dominion over the peoples' is the Second Temple promise that the righteous will share God's eschatological judging rule, paralleling the disciples on thrones.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'In the regeneration (palingenesia)'—the renewed cosmos—echoes Isaiah's 'I create new heavens and a new earth'; the eschatological re-creation in which the thrones are set.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: 'The new heavens and the new earth which I will make shall remain' reinforces the 'regeneration' framework of the promised renewal.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'Will inherit eternal life' echoes Daniel's resurrection to 'everlasting life,' the OT locus for that phrase informing the disciples' reward.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: 'Many first will be last, and last first' resonates with Hannah's reversal song—the LORD raises the poor from the dust and seats them with princes.

echoes.text: Yahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before. Then came there to him all his brothers, and all his sisters, and all those who had been of his acquaintance before, and ate bread with him in his house. They comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that Yahweh had brought on him. Everyone also gave him a piece of money, and everyone a ring of gold. So Yahweh blessed the […]
echoes.note: The hundredfold restoration to those who left all faintly recalls Job's twofold/restored fortunes after loss; reward-after-renunciation pattern.

echoes.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
echoes.note: Leaving 'houses... father, mother... lands' for Jesus' name's sake to inherit reward retraces Abraham's call to leave country and kindred for a promised inheritance.

pericopes.text: “For the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who was the master of a household, who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. When he had agreed with the laborers for a denariusa day, he sent them into his vineyard. He went out about the third hour,and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. To them he said, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you.’ So they went their way. Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour,and did likewise. About the eleventh hourhe went out, and found others standing idle. He said to them, ‘Why do you stand here all day idle?’ “They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ “He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and you will receive whatever is right.’ When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first.’ “When those who were hired at about the eleventh hour came, they each received a denarius. When the first came, they supposed that they would receive more; and they likewise each received a denarius. When they received it, they murmured against the master of the household, saying, ‘These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!’ “But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree with me for a denarius? Take that which is yours, and go your way. It is my desire to give to this last just as much as to you. Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’ So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The vineyard (ampelon) is the master's estate where laborers are hired; Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard establishes the vineyard as Israel/God's people under his care and reckoning. Matthew reuses this stock symbol (cf. the next parable, 21:33-41, which quotes Isa 5 directly), framing the kingdom under the imagery of God's vineyard.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine/vineyard brought out of Egypt and tended by God is part of the same symbolic field; faint thematic resonance behind the kingdom-as-vineyard image rather than verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates. In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: The Torah commands paying a hired laborer his wages the same day, before sundown: 'When evening had come... pay them their wages' (20:8) directly enacts this hired-laborer wage law, giving the parable its legal verisimilitude and its concern with what is 'right' (dikaion).

echoes.text: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
echoes.note: Parallel wage-law ('the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning'); reinforces the same-day payment background of 20:8.

echoes.text: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing; and he cry to Yahweh against you, and it be sin to you.
echoes.note: 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' (20:15) uses the Semitic idiom of the 'evil eye' (ophthalmos ponēros) for grudging stinginess; Deut 15:9 warns against the eye being 'evil' (begrudging) toward a needy brother — the exact moral idiom Jesus inverts (here it is the workers who begrudge the master's generosity).

echoes.text: Don’t eat the food of him who has a stingy eye, and don’t crave his delicacies:
echoes.note: 'Do not eat the bread of him who has an evil eye' — same 'evil eye'=miserly idiom standing behind 20:15; faint, idiomatic rather than allusive.

echoes.text: He said, “I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim Yahweh’s name before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.”
echoes.note: 'It is my desire to give... Isn't it lawful for me to do what I want with what I own?' (20:14-15) echoes God's sovereign freedom in mercy ('I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious'); thematic, disputed.

echoes.text: When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he fainted, and requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
echoes.note: 'The burden of the day and the scorching heat' (20:12) faintly recalls the scorching east wind/heat motif; very weak, likely just realistic detail of agricultural labor.

pericopes.text: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and will hand him over to the Gentiles to mock, to scourge, and to crucify; and the third day he will be raised up.”

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: The Son of Man 'will be delivered/handed over' (paradothēsetai) to the authorities and Gentiles; paradidōmi is the verb the Greek of Isaiah 53 uses for the Servant being 'handed over' for sins (Isa 53:6,12 LXX), coloring the passion prediction with Servant theology.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: 'to mock, to scourge' (20:19) corresponds to the Servant who gives his back to those who strike and his face to mocking/spitting; the catalog of mistreatment draws on the third Servant Song.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'the third day he will be raised up' (20:19) echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him'; widely read as the scriptural background for the 'third day' resurrection formula.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'the Son of Man' (20:18) carries the Danielic title; here paradoxically the exalted Danielic figure is the one delivered up to death, a Matthean recurrence of the title.

pericopes.text: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, kneeling and asking a certain thing of him. He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand, and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom.” But Jesus answered, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?” They said to him, “We are able.” He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with, but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give; but it is for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: 'the cup that I am about to drink' (20:22) is the prophetic 'cup of wrath/staggering' that Jerusalem drinks (Isa 51:17,22); Jesus takes upon himself the cup of judgment, the dominant OT background for the passion-cup.

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: The cup of foaming wine of God's wrath that the wicked drink to the dregs; supplies the 'cup' = divine judgment imagery behind 20:22-23.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it.
echoes.note: 'Take this cup of the wine of wrath from my hand, and make all the nations drink it' — the cup of wrath passed to the nations; reinforces the cup-of-judgment field Jesus says he must drink.

echoes.text: You have walked in the way of your sister; therefore will I give her cup into your hand. Thus says the Lord Yahweh: You will drink of your sister’s cup, which is deep and large; you will be ridiculed and held in derision; it contains much. You shall be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, with the cup of astonishment and desolation, with the cup of your sister Samaria. You shall even drink it and drain it out, and you shall gnaw the broken pieces of it, […]
echoes.note: The cup of horror and desolation that Jerusalem must drink to the dregs; same cup-of-wrath motif, fainter parallel.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The request to sit at Jesus' right hand and left in his kingdom faintly invokes enthronement-at-the-right-hand language; weak, the verbal contact is only 'right hand.'

echoes.text: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck! I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
echoes.note: The 'baptism' of overwhelming suffering pairs with the cup; the engulfing-waters imagery of the righteous sufferer ('the waters have come up to my neck') is a faint background for being 'baptized' with suffering.

pericopes.text: When the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers. But Jesus summoned them, and said, “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall beyour servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: KEY allusion. 'The Son of Man came... to give his life as a ransom for many' (20:28) compresses the fourth Servant Song: the Servant 'pours out his soul to death' and 'bears the sin of many' (Isa 53:12), making his life an offering (asham, 53:10). 'Give his life' (dounai tēn psychēn) + 'for many' (anti pollōn) maps onto the LXX Servant who is handed over for the 'many' (polloi, Isa 53:11-12). Vicarious, substitutionary death — the figural fulfillment of the Servant.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: Jesus identifies himself as the one who came 'to serve' (diakonēsai); the title 'Son of Man' is overlaid on the exalted 'my Servant' (pais) of Isaiah, framing his whole mission as the Servant of YHWH who suffers and is exalted.

echoes.text: You haven’t strengthened the diseased, neither have you healed that which was sick, neither have you bound up that which was broken, neither have you brought back that which was driven away, neither have you sought that which was lost; but with force and with rigor you have ruled over them.
echoes.note: 'The rulers of the nations lord it over them... it shall not be so among you' (20:25-26) inverts the false shepherds of Israel who 'with force and harshness ruled them'; Jesus contrasts domineering rule with self-giving service in the shepherd-leadership idiom of Ezek 34.

echoes.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem: for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. When Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was yet in Egypt, where he had fled from the presence of king Solomon, and Jeroboam lived in Egypt, and they sent and called him), Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came, and spoke to Rehoboam, saying, “Your father made our yoke grievous: now therefore make you the grievous service of your father, and his heavy yoke which […]
echoes.note: Rehoboam's choice to make his yoke heavier and rule harshly over against serving the people is a narrative type of lordly domination Jesus repudiates; thematic, disputed.

echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I have given Egypt as your ransom, Ethiopia and Seba in your place. Since you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you; therefore I will give people in your place, and nations instead of your life.
echoes.note: God 'gave Egypt as your ransom (LXX allagma/lytron), Cush and Seba in exchange for you... I give people in return for your life'; supplies the ransom-in-exchange-for-life logic of lytron anti pollōn in 20:28.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: Each Israelite gives a 'ransom (lytra) for his life' at the census so that no plague falls; background to the ransom-price (lytron) vocabulary, though Jesus' self-gift transcends the cultic fee.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: 'No man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him, for the redemption of their life is costly'; Jesus' ransom answers the impossibility the psalm laments — faint, ironic counterpoint.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'the Son of Man' (20:28) again carries the Danielic title; the one given dominion and service by the nations is here the one who himself comes to serve, a deliberate Matthean inversion of the Danielic enthronement.

pericopes.text: As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him. Behold, two blind men sitting by the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!” The multitude rebuked them, telling them that they should be quiet, but they cried out even more, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!” Jesus stood still, and called them, and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?” They told him, “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” Jesus, being moved with compassion, touched their eyes; and immediately their eyes received their sight, and they followed him.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped.
echoes.note: 'that our eyes may be opened... their eyes received their sight' (20:33-34) enacts the messianic-age promise 'then the eyes of the blind shall be opened'; the healing functions as a sign that the awaited deliverance has arrived (cf. Matt 11:5).

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant is called 'to open the eyes that are blind'; the blind men's healing realizes the Servant's commission — tying this episode back to the Servant theme just sounded in 20:28.
