echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: 'Son of David, have mercy on us!' (20:30-31) invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's seed; the blind confess Jesus as the messianic Son of David.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The 'shoot from the stump of Jesse' stands behind the Son-of-David / Davidic-messiah confession; thematic support for the title in 20:30.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: 'the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity' — additional eschatological sight-restoration promise reinforcing the Isaianic background of the healing.

echoes.text: Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us, for we have endured much contempt.
echoes.note: 'Have mercy on us (eleēson hēmas), O LORD, have mercy on us' — the doubled cry of the blind (20:30-31) reuses the stock psalmic plea for mercy; idiomatic rather than a specific citation.

pericopes.text: When they drew near to Jerusalem, and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them, and bring them to me. If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and immediately he will send them.” All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “Tell the daughter of Zion, behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” The disciples went, and did just as Jesus commanded them, and brought the donkey and the colt, and laid their clothes on them; and he sat on them. A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road. Others cut branches from the trees, and spread them on the road. The multitudes who went before him, and who followed kept shouting, “Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” When he had come into Jerusalem, all the city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” The multitudes said, “This is the prophet, Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.”

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: Matthew's formula citation (21:4-5) of the prophesied king who comes 'humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.' Matthew uniquely reads the Hebrew parallelism woodenly, producing two animals (donkey and colt), which shapes his narrative of two beasts (21:7).

echoes.text: Behold, Yahweh has proclaimed to the end of the earth, “Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your salvation comes. Behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.’”
echoes.note: The opening of the citation, 'Tell the daughter of Zion, behold...,' is drawn from Isaiah 62:11 ('Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your salvation comes') rather than from Zechariah, whose own opening is 'Rejoice greatly.' Matthew blends Isaiah 62:11 with Zechariah 9:9 into a single quotation.

echoes.text: Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh! Yahweh, we beg you, send prosperity now. Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The crowd's cry (21:9) quotes Psalm 118:25-26: 'Hosanna' transliterates the Hebrew 'hoshia-na' ('save now,' Ps 118:25), and 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD' is verbatim from Ps 118:26 (LXX), a Hallel pilgrimage acclamation.

echoes.text: Then they hurried, and took every man his garment, and put it under him on the top of the stairs, and blew the trumpet, saying, “Jehu is king.”
echoes.note: Spreading garments on the road as an act of royal acclamation: at Jehu's anointing the men 'took every man his garment, and put it under him... and blew the trumpet, saying, Jehu is king.' The crowd's gesture (21:8) enacts an enthronement.

echoes.text: The king said to them, “Take with you the servants of your lord, and cause Solomon my son to ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel. Blow the trumpet, and say, ‘Long live king Solomon!’ Then you shall come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne; for he shall be king in my place. I have appointed him to be prince over Israel and over Judah.” Benaiah the […]
echoes.note: Solomon is mounted on the king's mule and led to be made king amid rejoicing; the royal son of David enters his city riding a humble mount to acclamation, the pattern Jesus' entry evokes.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The repeated acclamation 'son of David' (21:9) invokes the Davidic covenant promise of an everlasting throne to David's offspring, framing Jesus' entry as the coming of the promised Davidic king.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Jacob's blessing on Judah, 'binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine,' was read messianically (donkey + colt motif) in Jewish tradition and may stand behind the donkey imagery alongside Zechariah 9:9.

echoes.text: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. Yahweh has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, Yahweh, is in your midst. You will not be afraid of evil any more.
echoes.note: 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion... the King of Israel, even the LORD, is in your midst': a 'daughter of Zion' oracle announcing the arrival of the divine king, thematically resonant with the entry.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The crowd's identification of Jesus as 'the prophet' (21:11) may echo the promise of a prophet like Moses whom the people must heed.

echoes.text: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.
echoes.note: Simon's entry into the Jerusalem citadel 'with praise and palm branches' provides a Second Temple template for entering the holy city with branches and acclamation, paralleling the multitude cutting and spreading branches (21:8).

echoes.text: Wherefore bearing wands wreathed with leaves, and fair boughs, and palms also, they offered up hymns of thanksgiving to him that had prosperously brought to pass the cleansing of his own place.
echoes.note: At the temple's rededication the people carried 'branches and beautiful boughs and palms' with hymns, a Hanukkah-style festal procession resembling the branch-waving acclamation of Jesus.

pericopes.text: Jesus entered into the temple of God, and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves. He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’but you have made it a den of robbers!” The blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the son of David!” they were indignant, and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of babes and nursing babies you have perfected praise?’” He left them, and went out of the city to Bethany, and lodged there.

echoes.text: even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar; for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
echoes.note: Jesus' citation 'My house shall be called a house of prayer' (21:13) quotes Isaiah 56:7 verbatim, an oracle of the temple as a house of prayer for all peoples; the act of cleansing enacts the eschatological temple ideal.

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'But you have made it a den of robbers' (21:13) quotes Jeremiah 7:11 from the Temple Sermon, where cultic activity masks injustice and invites judgment; the borrowed indictment imports Jeremiah's threat of the temple's destruction.

echoes.text: From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength, because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger.
echoes.note: Jesus answers the indignant priests by citing Psalm 8:2 (21:16): 'Out of the mouth of babes and nursing babies you have perfected praise' (the LXX form 'perfected praise' rather than MT 'established strength'), legitimating the children's Hosanna as God-ordained praise.
echoes.lxxText: Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings hast thou perfected praise, because of thine enemies; that thou mightest put down the enemy and avenger.

echoes.text: Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to Yahweh of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'There shall no longer be a trader (Canaanite/merchant) in the house of the LORD of hosts on that day': the eschatological purging of commerce from the temple is the closest prophetic charter for driving out sellers and money-changers.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap; and he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and […]
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... he will purify the sons of Levi': the messenger/Lord coming to purify temple worship undergirds Jesus' purifying intervention.

echoes.text: David said on that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him get up to the watercourse, and strike the lame and the blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame can’t come into the house.”
echoes.note: The proverb that 'the blind and the lame' shall not come into the house is pointedly reversed: 'the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them' (21:14), so that the excluded are restored at the purified temple.

echoes.text: “‘If he can’t afford a lamb, then he shall bring his trespass offering for that in which he has sinned, two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, to Yahweh; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.
echoes.note: The doves/pigeons sold (21:12) are the offering prescribed for the poor (also Lev 12:8); their sellers' tables being overthrown touches the cult of the poor at the temple.

echoes.text: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house. It grieved me severely: therefore I threw all the household stuff of Tobiah out of the room. Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms: and there brought I again the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense.
echoes.note: Nehemiah's expulsion of Tobiah's goods and his cleansing of the temple chambers offers a precedent of zealous reform purging defilement from the temple precincts.

pericopes.text: Now in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry. Seeing a fig tree by the road, he came to it, and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “Let there be no fruit from you forever!” Immediately the fig tree withered away. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree immediately wither away?” Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, if you have faith, and don’t doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you told this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it would be done. All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

echoes.text: I will utterly consume them, says Yahweh: no grapes shall be on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and the things that I have given them shall pass away from them.
echoes.note: 'When I would gather them... there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf is withered': a judgment oracle on fruitless Israel whose figs and leaves fail, the closest prophetic backdrop to the cursed, leafy-but-fruitless fig tree (21:19).

echoes.text: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree at its first season; but they came to Baal Peor, and consecrated themselves to the shameful thing, and became abominable like that which they loved.
echoes.note: 'I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the first ripe in the fig tree,' followed by their apostasy and barrenness; the fig tree symbolizes Israel's spoiled fruit, the figural sense Matthew gives the withered tree.

echoes.text: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard: There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.
echoes.note: 'There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe fig' — the prophet finding no fruit on Israel, mirroring Jesus hungry and 'finding nothing on it but leaves' (21:19).

echoes.text: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.
echoes.note: The fig tree laid waste and withered in the day of judgment supplies the imagery of a suddenly dried-up fig tree as a sign of devastation.

echoes.text: The fading flower of his glorious beauty, which is on the head of the fertile valley, shall be like the first-ripe fig before the summer; which someone picks and eats as soon as he sees it.
echoes.note: The 'first-ripe fig' that is quickly consumed/fails contributes to the prophetic stock of fig imagery for judgment on Israel.

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain': prophetic precedent for the leveling of a mountain by faith/divine word, paralleling 'tell this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea' (21:21).

echoes.text: Therefore we won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas;
echoes.note: 'Though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea' supplies the very image of a mountain cast into the sea used in Jesus' saying on faith.

echoes.text: For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls:
echoes.note: 'Though the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines' — a fruitless fig tree as a figure of scarcity and testing, a faint resonance.

pericopes.text: When he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?” Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, which if you tell me, I likewise will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John, where was it from? From heaven or from men?” They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will ask us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From men,’ we fear the multitude, for all hold John as a prophet.” They answered Jesus, and said, “We don’t know.” He also said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

echoes.text: He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
echoes.note: The challenge 'By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?' (21:23) faintly recalls the recurring biblical motif of authority contested ('Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?'), the leader's commission questioned by his own people.

echoes.text: They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them, “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them! Why do you lift yourselves up above Yahweh’s assembly?”
echoes.note: Korah's challenge to Moses and Aaron, 'Why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly?,' is a paradigmatic disputing of divinely given authority, distantly resonant with the priests' interrogation.

pericopes.text: But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first, and said, ‘Son, go work today in my vineyard.’ He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind, and went. He came to the second, and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I go, sir,’ but he didn’t go. Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into the Kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you didn’t believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. When you saw it, you didn’t even repent afterward, that you might believe him.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The father's command 'go work today in my vineyard' (21:28) uses the standing prophetic image of the vineyard as Israel and its work as covenant obedience, preparing for the explicit vineyard parable that follows.

echoes.text: But if the wicked turn from all his sins that he has committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. None of his transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him: in his righteousness that he has done he shall live. Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live? But when the righteous […]
echoes.note: The contrast between the son who says no but repents and obeys, and the son who professes obedience but does not act, dramatizes Ezekiel's teaching that the wicked who turns shall live and the righteous who turns away shall die — repentance, not initial profession, is decisive.

echoes.text: I walk in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of justice;
echoes.note: 'John came to you in the way of righteousness' (21:32) employs the Wisdom/sapiential idiom 'the way of righteousness' (cf. Prov 12:28; 21:16) for the path of life that the hearers refused.

pericopes.text: “Hear another parable. There was a man who was a master of a household, who planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, dug a wine press in it, built a tower, leased it out to farmers, and went into another country. When the season for the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the farmers, to receive his fruit. The farmers took his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they treated them the same way. But afterward he sent to them his son, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ But the farmers, when they saw the son, said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him, and seize his inheritance.’ So they took him, and threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?” They told him, “He will miserably destroy those miserable men, and will lease out the vineyard to other farmers, who will give him the fruit in its season.” Jesus said to them, “Did you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner. This was from the Lord. It is marvelous in our eyes?’ “Therefore I tell you, the Kingdom of God will be taken away from you, and will be given to a nation producing its fruit. He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust.” When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he spoke about them. When they sought to seize him, they feared the multitudes, because they considered him to be a prophet.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The parable's setup (21:33) reproduces the Song of the Vineyard almost verbatim from Isaiah 5:2 (LXX): a man planted a vineyard, set a hedge/fence about it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. The whole parable presupposes Isaiah's allegory of the vineyard as Israel/Judah and its expected fruit.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.
echoes.note: Jesus cites Psalm 118:22-23 verbatim (21:42): 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner. This was from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' interpreting the rejected/vindicated son as the rejected/exalted cornerstone (same Psalm 118 quoted at the entry, 21:9).

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: 21:44, 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust,' draws on Daniel's stone cut without hands that smashes the kingdoms and whose fragments become chaff blown away — the stone that both judges and inaugurates God's kingdom.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' on which many 'shall fall, and be broken' supplies the first half of 21:44 ('he who falls on this stone will be broken'), fusing with the Psalm 118 cornerstone into a composite stone-testimonium.

echoes.text: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
echoes.note: The tenants' deliberation, 'This is the heir. Come, let's kill him, and seize his inheritance' (21:38), closely echoes Joseph's brothers: 'Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now, let us kill him' — the heir/beloved son plotted against by his own.

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: 'I sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them, yet they did not listen' (cf. Jer 25:4) is the prophetic pattern behind the householder repeatedly sending servants who are beaten and killed (21:34-36).

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, sent by God to the people, was stoned to death in the court of the temple — a concrete instance of a divine messenger stoned, matching 'stoned another' (21:35).

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel's confession that 'they slew your prophets which testified against them to turn them to you' summarizes the rejected-and-killed-emissaries pattern the parable allegorizes.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine brought out of Egypt and planted, whose hedges God then breaks down so passers-by pluck it, is a second vineyard-as-Israel song reinforcing Isaiah 5 and the threat to remove the vineyard's protection (21:43).

echoes.text: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.
echoes.note: 'The LORD testified against Israel... by all the prophets... yet they would not hear, but hardened their necks' — the deuteronomistic summary of prophets sent and rejected, paralleling the servants' fate.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'precious cornerstone' laid in Zion as a sure foundation belongs to the same stone-testimonia cluster (with Ps 118:22) that early Christians combined to interpret Christ as the cornerstone.

echoes.text: Yahweh will enter into judgment with the elders of his people, and their leaders: “It is you who have eaten up the vineyard. The plunder of the poor is in your houses.
echoes.note: 'You have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses' — Israel's leaders arraigned for plundering the vineyard, resonant with the tenants who seize the produce and inheritance.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd' as the divinely sent figure who is struck may faintly inform the killing of the beloved son, though the imagery differs.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to 'a nation producing its fruit' (21:43) faintly recalls Daniel's everlasting kingdom given to the people of the saints, the transfer of dominion to a faithful nation.

pericopes.text: Jesus answered and spoke again in parables to them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who made a marriage feast for his son, and sent out his servants to call those who were invited to the marriage feast, but they would not come. Again he sent out other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “Behold, I have prepared my dinner. My cattle and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the marriage feast!”’ But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his merchandise, and the rest grabbed his servants, and treated them shamefully, and killed them. When the king heard that, he was angry, and sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. “Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding is ready, but those who were invited weren’t worthy. Go therefore to the intersections of the highways, and as many as you may find, invite to the marriage feast.’ Those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together as many as they found, both bad and good. The wedding was filled with guests. But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man who didn’t have on wedding clothing, and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here not wearing wedding clothing?’ He was speechless. Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and throw him into the outer darkness; there is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.’ For many are called, but few chosen.”

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet — the LORD makes 'a feast of fat things' (fatlings/oxen killed, 22:4) for all peoples on his mountain. The king's marriage feast for his son draws on this prophetic image of the messianic/end-time banquet; the killing of fatlings matches Isaiah's 'fat things full of marrow.'

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests. It will happen in the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice, that I will punish the princes, the king’s sons, and all those who are clothed with foreign clothing.
echoes.note: The LORD 'has prepared a sacrifice' and bids his guests, and on that day will punish 'all such as are clothed with strange apparel' — a striking double parallel to the prepared feast (22:4) AND the man cast out for improper garment (22:11-13). Likely source for the wedding-clothing judgment.

echoes.text: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars. She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table. She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him, “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed! Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of […]
echoes.note: Wisdom builds her house, 'kills her beasts,' mixes her wine, and sends out maidservants to invite the simple to her feast — close structural echo of slaughtered cattle (22:4) and servants sent to call guests (22:3-4,9).

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
echoes.note: Open invitation to come freely to a banquet of rich food — thematic echo of the wide call to the highways (22:9), the unworthy invited replaced by all comers.

echoes.text: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear. The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the […]
echoes.note: Prophets/servants sent to call Israel back are seized and killed (Zechariah stoned in the temple court) — the king's servants beaten and murdered (22:6) figure the rejected prophets, a deuteronomistic pattern Matthew develops (cf. 23:34-37).

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: God 'sent unto you all my servants the prophets... yet they hearkened not' but treated them shamefully — the repeated sending of servants who are spurned and killed (22:3-6) reuses this prophetic-rejection schema.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel 'slew thy prophets which testified against them' — same servants-as-prophets motif behind the murdered messengers (22:6).

echoes.text: He burnt Yahweh’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, burnt he with fire.
echoes.note: Burning of the rebellious city (Jerusalem by Babylon) — the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city (22:7), echoing the prophetic-historical pattern of a city torched in judgment.

echoes.text: I will greatly rejoice in Yahweh, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
echoes.note: 'He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself' — wedding-garment imagery (22:11-12) as the required clothing of righteousness/salvation for the marriage feast.

echoes.text: There be many created, but few shall be saved.
echoes.note: 'Many have been created, but few shall be saved' (Fourth Ezra) — a near-formulaic Second Temple parallel to 'many are called, but few are chosen' (22:14).

pericopes.text: Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entrap him in his talk. They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are honest, and teach the way of God in truth, no matter whom you teach, for you aren’t partial to anyone. Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test me, you hypocrites? Show me the tax money.” They brought to him a denarius. He asked them, “Whose is this image and inscription?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” When they heard it, they marveled, and left him, and went away.

echoes.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: Jesus' question 'whose image (eikon) and inscription?' (22:20) plays on imago Dei: the coin bears Caesar's image and is owed to Caesar, but humanity bears God's image and is owed wholly to God — 'render to God the things that are God's' (22:21).

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof' — undergirds the claim that what is God's (everything, including the bearer of his image) belongs to God (22:21).

echoes.text: I say, “Keep the king’s command!” because of the oath to God.
echoes.note: Counsel to keep the king's commandment because of one's oath to God — faint wisdom backdrop to the dual obligation to Caesar and to God (22:21).

pericopes.text: On that day Sadducees (those who say that there is no resurrection) came to him. They asked him, saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed for his brother.’ Now there were with us seven brothers. The first married and died, and having no seed left his wife to his brother. In the same way, the second also, and the third, to the seventh. After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection therefore, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.” But Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven. But concerning the resurrection of the dead, haven’t you read that which was spoken to you by God, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?’God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” When the multitudes heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.

echoes.text: If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies, and has no son, the wife of the dead shall not be married outside to a stranger. Her husband’s brother shall go in to her, and take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her.
echoes.note: The Sadducees quote the levirate law nearly verbatim: 'If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed for his brother' (22:24) = Deuteronomy 25:5-6.

echoes.text: Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up seed to your brother.”
echoes.note: Judah commands Onan to 'go in unto thy brother's wife... and raise up seed to thy brother' — the narrative instance of levirate duty behind the Sadducees' test case (22:24-28).

echoes.text: Moreover he said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God.
echoes.note: Jesus' clinching scriptural proof, formula-cited ('that which was spoken to you by God'): 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (22:32) — verbatim from God at the bush; Jesus argues the patriarchs live to God.

echoes.text: God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.
echoes.note: The same divine self-naming as 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' is repeated and declared God's everlasting memorial name — reinforces the citation in 22:32.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many of them that sleep in the dust shall awake' — the canonical OT resurrection text behind the whole resurrection controversy the Sadducees deny (22:23,28-31).

echoes.text: because that she had been given to seven husbands, and Asmodaeus the evil spirit killed them, before they had lain with her. And they said to her, “Do you not know that you strangle your husbands? You have had already seven husbands, and you haven’t borne the name of any one of them.
echoes.note: Sarah had been given to seven husbands, each killed before consummation (Tobit 3:8; 7:11) — a Second Temple narrative of a woman successively wed to seven men, strikingly close to the Sadducees' seven-brothers scenario (22:25-27).

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: The martyred brothers' hope that 'the King of the world shall raise us up... unto everlasting life' — a Second Temple affirmation of bodily resurrection contested by the Sadducees here (22:23-32).

echoes.text: God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.
echoes.note: 'Sons of God' / angels — faint backdrop to 'they are as the angels of God in heaven' (22:30); largely thematic and disputed.

pericopes.text: But the Pharisees, when they heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered themselves together. One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him. “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.”

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's love command quoted as the first and great commandment: 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind' (22:37).

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The second commandment quoted verbatim: 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' (22:39).

echoes.text: Now, Israel, what does Yahweh your God require of you, but to fear Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
echoes.note: 'To love him, to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul' — reinforces the whole-being love demanded in 22:37.

echoes.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
echoes.note: Command to 'love the LORD your God... with all your heart and with all your soul' — another canonical restatement standing behind 22:37.

pericopes.text: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “Of David.” He said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, sit on my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet?’ “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” No one was able to answer him a word, neither did any man dare ask him any more questions from that day forward.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Formula-cited as David speaking 'in the Spirit': 'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool' (22:44) — the crux for showing the Christ is more than David's son.

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: The Davidic covenant promising David a 'seed' whose throne God establishes and who will be God's son — the basis for the crowd's answer that the Christ is the son of David (22:42).

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'Thou art my Son' — royal/messianic sonship that, paired with Psalm 110, presses Jesus' question of how David's son can also be David's Lord (22:43-45).

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: The messianic 'rod out of the stem of Jesse' — Davidic-descent expectation underlying 'whose son is he? ... Of David' (22:42).

pericopes.text: Then Jesus spoke to the multitudes and to his disciples, saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ seat. All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do. For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them. But all their works they do to be seen by men. They make their phylacteries broad, enlarge the fringesof their garments, and love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues, the salutations in the marketplaces, and to be called ‘Rabbi, Rabbi’ by men. But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers. Call no man on the earth your father, for one is your Father, he who is in heaven. Neither be called masters, for one is your master, the Christ. But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.
echoes.note: "Moses' seat" (v2) as the locus of teaching/judging authority evokes Moses sitting to adjudicate for the people; the chair becomes a metaphor for inherited Mosaic teaching office.

echoes.text: You shall do according to the decisions of the verdict which they shall give you from that place which Yahweh chooses. You shall observe to do according to all that they shall teach you: according to the decisions of the law which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the sentence which they shall show you, to the right hand, nor to the left.
echoes.note: The duty to do all that the Levitical judges 'at that place' tell you, not turning aside, underlies Jesus' 'observe and do whatever they tell you' (v3) even while condemning their conduct.

echoes.text: You shall bind them for a sign on your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes.
echoes.note: "They make their phylacteries broad" (v5) directly references tefillin, the binding of the words 'as a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes'; Jesus targets the ostentatious enlargement of this commanded practice.

echoes.text: It shall be for a sign on your hand, and for symbols between your eyes: for by strength of hand Yahweh brought us out of Egypt.”
echoes.note: Parallel phylactery command ('a sign on your hand and frontlets between your eyes') stands behind the broadened phylacteries of v5.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: "Enlarge the fringes of their garments" (v5) references the commanded tassels (tzitzit) on the corners of garments, given as a reminder of the commandments; the abuse is enlarging them for show.

echoes.text: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men; for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.
echoes.note: "They love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats" (v6) inverts the wisdom counsel not to claim the place of the great but to be invited up; same banqueting-status imagery Jesus uses elsewhere (Luke 14).

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: "Call no man your father... one is your Father" (v9) echoes 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' — the prophetic insistence on a single divine paternity over the covenant community.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: "You, O LORD, are our Father" supports the one-Father claim of v9 against human honorifics.

echoes.text: All your children shall be taught of Yahweh; and great shall be the peace of your children.
echoes.note: "All your children shall be taught by the LORD" undergirds 'one is your teacher' (v8); divine, not rabbinic, instruction is the eschatological norm.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.
echoes.note: Hannah's song ('The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and exalts') anticipates the reversal of v12, that the self-exalting are humbled and the humble exalted.

echoes.text: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
echoes.note: "A man's pride will bring him low, but the humble in spirit will obtain honor" is the proverbial substrate of v12's exaltation/humiliation reversal.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: "Exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high" supplies the prophetic reversal formula behind v12.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: "He saves the humble... God saves the lowly" parallels the exalt/humble logic of v12.

echoes.text: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day. For there will be a day of Yahweh of Armies for all that is proud and haughty, and for all that is lifted up; and it shall be brought low: For all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, For all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, For every lofty tower, for every […]
echoes.note: The Day of the LORD theme that 'the haughtiness of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone exalted' resonates with v12.

pericopes.text: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses, and as a pretense you make long prayers. Therefore you will receive greater condemnation. “But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! Because you shut up the Kingdom of Heaven against men; for you don’t enter in yourselves, neither do you allow those who are entering in to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel around by sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much of a son of Gehennaas yourselves. “Woe to you, you blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is obligated.’ You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold? ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on it, he is obligated?’ You blind fools! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? He therefore who swears by the altar, swears by it, and by everything on it. He who swears by the temple, swears by it, and by him who was livingin it. He who swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God, and by him who sits on it.

echoes.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
echoes.note: "Son of Gehenna" (v15) presupposes the Valley of Hinnom (ge-hinnom), defiled by Josiah, as the topographic origin of the eschatological place of judgment.

echoes.text: therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that this place shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter.
echoes.note: The renaming of the Valley of the Son of Hinnom as 'the Valley of Slaughter' supplies the dark connotation behind 'son of Gehenna' (v15).

echoes.text: His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.
echoes.note: "Blind guides" / 'his watchmen are blind' — the prophetic indictment of sightless religious leaders stands behind the repeated 'blind guides, blind fools' (vv16-19,24).

echoes.text: “‘You shall not swear by my name falsely, and profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: "You shall not swear by my name falsely" grounds the whole oath casuistry of vv16-22; the Pharisaic gradations of binding vs. non-binding oaths violate the simple seriousness of vowing.

echoes.text: When you vow a vow to Yahweh your God, you shall not be slack to pay it; for Yahweh your God will surely require it of you; and it would be sin in you. But if you refrain from making a vow, it shall be no sin in you. You shall observe and do that which has gone out of your lips. Whatever you have vowed to Yahweh your God as a freewill offering, which you have promised with your mouth, you must do.
echoes.note: The law that a vow to the LORD must be paid and is not to be trifled with underlies Jesus' attack on evasive oath distinctions (vv16-22).

echoes.text: Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar, and sanctify it: and the altar shall be most holy; whatever touches the altar shall be holy.
echoes.note: "The altar... whatever touches the altar shall be holy" is the precise principle Jesus invokes in v19: the altar sanctifies the gift, so swearing by the altar binds by all on it.

echoes.text: I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
echoes.note: Solomon's temple as the 'place for you to dwell in forever' undergirds v21, swearing 'by him who dwells in it'; cf. the tension with 8:27 that heaven cannot contain God.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what kind of house will you build to me? and what place shall be my rest?
echoes.note: "Heaven is my throne" directly grounds v22: to swear by heaven is to swear by the throne of God and by him who sits on it.

echoes.text: Yahweh has established his throne in the heavens. His kingdom rules over all.
echoes.note: "The LORD has established his throne in the heavens" supports the heaven-as-throne identification of v22.

pericopes.text: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone. You blind guides, who strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel! “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness. You blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and of the platter, that its outside may become clean also. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness. Even so you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

echoes.text: “‘All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh’s. It is holy to Yahweh.
echoes.note: "The tithe of the land... is the LORD's" grounds v23; the Pharisees scrupulously tithe even garden herbs (mint, dill, cumin), extending the produce-tithe to the smallest plants.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: "The weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith(fulness)" (v23) closely echoes 'to do justice, and to love mercy (hesed), and to walk humbly' — the prophetic distillation of true Torah.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" — Matthew's signature prophetic text (cf. 9:13; 12:7) — underlies the priority of mercy over ritual scruple in v23.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother.
echoes.note: "Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy" parallels the triad of justice/mercy/faith as the weightier matters of v23.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: Execute justice and righteousness, and deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence, to the foreigner, the fatherless, nor the widow; neither shed innocent blood in this place.
echoes.note: "Do justice and righteousness... do no wrong" reinforces the justice/mercy demand neglected in v23.

echoes.text: “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is unclean to you.
echoes.note: The camel is explicitly named unclean; 'strain out a gnat and swallow a camel' (v24) plays on the largest and (via Lev 11:23,41) the smallest unclean creatures, an absurd inversion of purity scruple.

echoes.text: “Whoever in the open field touches one who is slain with a sword, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days.
echoes.note: Touching a grave or human bones renders one unclean seven days; the 'whitewashed tombs... full of dead men's bones' (v27) trades on corpse-impurity, the very thing graves were whitewashed to warn passersby against.

echoes.text: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash: tell those who plaster it with whitewash, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and you, great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall tear it. Behold, when the wall has fallen, shall it not be said to you, Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it? Therefore […]
echoes.note: The false prophets who 'whitewash' a flimsy wall to make it look sound, only for it to be torn down, supply the controlling image of v27's whitewashed tombs concealing inner corruption.

echoes.text: On whatever any of them falls when they are dead, it shall be unclean; whether it is any vessel of wood, or clothing, or skin, or sack, whatever vessel it is, with which any work is done, it must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it will be clean. Every earthen vessel, into which any of them falls, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. All food which may be eaten, that on which water comes, shall be […]
echoes.note: Purity rules for vessels (cups, dishes) that contract uncleanness stand behind the inside/outside-of-the-cup imagery of vv25-26.

pericopes.text: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and decorate the tombs of the righteous, and say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we wouldn’t have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.’ Therefore you testify to yourselves that you are children of those who killed the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. You serpents, you offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? Therefore behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify; and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city; that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the sanctuary and the altar. Most certainly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: God 'sent persistently to them by his messengers... but they kept mocking the messengers... and scoffing at his prophets' — the Chronicler's summation of prophet-rejection frames vv29-37's prophet-killing generation.

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: "They killed your prophets who had warned them" — the confessional memory of slain prophets undergirds vv30-31,34-37.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's complaint 'they have killed your prophets with the sword' is part of the prophet-martyr tradition behind vv31,37.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: The prophet Uriah son of Shemaiah killed by the king is a concrete instance of the prophet-killing the woe presupposes (vv31,34).

echoes.text: In the fourth generation they will come here again, for the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.”
echoes.note: "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" supplies the 'measure not yet full' logic of v32, 'fill up the measure of your fathers.'

echoes.text: In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
echoes.note: "When the transgressors have reached their full measure" parallels the filling-up-of-iniquity idiom of v32.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: "You serpents" (v33) may evoke the primeval serpent and its 'seed,' casting the opponents as offspring of the deceiver.

echoes.text: Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent.
echoes.note: "From the serpent's root comes forth an adder, and its fruit a flying serpent" supplies the viper-offspring image of 'offspring of vipers' (v33; cf. 3:7; 12:34).

echoes.text: They hatch adders’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web: he who eats of their eggs dies; and that which is crushed breaks out into a viper.
echoes.note: The wicked who 'hatch adders' eggs' parallels the 'offspring of vipers' charge (v33), linking venomous brood to deeds of bloodshed (Isa 59:7).

echoes.text: Their wine is the poison of serpents, the cruel venom of asps.
echoes.note: "Their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps' from the Song of Moses colors the serpent/viper invective of v33.

echoes.text: Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh; and they testified against them: but they would not give ear.
echoes.note: "He sent prophets among them to bring them back to the LORD... they would not listen" stands directly before the Zechariah martyrdom and parallels 'I send to you prophets' (v34).

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: "I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets... yet they did not listen' parallels the divine sending of prophets, wise men, and scribes in v34.

echoes.text: Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
echoes.note: "The blood of righteous Abel" (v35) cites the first murder, whose blood 'cries to me from the ground' — the inaugural shed innocent blood opening the canonical span of martyrdom.

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house. Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his […]
echoes.note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, stoned 'in the court of the house of the LORD' (between sanctuary and altar), dying with 'May the LORD see and avenge' — the closing martyrdom of the Hebrew canon (Chronicles last); v35's Abel-to-Zechariah spans Genesis to Chronicles. The patronym 'son of Berechiah' likely conflates with the prophet of Zech 1:1.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: "A crooked and twisted generation" from the Song of Moses lies behind the verdict on 'this generation' (v36).

echoes.text: But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, Because he is of disservice to us, And is contrary to our works, And upbraids us with sins against the law, And lays to our charge sins against our discipline. He professes to have knowledge of God, And names himself servant of the Lord. He became to us a reproof of our thoughts. He is grievous to us even to behold, Because his life is unlike other men’s, And his paths are of strange fashion. We were accounted […]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical plot of the wicked conspiring to condemn the righteous one to a shameful death anticipates the persecution/killing of the sent righteous in vv34-35.

echoes.text: For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord does with longsuffering forbear, until that he punish them when they have attained to the full measure of their sins; but not so judged he as touching us,
echoes.note: God waiting 'until they have reached the full measure of their sins' parallels the filling-up of the fathers' measure (v32).

pericopes.text: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets, and stones those who are sent to her! How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not! Behold, your house is left to you desolate. For I tell you, you will not see me from now on, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

echoes.text: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: "They stoned him... in the court of the house of the LORD" — Zechariah's stoning is a concrete referent for 'Jerusalem... who stones those sent to her' (v37).

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: The confession that they 'killed your prophets' frames the apostrophe to prophet-killing Jerusalem (v37).

echoes.text: As an eagle that stirs up her nest, that flutters over her young, he spread abroad his wings, he took them, he bore them on his feathers.
echoes.note: The eagle that 'spreads its wings... catches them, bears them on its pinions' from the Song of Moses is the maternal bird-protection image behind 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings' (v37).

echoes.text: He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge. His faithfulness is your shield and rampart.
echoes.note: "He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge" supplies the sheltering-wings imagery of v37 directly.

echoes.text: May Yahweh repay your work, and a full reward be given you from Yahweh, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.”
echoes.note: "Under whose wings you have come to take refuge" is part of the wing-shelter cluster behind v37.

echoes.text: Keep me as the apple of your eye. Hide me under the shadow of your wings,
echoes.note: "Hide me in the shadow of your wings" belongs to the protective-wings imagery gathered in v37.

echoes.text: As birds hovering, so Yahweh of Armies will protect Jerusalem. He will protect and deliver it. He will pass over and preserve it.”
echoes.note: "Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem' — a bird-protection-of-Jerusalem image poignantly inverted when Jerusalem refuses gathering (v37).

echoes.text: But if you will not hear these words, I swear by myself, says Yahweh, that this house shall become a desolation.
echoes.note: "This house shall become a desolation" — the LORD's oath against the royal house — is closely echoed in 'your house is left to you desolate' (v38).

echoes.text: I have forsaken my house, I have cast off my heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
echoes.note: "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage" supplies the abandonment/desolation of the house in v38.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The warning that the temple will become 'a heap of ruins' and Israel a byword if they forsake the LORD informs the desolation pronounced in v38.

echoes.text: Let their habitation be desolate. Let no one dwell in their tents.
echoes.note: "May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents" parallels the desolate-house verdict of v38.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory went out from over the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim. The cherubim lifted up their wings, and mounted up from the earth in my sight when they went out, and the wheels beside them: and they stood at the door of the east gate of Yahweh’s house; and the glory of the God of Israel was over them above.
echoes.note: The departure of the glory of the LORD from the temple is the theological backdrop to the house being 'left desolate' in v38.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh’s name! We have blessed you out of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD" is quoted verbatim in v39 — the Hallel acclamation (already shouted at the entry, 21:9) whose future utterance conditions Jerusalem's seeing of Jesus again.

pericopes.text: Jesus went out from the temple, and was going on his way. His disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple. But he answered them, “You see all of these things, don’t you? Most certainly I tell you, there will not be left here one stone on another, that will not be thrown down.” As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?”

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: The prophecy that not one stone of the temple will be left on another reprises Micah's oracle that 'Zion shall be plowed as a field, Jerusalem shall become heaps,' the classic prophetic word of the temple's destruction; Jeremiah cites Micah 3:12 in his temple sermon (Jer 26:18), making it the paradigmatic temple-doom text.

echoes.text: therefore will I do to the house which is called by my name, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon threatens to do to the Jerusalem house what was done to Shiloh; Jesus' prediction of the temple's total demolition stands in this prophetic tradition of judgment on a temple presumed inviolable.

echoes.text: Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah; and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Zion shall be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's recitation of Micah's temple-destruction oracle before the elders forms the precedent for a prophet announcing the razing of the temple and being threatened for it.

echoes.text: His feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in two, from east to west, making a very great valley. Half of the mountain will move toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
echoes.note: Jesus delivers the discourse seated on the Mount of Olives, the very mountain on which Zechariah says the LORD's feet will stand on the day of judgment, splitting it in two; the eschatological setting is deliberately Zecharian.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory went up from the midst of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.
echoes.note: The glory of the LORD departs the temple and rests on 'the mountain east of the city' (the Mount of Olives); Jesus leaving the temple and seating himself on that mountain to pronounce its doom evokes the departure of the divine presence.

echoes.text: But you, Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run back and forth, and knowledge shall be increased.”
echoes.note: The disciples' question about the sign of 'the end of the age' uses the apocalyptic 'time of the end' vocabulary that pervades Daniel 8-12, framing the whole discourse in Danielic eschatological terms.

pericopes.text: Jesus answered them, “Be careful that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will lead many astray. You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you aren’t troubled, for all this must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of birth pains.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' closely matches 2 Chronicles 15:6, 'nation was crushed by nation and city by city,' a description of the LORD troubling them with every distress; the verbal pairing is the source idiom for the upheaval motif.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: 'I will stir up Egyptian against Egyptian... city against city, kingdom against kingdom' supplies the same nation-against-nation / kingdom-against-kingdom formula for divine judgment producing internal strife.

echoes.text: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
echoes.note: 'the beginning of birth pains' draws on the prophetic figure of the Day of the LORD as labor pangs; Isaiah 13:8 has the doomed seized by 'pangs and agony... like a woman in labor' in the oracle against Babylon, a passage Matthew 24:29 mines again for cosmic darkening.

echoes.text: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!
echoes.note: The 'birth pains' metaphor for the onset of judgment is a recurring Jeremianic figure (also Jer 4:31; 6:24; 13:21), reinforcing 'beginning of birth pains' as prophetic shorthand for the throes preceding the end.
