echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'all this must happen' (Greek dei genesthai) echoes Daniel's 'what must take place' / 'what will be in the latter days,' the apocalyptic language of divinely fixed events; the necessity (dei) is Danielic determinism.

echoes.text: But news out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him; and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.
echoes.note: 'rumors' troubling the king and the eschatological wars of Daniel 11 stand behind the 'wars and rumors of wars' that must occur before the end without yet being the end.

echoes.text: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized.
echoes.note: 'See that you aren't troubled' recalls Isaiah's 'do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread,' the prophetic reassurance not to be terrified by the threats of the nations.

echoes.text: ‘If evil comes on us—the sword, judgment, pestilence, or famine—we will stand before this house, and before you, (for your name is in this house), and cry to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.’
echoes.note: The triad of sword (war), famine, and pestilence/plague is the standard prophetic judgment cluster (sword-famine-pestilence) found throughout Jeremiah and Ezekiel; 'famines, plagues, and earthquakes' draws on this covenant-curse vocabulary.

echoes.text: A third part of you shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in your midst; and a third part shall fall by the sword around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds, and will draw out a sword after them.
echoes.note: The sword-famine-pestilence triad that Jesus lists as preliminary woes is Ezekiel's signature judgment formula (also Ezek 6:11-12; 7:15; 14:21), the covenant curses unleashed on Jerusalem.

pericopes.text: Then they will deliver you up to oppression, and will kill you. You will be hated by all of the nations for my name’s sake. Then many will stumble, and will deliver up one another, and will hate one another. Many false prophets will arise, and will lead many astray. Because iniquity will be multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. But he who endures to the end, the same will be saved. This Good News of the Kingdom will be preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: The handing over to tribulation and the promise that 'he who endures to the end will be saved' echoes Daniel 12:1, where after a time of unequaled trouble 'your people shall be delivered, everyone found written in the book'; deliverance comes through, not around, the tribulation.

echoes.text: Those who are wise among the people shall instruct many; yet they shall fall by the sword and by flame, by captivity and by plunder, many days.
echoes.note: 'they will deliver you up... and will kill you' matches Daniel 11:33, where 'those who are wise... shall fall by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder' during the persecution, the maskilim suffering before vindication.

echoes.text: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.
echoes.note: The wise who 'stumble' so as to be refined 'until the time of the end' (Dan 11:35) stands behind 'many will stumble' under persecution before the end comes.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 'will deliver up one another, and will hate one another' draws on Micah 7:6, where son dishonors father and a man's enemies are his own household, the eschatological breakdown of kinship loyalty Jesus cites explicitly in Matthew 10:21,35-36.

echoes.text: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.
echoes.note: 'many will be purified... but the wicked shall act wickedly' (Dan 12:10) parallels the sifting in which many stumble and love grows cold while some endure to be saved.

echoes.text: I will bring the third part into the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will test them like gold is tested. They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, ‘It is my people;’ and they will say, ‘Yahweh is my God.’”
echoes.note: The refining of a remnant through fire so that those who endure are saved while two-thirds perish (Zech 13:8-9) supplies the testing-and-remnant pattern behind enduring to the end for salvation.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The gospel 'preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations' before the end resonates with the Servant being given as 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.'

echoes.text: Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples.
echoes.note: Proclaiming God's glory and salvation 'among all the nations' anticipates the worldwide witness to the nations that must precede the end.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: How much more when I send my four severe judgments on Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the evil animals, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and animal!
echoes.note: The intensifying judgments and the universal hatred for the name belong to the prophetic scenario of covenant judgment poured on a faithless world, of which Ezekiel's four deadly acts are emblematic.

pericopes.text: “When, therefore, you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let him who is on the housetop not go down to take out things that are in his house. Let him who is in the field not return back to get his clothes. But woe to those who are with child and to nursing mothers in those days! Pray that your flight will not be in the winter, nor on a Sabbath, for then there will be great oppression, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, nor ever will be. Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones, those days will be shortened.

echoes.text: He shall make a firm covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease; and on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate; and even to the full end, and that determined, shall wrath be poured out on the desolate.
echoes.note: 'the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet' is an explicit, attributed citation; Daniel 9:27 reads that 'on the wing of abominations shall come one who makes desolate' (LXX bdelygma ton eremoseon), the precise phrase Jesus quotes.

echoes.text: Forces shall stand on his part, and they shall profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and shall take away the continual burnt offering, and they shall set up the abomination that makes desolate.
echoes.note: The same 'abomination that makes desolate' is set up in the temple in Daniel 11:31, the historical referent in the Antiochene desecration; Jesus' explicit Danielic citation conflates 11:31 with 9:27 and 12:11 as the prophetic source.

echoes.text: From the time that the continual burnt offering shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate set up, there shall be one thousand two hundred ninety days.
echoes.note: Daniel 12:11 dates 'the abomination that makes desolate' set up after the daily sacrifice is taken away; together with 9:27 and 11:31 this is the named Danielic prophecy Jesus invokes for the desecration standing in the holy place.

echoes.text: Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, How long shall be the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot?
echoes.note: Daniel 8:13's 'transgression that makes desolate' giving over the sanctuary and host to be trampled is part of the same Danielic abomination complex underlying the desecration of the holy place.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: 'great oppression, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, nor ever will be' is a near-verbatim rendering of Daniel 12:1, 'a time of trouble such as never has been since there was a nation till that time'; this is the controlling source for the unequaled-tribulation clause.

echoes.text: And on the fifteenth day of Chislev, in the hundred and forty and fifth year, they built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah on every side they built idol altars.
echoes.note: 1 Maccabees 1:54 narrates the fulfillment of Daniel: Antiochus 'erected a desolating sacrilege (bdelygma eremoseos) on the altar of burnt offering,' the deuterocanonical realization of the abomination phrase Jesus reuses for a future desecration.

echoes.text: Behold, tomorrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as has not been in Egypt since the day it was founded even until now.
echoes.note: The 'such as has never been... nor ever will be' formula is itself a stock superlative of unprecedented disaster (Exod 9:18, the hail; 10:14, the locusts; 11:6, the death of the firstborn), reinforcing the tribulation's incomparability.

echoes.text: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.
echoes.note: Joel's Day of the LORD is 'a day of darkness... such as has never been, nor will be again after them through the years,' the same unequaled-distress superlative attached to the eschatological day.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: 'flee to the mountains' and do not turn back to take anything echoes the angelic command to Lot, 'Flee to the hills... do not look back,' the paradigm of urgent escape from a doomed place before destruction falls.

echoes.text: And he and his sons fled into the mountains, and forsook all that they had in the city.
echoes.note: Mattathias and his sons 'fled to the mountains' to escape the persecution and desecration, a Maccabean precedent for fleeing to the hills when the abomination stands in the holy place.

echoes.text: But those of those who escape shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, every one in his iniquity.
echoes.note: 'those who survive shall escape and be on the mountains' when judgment falls on the land parallels the command to flee to the mountains in the day of desolation.

echoes.text: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
echoes.note: The warnings not to go down from the housetop or turn back in the field for one's goods recall Lot's wife, who looked back toward Sodom and perished; the danger of delay for possessions is the Sodom-escape topos.

echoes.text: The hands of the pitiful women have boiled their own children; They were their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.
echoes.note: The woe to pregnant and nursing women in those days resonates with Lamentations' horrors of the siege of Jerusalem, where mothers and infants suffer the extremity of the city's fall.

echoes.text: Samaria will bear her guilt; for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”
echoes.note: The special woe to pregnant women and the dashing of infants in the day of judgment (Hosea 13:16) underlies the lament for those with child and nursing mothers in the days of tribulation.

echoes.text: You will eat the fruit of your own body, the flesh of your sons and of your daughters, whom Yahweh your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies will distress you.
echoes.note: The covenant-curse siege horrors falling especially on the tender and pregnant (Deut 28:53-57) form the Deuteronomic backdrop for the woe to mothers in those days.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one says, ‘Don’t destroy it, for a blessing is in it:’ so will I do for my servants’ sake, that I may not destroy them all.
echoes.note: The days being 'shortened for the sake of the chosen ones' so that some flesh is saved echoes the prophetic logic of God preserving a remnant 'for my servants' sake' rather than destroying all.

pericopes.text: “Then if any man tells you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ don’t believe it. For there will arise false christs, and false prophets, and they will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones. “Behold, I have told you beforehand. If therefore they tell you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ don’t go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ don’t believe it. For as the lightning flashes from the east, and is seen even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For wherever the carcass is, there is where the vultures gather together.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder,
echoes.note: 'false christs and false prophets will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray' draws on Deuteronomy 13:1-3, the warning about a prophet who gives a sign or wonder to lead Israel astray after other gods; the criterion is fidelity, not the marvel.

echoes.text: That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which Yahweh your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from your midst.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic insistence that even a wonder-working prophet who leads astray must be rejected reinforces 'don't believe it' against the seductive signs of false messiahs.

echoes.text: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.
echoes.note: The deceivers leading astray 'even the chosen ones, if possible' parallels Daniel's wise being tested and some falling away amid the deceits of the end-time tribulation.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Expectation of the eschatological prophet/messiah in the wilderness or hidden chamber plays against authentic prophetic anticipation; the 'wilderness' rumor (v.26) trades on Elijah-style wilderness expectation.

echoes.text: Their horses also are swifter than leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves. Their horsemen press proudly on. Yes, their horsemen come from afar. They fly as an eagle that hurries to devour.
echoes.note: 'wherever the carcass is, there is where the vultures gather' evokes the swift birds of prey swooping to the kill in Habakkuk's vision of judgment, the inevitability and visibility of the coming devastation.

echoes.text: His young ones also suck up blood. Where the slain are, there he is.”
echoes.note: 'where the slain are, there is he' (the eagle/vulture over the carcass, Job 39:30) is a likely source for the proverb of the gathering vultures, an image of unmistakable, inevitable convergence.

echoes.text: You, son of man, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Speak to the birds of every sort, and to every animal of the field, Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I do sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, that you may eat flesh and drink blood.
echoes.note: The birds gathering to the great slaughter-sacrifice in the day of the LORD (Ezek 39:4,17-20) lies behind the carcass-and-vultures image of eschatological judgment that none will miss.

pericopes.text: But immediately after the oppression of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory. He will send out his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the sky to the other.

echoes.text: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
echoes.note: 'the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light' is a near-quotation of Isaiah 13:10, 'the stars of the heavens... will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising and the moon will not shed its light,' the cosmic collapse in the Day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: 'the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken' renders Isaiah 34:4, 'all the host of heaven shall rot away... all their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine,' the dissolution of the heavenly host in judgment.

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: Joel 2:10 (and 3:15) 'the sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' supplies the same triad of darkened sun, moon, and stars as the heralds of the Day of the LORD.

echoes.text: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'the sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD' is part of the Joel cluster behind the cosmic-portent language of the Son of Man's coming.

echoes.text: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light.
echoes.note: Ezekiel 32:7-8, 'I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light,' is a direct parallel to the darkening of sun, moon, and stars over a fallen power.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory' is a strong allusion to Daniel 7:13, 'one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven,' to whom dominion and glory are given; the title and the cloud-coming are Danielic.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The 'power and great glory' and the gathering of all peoples reflects Daniel 7:14, where the son of man receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples should serve.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn.
echoes.note: 'all the tribes of the earth will mourn' draws on Zechariah 12:10-14, 'they shall look on him whom they have pierced, and mourn... the land shall mourn, each family by itself,' the eschatological mourning of the tribes/families at the appearance of the one they pierced.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son.

echoes.text: The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart;
echoes.note: The enumeration of mourning 'families/tribes' in Zechariah 12:12-14 is specifically behind 'all the tribes (phylai) of the earth will mourn,' Matthew's universalizing of Zechariah's clan-by-clan lament.

echoes.text: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.
echoes.note: 'they will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the sky to the other' echoes Deuteronomy 30:4, 'though you are driven to the farthest parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you,' the promise of regathering the scattered elect.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have spread you abroad like the four winds of heaven' (Zech 2:6) supplies the 'four winds' as the dispersion-points from which the elect are gathered at the end.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost... will come and worship the LORD' (Isa 27:13) is the source for the trumpet that summons the dispersed elect to be gathered at the Son of Man's coming.

echoes.text: He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: The LORD raising a signal/sign and 'gathering the dispersed of Israel... from the four corners of the earth' (Isa 11:12) parallels both the 'sign of the Son of Man' and the gathering of the elect from the four winds.

echoes.text: Yahweh will be seen over them; and his arrow will go flash like lightning; and the Lord Yahweh will blow the trumpet, and will go with whirlwinds of the south.
echoes.note: 'the Lord GOD will sound the trumpet' in the day of his appearing (Zech 9:14) reinforces the eschatological trumpet that accompanies the gathering.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: The 'powers of the heavens shall be shaken' specifically draws on the shaking and dissolution of the heavenly host in Isaiah 34:4, distinct from the falling stars, emphasizing cosmic powers undone.

echoes.text: For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: ‘Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
echoes.note: 'I will shake the heavens and the earth' (Hag 2:6) is part of the prophetic shaking-of-the-cosmos tradition behind 'the powers of the heavens will be shaken.'

echoes.text: Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed; for Yahweh of Armies will reign on Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem; and before his elders will be glory.
echoes.note: Isaiah 24:23, the moon abashed and the sun ashamed when the LORD reigns in glory on Zion, belongs to the same Isaianic cluster of luminaries failing at the LORD's appearing.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: The gathering of the chosen and the kingdom given to the saints (Dan 7:27) underlies the assembling of the elect at the Son of Man's coming.

echoes.text: When you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets. Then you will be remembered before Yahweh your God, and you will be saved from your enemies.
echoes.note: The trumpet sounded so that Israel is remembered and gathered/delivered (Num 10:9; cf. Lev 23:24) supplies the cultic trumpet-of-assembly background to the angels' trumpet gathering the elect.

echoes.text: “Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.”
echoes.note: 'Gather my faithful ones to me' as God comes in judgment with consuming fire (Ps 50:3-5) parallels the gathering of the chosen at the Son of Man's glorious advent.

pericopes.text: “Now from the fig tree learn this parable. When its branch has now become tender, and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near. Even so you also, when you see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors. Most certainly I tell you, this generationwill not pass away, until all these things are accomplished. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.
echoes.note: The fig tree (and vine) yielding its fruit as a sign of the turning season (Joel 2:22) lies loosely behind the fig-tree parable's reading of budding branches as the nearness of the appointed time.

echoes.text: The fig tree ripens her green figs. The vines are in blossom. They give out their fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.” Lover
echoes.note: 'The fig tree puts forth its figs... arise, my love' (Song 2:13) marks the fig's leafing as the herald of the season's arrival, the natural sign-reading the parable trades on.

echoes.text: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away' draws on Isaiah 40:8, 'the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever,' contrasting transient creation with God's enduring word.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
echoes.note: Isaiah 51:6, 'the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out... but my salvation will be forever,' parallels the passing of heaven and earth set against the permanence of Jesus' word.

echoes.text: They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed.
echoes.note: Psalm 102:26-27, 'they will perish, but you remain... they will pass away, but you are the same,' contributes to the heaven-and-earth-pass-away / my-words-remain antithesis.

pericopes.text: But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven,but my Father only. “As the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in those days which were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship, and they didn’t know until the flood came, and took them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left; two women grinding at the mill, one will be taken and one will be left.

echoes.text: Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters.
echoes.note: 'As the days of Noah were... eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship, and they didn't know until the flood came and took them all away' is a sustained allusion to Genesis 6-7, the flood narrative; the unsuspecting world swept away while Noah enters the ark is the controlling typology.

echoes.text: Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
echoes.note: The flood that 'took them all away' (every living thing blotted out, only Noah and those with him remaining, Gen 7:23) is the precise source for the sudden, total, unexpected sweeping-away that figures the Son of Man's coming.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: The heedless eating, drinking, and marrying corresponds to the corrupt complacency of Noah's generation (Gen 6:5,11-12), heightening the contrast with the abrupt judgment.

echoes.text: In the same day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth—the sons of Noah—and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, entered into the ship—
echoes.note: 'the day that Noah entered the ark' (Gen 7:13) marks the decisive divide between the saved and the swept-away that the parable applies to the day of the Son of Man.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.
echoes.note: The withholding of the precise time even from heavenly beings, known only to God, resonates with Daniel sealing the appointed time until the end, knowledge reserved to God alone.

echoes.text: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.
echoes.note: 'a day known to the LORD' alone (Zech 14:7) parallels 'no one knows of that day and hour... but my Father only,' the day's timing reserved to God.

pericopes.text: Watch therefore, for you don’t know in what hour your Lord comes. But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have watched, and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore also be ready, for in an hour that you don’t expect, the Son of Man will come.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The sudden, unanticipated arrival of the Lord who 'will suddenly come to his temple' (Mal 3:1) resonates with the Lord coming at an unexpected hour for which one must be ready.

echoes.text: If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? if thieves by night, wouldn’t they destroy until they had enough?
echoes.note: The thief-in-the-night image of unexpected nocturnal plunder (cf. Jer 49:9; Obad 5, thieves who take only what they want by night) supplies the figure of the thief whose hour the householder cannot predict.

echoes.text: The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief.
echoes.note: The thief/murderer who rises in the dark and breaks into houses (Job 24:14,16) furnishes the burglary imagery for the unexpected coming for which one must keep watch.

pericopes.text: “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes. Most certainly I tell you that he will set him over all that he has. But if that evil servant should say in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, and eat and drink with the drunkards, the lord of that servant will come in a day when he doesn’t expect it, and in an hour when he doesn’t know it, and will cut him in pieces, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. There is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.
echoes.note: The faithful and wise servant whom the master sets over his household to provision it recalls Joseph set over Potiphar's house and over all Egypt's storehouses to give out food in due season (Gen 39:4-6; 41:40-41), the trusted-steward type.

echoes.text: These all wait for you, that you may give them their food in due season.
echoes.note: Giving the household 'their food in due season' echoes the providential idiom of Psalm 104:27 (and 145:15), 'you give them their food in due season,' applied to the steward's faithful provisioning.

echoes.text: She rises also while it is yet night, gives food to her household, and portions for her servant girls.
echoes.note: The wise household manager who rises to provide food/portions for the household (Prov 31:15) parallels the faithful and wise servant dispensing the household's food at the right time.

echoes.text: Then the king made Daniel great, and gave him many great gifts, and made him to rule over the whole province of Babylon, and to be chief governor over all the wise men of Babylon.
echoes.note: The faithful, wise servant being promoted to be set 'over all that he has' resembles the wise Daniel exalted to rule the whole province as reward for faithful discernment.

echoes.text: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
echoes.note: The wicked servant's reasoning that 'my lord is delaying' so that he turns to abuse and drunkenness reflects Qoheleth's observation that when judgment is delayed the heart is emboldened to do evil.

echoes.text: I will thrust you from your office. You will be pulled down from your station.
echoes.note: The unfaithful steward thrust from his office and his place given to another (Shebna deposed, Isa 22:15-19) parallels the evil servant cut off and assigned his portion with the hypocrites.

echoes.text: The wicked will see it, and be grieved. He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away. The desire of the wicked will perish.
echoes.note: 'the wicked will see it and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and melt away' (Ps 112:10) lies behind the recurring Matthean punishment-formula 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' assigned to the evil servant.

pericopes.text: “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins, who took their lamps, and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them, but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept. But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’ Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps. The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’ While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’ Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: The bridegroom motif organizing the whole parable draws on the prophetic image of God/Messiah as bridegroom: 'as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.' Matthew makes the coming bridegroom the figure for the returning Son of Man, joining the eschatological wedding feast to messianic arrival.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: God's betrothal of Israel ('I will betroth you to me forever') stands behind the bridegroom-and-attendants imagery; the marriage covenant is the controlling metaphor for the eschatological union the wise virgins enter and the foolish miss.

echoes.text: Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all spices of the merchant? Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage! Sixty mighty men are around it, of the mighty men of Israel. They all handle the sword, and are expert in war. Every man has his sword on his thigh, because of fear in the night. King Solomon made himself a carriage of the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, its bottom of […]
echoes.note: The nocturnal coming of the bridegroom in procession, the cry going up, and the wedding of King Solomon supply a scriptural scene of a bridegroom arriving by night to be met by attendants. Verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him. Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?
echoes.note: The reversal whereby those who presume entry are shut out ('Lord, Lord, open to us' / 'I don't know you') resonates with the prophetic Day of the LORD warning that the day will be darkness for the complacent, not the light they expected.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies. “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... but who can endure the day of his coming?' supplies the pattern of a sudden, testing arrival of the Lord for which one must be prepared; the delay-then-sudden-cry structure of the parable echoes this.

echoes.text: For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: 'Though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not delay' frames the theme of the bridegroom's delay (v.5) and the call to keep ready through the apparent postponement of the appointed time.
echoes.lxxText: For the vision is yet for a time, and it shall shoot forth at the end, and not in vain: though he should tarry, wait for him; for he will surely come, and will not tarry.

echoes.text: “You shall command the children of Israel, that they bring to you pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually. In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil which is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall keep it in order from evening to morning before Yahweh: it shall be a statute forever throughout their generations on the behalf of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: The provision of pure oil to keep the lamp burning continually 'from evening to morning' supplies the cultic background for oil-as-fidelity that keeps the light alive through the night of waiting.

echoes.text: The princess inside is all glorious. Her clothing is interwoven with gold. She shall be led to the king in embroidered work. The virgins, her companions who follow her, shall be brought to you. With gladness and rejoicing they shall be led. They shall enter into the king’s palace.
echoes.note: The royal wedding psalm, with virgin companions led in procession to the king's palace amid gladness, provides a scriptural template for virgins escorting a bridegroom into the marriage feast.

pericopes.text: “For it is like a man, going into another country, who called his own servants, and entrusted his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one; to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey. Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents. In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two. But he who received the one went away and dug in the earth, and hid his lord’s money. “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and reconciled accounts with them. He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents besides them.’ “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ “He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents besides them.’ “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ “He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you did not scatter. I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’ “But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter. You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest. Take away therefore the talent from him, and give it to him who has the ten talents. For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away. Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he […]
echoes.note: Joseph entrusted with all his master's goods and proving faithful as a steward supplies a narrative type of the trusted servant set over his lord's property, rewarded with greater authority.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The condemnation of the 'slothful' servant (v.26) and the praise of diligent gain echoes wisdom's contrast between the industrious and the sluggard whose laziness brings ruin.

echoes.text: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth. He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during the harvest is a son who causes shame.
echoes.note: 'A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich; he who gathers in summer is a prudent son' undergirds the parable's reward of the productive servants and reproach of the one who buried his trust.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: The judgment-language of the parable's frame (joy of the lord vs. outer darkness) participates in the apocalyptic two-fold destiny of the wise who shine and others who go to shame, the eschatological backdrop Matthew assumes.

echoes.text: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who adorn yourselves with torches around yourselves; walk in the flame of your fire, and among the brands that you have kindled. You shall have this of my hand; you shall lie down in sorrow.
echoes.note: The motif of being cast into darkness as judgment ('you shall lie down in torment') faintly underlies the 'outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth' fate of the unprofitable servant.

pericopes.text: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory. Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left. Then the King will tell those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you took me in. I was naked, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me.’ “Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, and feed you; or thirsty, and give you a drink? When did we see you as a stranger, and take you in; or naked, and clothe you? When did we see you sick, or in prison, and come to you?’ “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ Then he will say also to those on the left hand, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry, and you didn’t give me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; I was a stranger, and you didn’t take me in; naked, and you didn’t clothe me; sick, and in prison, and you didn’t visit me.’ “Then they will also answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and didn’t help you?’ “Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you didn’t do it to one of the least of these, you didn’t do it to me.’ These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The Son of Man coming in glory and seated on his throne, before whom all nations/peoples are gathered to serve him, is the direct backbone of v.31-32. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' receives dominion, glory, and kingdom over all peoples, nations, and languages; Matthew transposes this enthronement into the scene of universal judgment.

echoes.text: As for you, O my flock, thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats.
echoes.note: 'I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats' is the explicit verbal and conceptual source for 'he will separate them... as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats' (v.32-33). The shepherd-judge distinguishing the flock animals is unmistakable.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh to them: Behold, I, even I, will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you thrust with side and with shoulder, and push all the diseased with your horns, until you have scattered them abroad; therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: The LORD 'will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep,' saving the weak from those who shove with side and shoulder. This grounds the criterion of judgment on treatment of the vulnerable and the shepherd-king's vindication of the mistreated, mirrored in care for the hungry, naked, sick, and imprisoned.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: The promise of one shepherd, 'my servant David,' set over the flock as prince, is typologically fulfilled in the Son of Man / King who shepherds and judges the nations. The Davidic shepherd-king of Ezekiel 34 is the figure Matthew casts Jesus as embodying.

echoes.text: I will gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and I will execute judgment on them there for my people, and for my heritage, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations. They have divided my land,
echoes.note: 'I will gather all the nations... and I will enter into judgment with them there' supplies the assize of the nations gathered before the throne (v.32), where they are judged on how they treated God's people.

echoes.text: “Let the nations arouse themselves, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat; for there will I sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
echoes.note: 'Let the nations be roused and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.' The enthroned divine Judge seated to judge the assembled nations directly parallels the Son of Man sitting on the throne of his glory to judge all the nations.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.' This supplies the retinue of v.31, 'the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him,' for the day of the LORD's appearing.

echoes.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: The acts of true fasting/righteousness — 'share your bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, when you see the naked, cover him' — closely match the King's catalog of hungry/stranger/naked in v.35-36. Isaiah 58 is the strongest verbal parallel for the works that mark the righteous.

echoes.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail, or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, her have I guided from my mother’s womb); if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering; if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece; if I have lifted up my hand […]
echoes.note: Job's oath of innocence — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for the needy ('if I have not given the poor their portion... if I have seen any perish for lack of clothing') — supplies a near-checklist of the deeds of mercy that define the sheep.

echoes.text: and if you draw out your soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul: then your light shall rise in darkness, and your obscurity be as the noonday;
echoes.note: 'If you pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness' reinforces the same Isaian ethic of self-giving to the afflicted as the substance of righteousness rewarded by God.

echoes.text: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
echoes.note: The righteous man 'gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment' — Ezekiel's catalog of the deeds that mark the just from the wicked closely parallels the King's criteria and reinforces the Ezekielian frame already operative in the sheep/goats image.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' This is the precise theology of v.40 — kindness to the least is rendered to the King himself, who repays. The identification of the needy with the divine creditor is the conceptual hinge.

echoes.text: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.' The principle that treatment of the poor is treatment of God himself underwrites 'you did it to me' / 'you did not do it to me.'

echoes.text: For, behold, Yahweh will come with fire, and his chariots shall be like the whirlwind; to render his anger with fierceness, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire will Yahweh execute judgment, and by his sword, on all flesh; and the slain of Yahweh shall be many.
echoes.note: 'The LORD will come with fire... by fire will the LORD enter into judgment with all flesh' faintly underlies the 'eternal fire' prepared for the cursed and the universal judgment of all flesh/nations.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The closing image of the unquenched fire / undying worm for the rebellious provides scriptural background for the 'eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' of v.41, 46.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.' This two-fold eternal destiny is the source for v.46, 'these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.'

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The enthronement of the messianic Lord at God's right hand, with subjugation of enemies, underlies the royal session of the Son of Man on the throne of his glory and the placing of subjects at the right and left.

echoes.text: For he will deliver the needy when he cries; the poor, who has no helper. He will have pity on the poor and needy. He will save the souls of the needy. He will redeem their soul from oppression and violence. Their blood will be precious in his sight.
echoes.note: The royal psalm's portrait of the king who delivers the needy, the poor, and those who have no helper, redeeming their life from oppression, supplies the ideal of the just king whose rule is measured by care for the vulnerable — the standard the King applies.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines. He will destroy in this mountain the surface of the covering that covers all peoples, and the veil that is spread over all nations. He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, […]
echoes.note: The eschatological banquet on the mountain for all peoples, where death is swallowed up, faintly informs the inheritance/eternal-life reward into which the blessed are welcomed when all nations are gathered.

echoes.text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, And no torment will touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died; And their departure was accounted to be their hurt, And their journeying away from us to be their ruin: But they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they be punished, Their hope is full of immortality; And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and […]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical promise that the righteous are in God's hand, will be vindicated at the visitation, judge nations, and receive a kingdom/crown, parallels the righteous inheriting the kingdom and the eternal-life reward at the eschatological assize.

echoes.text: Also to the poor man stretch out your hand, That your blessing may be perfected. A gift has grace in the sight of every man living; And for a dead man keep not back grace. Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn. Be not slow to visit a sick man; For by such things you will gain love.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's exhortation to stretch out your hand to the poor, give to the needy, not neglect those who weep, and visit the sick supplies a deuterocanonical catalog of mercy-deeds strikingly close to the King's list (feed, clothe, visit the sick).

echoes.text: In the days of Enemessar, I did many alms deeds to my kindred: I gave my bread to the hungry, and my garments to the naked. If I saw any of my race dead, and cast forth on the wall of Ninevah, I buried him.
echoes.note: Tobit's acts of charity — giving bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and burying the dead — model the very deeds of mercy that mark the righteous and were understood in Second Temple piety as righteousness stored up before God.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's instruction to give alms from your possessions, for almsgiving 'is a good gift in the sight of the Most High' and lays up treasure against the day of necessity, reflects the same logic that deeds to the least are rendered to God and rewarded eschatologically.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds' / the scattering and gathering language of Zechariah faintly resonates with the gathering of all nations before the throne, though the dominant gathering source is Joel 3.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (v.34) presupposes the creation account as the temporal anchor — the kingdom planned since the world's founding, a protological framing of the inheritance.

pericopes.text: When Jesus had finished all these words, he said to his disciples, “You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” Then the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders of the people were gathered together in the court of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas. They took counsel together that they might take Jesus by deceit, and kill him. But they said, “Not during the feast, lest a riot occur among the people.”

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified' (v2) deploys the apocalyptic Son of Man title that Matthew unfolds fully at 26:64; here in a passion-prediction key the exalted figure is paradoxically handed over.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: 'after two days the Passover is coming' (v2) times Jesus' death to the Passover, setting up the lamb typology that the Last Supper (vv26-28) makes explicit; he is slain at the feast that commemorates the original deliverance.

echoes.text: The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed, saying,
echoes.note: 'the chief priests... took counsel together that they might take Jesus by deceit, and kill him' (vv3-4) echoes the rulers who 'take counsel together against the LORD and against his anointed'; Matthew's anointed (Christos) is the target.

echoes.text: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.
echoes.note: 'they took counsel together against me; they plotted to take away my life' is a lament topos the gathering of priests in deceit replays.

echoes.text: The wicked watches the righteous, and seeks to kill him.
echoes.note: 'the wicked watches the righteous and seeks to kill him' supplies the righteous-sufferer plot frame for the conspiracy.

pericopes.text: Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him having an alabaster jar of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he sat at the table. But when his disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? For this ointment might have been sold for much, and given to the poor.” However, knowing this, Jesus said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? Because she has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you; but you don’t always have me. For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial. Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her.”

echoes.text: For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
echoes.note: 'you always have the poor with you' (v11) quotes the Deuteronomic axiom 'the poor will never cease out of the land'; Jesus invokes the law's own realism not to dismiss the poor but to mark the unrepeatable hour of his presence.

echoes.text: They buried him in his own tombs, which he had dug out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art: and they made a very great burning for him.
echoes.note: the costly ointment 'to prepare me for burial' (v12) evokes the spices and aromatic anointing laid up for an honored burial, here pre-enacted on the living body.

echoes.text: While the king sat at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance.
echoes.note: 'while the king is at his table, my spikenard sent forth its fragrance' offers a banquet-anointing image behind the woman pouring fragrant ointment as Jesus reclines.

echoes.text: Then Samuel took the vial of oil, and poured it on his head, and kissed him, and said, “Isn’t it that Yahweh has anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?
echoes.note: pouring oil on the head is the gesture of royal anointing; the woman's act may carry a faint messianic (Christos = anointed) coloring as the priests plot against the unanointed-by-them king.

pericopes.text: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests, and said, “What are you willing to give me, that I should deliver him to you?” They weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver. From that time he sought opportunity to betray him.

echoes.text: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. Yahweh said to me, “Throw it to the potter, the handsome price that I was valued at by them!” I took the thirty pieces of silver, and threw them to the potter, in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: 'They weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver' (v15) borrows the exact wage of the rejected shepherd in Zechariah; Matthew makes the citation explicit at 27:9-10 when the money buys the potter's field, so the allusion is deliberately seeded here.

echoes.text: If the bull gores a male servant or a female servant, thirty shekels of silver shall be given to their master, and the ox shall be stoned.
echoes.note: thirty shekels of silver is the Torah's compensation for a slave gored by an ox; the price of betrayal is the price of a slave, ironizing the worth assigned to Jesus.

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: the table-companion turned betrayer is introduced here; the 'familiar friend who lifted his heel' is made explicit at the supper (v23) but the bargain begins now.

pericopes.text: Now on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” He said, “Go into the city to a certain person, and tell him, ‘The Teacher says, “My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.”’” The disciples did as Jesus commanded them, and they prepared the Passover.

echoes.note: 'the first day of unleavened bread' and 'prepare... to eat the Passover' (vv17-19) directly invoke the Exodus 12 ordinance for the feast of unleavened bread and the Passover meal.

echoes.text: You may not sacrifice the Passover within any of your gates, which Yahweh your God gives you; but at the place which Yahweh your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell in, there you shall sacrifice the Passover at evening, at the going down of the sun, at the season that you came out of Egypt. You shall roast and eat it in the place which Yahweh your God chooses. In the morning you shall return to your tents. Six days you shall eat unleavened bread. […]
echoes.note: the Deuteronomic command to keep the Passover 'in the place the LORD chooses' (Jerusalem) frames the disciples' search for the room within the city.

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever.
echoes.note: the memorial-meal command undergirds Jesus' reconstitution of the Passover as his own memorial in the verses that follow.

pericopes.text: Now when evening had come, he was reclining at the table with the twelve disciples. As they were eating, he said, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.” They were exceedingly sorrowful, and each began to ask him, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?” He answered, “He who dipped his hand with me in the dish, the same will betray me. The Son of Man goes, even as it is written of him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.” Judas, who betrayed him, answered, “It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You said it.”

echoes.text: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
echoes.note: 'He who dipped his hand with me in the dish... will betray me' (v23) closely renders 'my own familiar friend... who ate of my bread, has lifted up his heel against me'; sharing the bowl is the very act that names the betrayer.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he […]
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man goes, even as it is written of him' (v24) appeals to a scriptural script of the suffering one being handed over, the Servant 'led as a lamb to the slaughter.'

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: the title 'Son of Man' carries the Danielic resonance even as the figure is led to suffering, holding exaltation and humiliation together.

echoes.text: “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.’
echoes.note: 'It would be better for that man if he had not been born' (v24) echoes the wisdom lament cursing the day of one's birth, here turned as a woe on the betrayer.

echoes.text: Yes, better than them both is him who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.
echoes.note: 'better... is he who has not yet been' supplies the non-existence-is-preferable formula behind the woe of v24.

pericopes.text: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.” When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: 'this is my blood of the covenant' (v28) verbally appropriates Moses' words at Sinai, 'Behold the blood of the covenant which the LORD has made with you'; Jesus' blood ratifies the covenant as the sacrificial blood once did.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: the covenant inaugurated 'for the remission of sins' (v28) realizes Jeremiah's promised new covenant whose hallmark is 'I will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more'; many texts read 'new covenant' explicitly here.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'poured out for many for the remission of sins' (v28) draws on the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and 'bore the sin of many'; 'many' (rabbim) is Isaiah's vicarious-atonement vocabulary.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: the Passover bread and the slain lamb stand behind the bread Jesus identifies as 'my body' and the cup as 'my blood,' refiguring the seder elements around himself.

echoes.text: In this mountain, Yahweh of Armies will make all peoples a feast of fat things, a feast of choice wines, of fat things full of marrow, of well refined choice wines.
echoes.note: 'until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father's Kingdom' (v29) anticipates the eschatological 'feast of wines on the lees' on the LORD's mountain.

echoes.text: I will take the cup of salvation, and call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: 'I will take the cup of salvation' from the Hallel sung at Passover colors the cup of the covenant; the Hallel (Pss 113-118) is the hymn of v30.

echoes.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
echoes.note: 'by the blood of your covenant I have set your prisoners free' joins covenant blood to liberation, resonant with blood 'poured out for many.'

echoes.text: Praise Yah! Praise, you servants of Yahweh, praise Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: 'when they had sung a hymn' (v30) refers to the Hallel Psalms (113-118) sung at the close of the Passover meal.

echoes.text: David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered, and went barefoot: and all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up.
echoes.note: going out to the Mount of Olives (v30) faintly recalls David ascending Olivet weeping as he flees betrayal by Ahithophel, a betrayer-companion type.

pericopes.text: Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of me tonight, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.” But Peter answered him, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble.” Jesus said to him, “Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” All of the disciples also said likewise.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered' (v31) is a formula-introduced ('it is written') citation of Zechariah; the smitten shepherd and scattered flock script the disciples' desertion.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: 'they were scattered because there was no shepherd' supplies the broader scattered-flock-without-shepherd motif that the Zechariah citation concentrates.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: 'I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd' is a parallel image of leaderless dispersal behind v31.

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: the prayer that Israel not be 'as sheep which have no shepherd' is the source idiom of the scattered flock.

pericopes.text: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.” He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled. Then he said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here, and watch with me.” He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” He came to the disciples, and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again, a second time he went away, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.” He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to his disciples, and said to them, “Sleep on now, and take your rest. Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence. My God, my soul is in despair within me. Therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.
echoes.note: 'My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death' (v38) echoes the psalmist's refrain 'Why are you cast down, O my soul?... my soul is cast down within me'; Jesus prays the lament psalter in the garden.

echoes.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him: my Savior, my helper, and my God.
echoes.note: the same refrain 'Why are you in despair, O my soul?' recurs in Ps 43:5, reinforcing the borrowed lament language of v38.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
